[Theorem thm:gaussian-coordinate-orbit-calibration of arXiv:2608.16119, 'Fully nonlinear parabolic equations under a fixed reference diffusion: weighted \texorpdfs'] Let $A\in W^{1,1}(0,T;\mathsf{S}^d)$ satisfy
(equation eq:pure-time-covariance-class of the paper), and let $\omega_{A,K}$ be any
correction constructed in (equation eq:pure-time-correction of the paper) with
$K\geq K_{\mathrm{hom}}$.  Suppose that a reference pair
$(b^{\mathrm{orig}},a^{\mathrm{orig}})$, started from
$x_{\mathrm{orig}}$ and satisfying
Assumption~(ass:reference-diffusion of the paper), has reference process
$X^{\mathrm{orig}}$ and admits mutually inverse space--time
maps $\Phi,\Psi$ with the regularity required in
Theorem~(thm:coordinate-naturality of the paper).  Put
$y_0=\Phi_0(x_{\mathrm{orig}})$, let the model $(0,A)$ start from $y_0$, and
suppose, for every $(t,x)\in(0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$, that
\begin{equation*}
 \begin{aligned}
  A(t)&=D_x\Phi_t(x)a^{\mathrm{orig}}(t,x)D_x\Phi_t(x)^\top,\qquad
  0=\partial_t\Phi_t(x)+D_x\Phi_t(x)b^{\mathrm{orig}}(t,x)
      +\tfrac12a^{\mathrm{orig}}(t,x):D_x^2\Phi_t(x).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
The sharp calibration is then
\begin{equation*}
 C_{t^\alpha\omega_{A,K}}(X^{\mathrm{orig}})=C_\alpha^{\mathrm{Br}}
 \qquad\text{for every }\alpha\geq0.
\end{equation*}

body: In mathematical analysis and in probability theory, a σ-algebra is part of the formalism for defining sets that can be measured. In calculus and analysis, for example, σ-algebras are used to define the concept of sets with area or volume. In probability theory, they are used to define events for which a probability can be defined. In this way, σ-algebras help to formalize the notion of size.

body:
[Proposition 19 (Uniform convergence for the triangular ODE system) of arXiv:2511.01456, 'Zero distribution of multiplicative Hermite and Laguerre polynomials'] For each $n\in\mathbb{N}$, let
$\{\eta_{m;n}\}_{m=1}^\infty\subseteq C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ solve the ODE system~\eqref{eq:ODE_system_etas_finite_n}.
Let also $\{\eta_{m;\infty}\}_{m=1}^\infty\subseteq C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ solve~\eqref{eq:ODE_system_etas_infinite_n}.
Fix $A>0$.
Then, for every $k\in \mathbb N$ there exists a constant $C_{k,A}<\infty$ (depending only on $k$ and $A$)  such that
\[
\sup_{s\in [-A,A]} |\eta_{k;n}(s)-\eta_{k;\infty}(s)|  \le  \frac{C_{k,A}}{n}
\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb{N}.
\]
In particular, for every $k\in \mathbb N$ we have $\lim_{n\to\infty}\eta_{k;n}(s) = \eta_{k;\infty}(s)$ uniformly in $s\in [-A,A]$.
title: Uniform convergence for the triangular ODE system

body: In combinatorics, the inclusion–exclusion principle (commonly referred to as PIE) is a counting technique which generalizes the familiar method of obtaining the number of elements in the union of two finite sets; symbolically expressed as $|A\cup B|=|A|+|B|-|A\cap B|$ where A and B are two finite sets and |S| indicates the cardinality of a set S (which may be considered as the number of elements of the set, if the set is finite). The formula expresses the fact that the sum of the sizes of the two sets may be too large since some elements may be counted twice. The double-counted elements are those in the intersection of the two sets and the count is corrected by subtracting the size of the intersection.

[Lemma lem:coupleeb of arXiv:2411.10829, 'Airy$_\beta$ line ensemble and its Laplace transform'] For any $C_1>0$ and $C_2>1$, there is a constant $C_3=C_3(C_1,C_2)>0$, such that the following is true for all $N\in \mathbb Z_+$.
Take any $C_1N^{-2/3}<x<(C_2/2)^{10}$ and $0\le h,g < (C_2-x^{1/10})N^{1/100}$, and $X, H, G\in \mathbb Z_{\ge 0}$, such that $|X-xN^{2/3}|, |H-hN^{1/3}|, |G-gN^{1/3}|<C_2$, and $X+H+G$ is even.
Take $\mathfrak{f}:\llbracket 0,X\rrbracket\to \mathbb Z_{\ge 0}$ uniformly random from $\mathscr F(X;H,G)$, and a Brownian bridge $B$ on $[0,x]$ with $B(0)=h$, $B(x)=g$, conditional on $B\ge 0$. Then we can couple $\mathfrak{f}$ and $B$ together, such that with probability $>1-C_3\log(X)XN^{-7/10}$, we have $|\mathfrak{f}(Y)-N^{1/3}B(y)|<C_3\log(N)N^{3/10}+C_3\log(X)N^{1/10}$ for all $Y\in\llbracket 0, X\rrbracket$ and $y\in [0, x]$ with $|Y-yN^{2/3}|<1$.

[Definition 6 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] A \emph{limiting point} at time \(T\) is an element
\(\xi\in M_T\) of Bamler's metric-flow slice at the limiting time
\cite[Definition~2.32 and the paragraph following
equation~(2.34)]{BamlerStructure}.  We represent it by a probability
conjugate heat flow
\[
 \xi=(\mu_t)_{t<T},\qquad d\mu_t=v_t\,dV_{g(t)},
\]
where
\[
 \partial_tv_t=-\Delta_{g(t)}v_t+R_{g(t)}v_t,
 \qquad v_t>0,
 \qquad \int_Xv_t\,dV_{g(t)}=1.
\]
The representation has the following two properties of the limiting slice:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(P\arabic*)},leftmargin=3em]
\item \(\xi\) is a subsequential limit of point conjugate heat flows
whose pole times increase to \(T\);
\item for \(D=2n\),
\begin{equation}
 \Var_{g(t)}(\mu_t)

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For random walk in a random environment on Z^d satisfying a directional transience condition, such as Sznitman's condition (T) or the stronger (T') in a direction l, or a simpler ballisticity/non-nestling condition, one constructs regeneration times tau_1 < tau_2 < ... at which the walk achieves a new running maximum in direction l and never backtracks below that level afterward. Under condition (T'), or the weaker (T), the increments (X_{tau_{k+1}} - X_{tau_k}, tau_{k+1} - tau_k), for k >= 1, form an i.i.d. sequence, reducing the walk, which is not itself Markovian once the environment is averaged out, to a genuine i.i.d.-increment structure from which a law of large numbers (a deterministic limiting velocity) follows directly, and, with additional finite-moment control on the regeneration increments, a central limit theorem follows via classical tools for sums of i.i.d. variables. This does not establish the directional transience condition itself, verifying (T) or (T') for a given environment law is typically the hard remaining step; it does not directly give a central limit theorem without separately checking finite second moments of the regeneration increments, which can genuinely fail in slow or near-critical regimes; and it is specific to the static, fixed-in-time environment model. Typical failure: Assuming the regeneration increments automatically have finite variance, and hence a central limit theorem follows, once ballisticity or condition (T') has been established; ballisticity under (T') only guarantees a finite mean regeneration time, and a genuine central limit theorem requires an additional, often delicate, verification of finite second moments, a point on which the Kesten-Kozlov-Spitzer branching-with-migration machinery exists precisely because these moments can fail. Canonical reference: Sznitman and Zerner, 1999, Annals of Probability; Sznitman, 2002, Ecole d'Ete de Probabilites de Saint-Flour, Springer Lecture Notes in Mathematics.

\mathbb{E}\left\|I(f)\right\|_{W^{\alpha,p}_{[0,T]}H}^p

[Theorem 10 (Operational state-selection theorem) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] Let $\mathfrak R$ be a declared response program on
$(\mathsf U_0,\mathbb I)$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.5em]
\item Every compatible primitive response factors uniquely through the
information quotient.  All algebraic, causal, restart, and uniformly continuous
postcomposition identities descend with it.
\item Let $\mathbf R^{\mathbb I}$ be the descended joint profile and put
\[
 u\sim_{\mathfrak R}v
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \mathbf R^{\mathbb I}(u)=\mathbf R^{\mathbb I}(v).
\]
The quotient by this response congruence carries the Hausdorff initial
uniformity generated by the responses.  The closure of its joint response image
in the product target is the completed response state, and every uniformly
continuous descended constructor extends uniquely to it.  If the program is
causally calibrated in the sense of
\Cref{def:causally-calibrated-response-program}, then the quotient and its
completion inherit the induced truncations, and every equivariant uniformly
continuous constructor extends as a stable-causal map.
\item If a required response fails information descent, no pointwise
realization on the full raw carrier that factors through $q_{\mathbb I}$ can
realize the program.  A probabilistic implementation relative to $\cP$ may
instead impose descent on the realized support; that is a support-relative
program rather than a realization of the full raw one.
\item The calibrated completion is unique in the following precise sense.  Every
complete faithful realization of the descended response presentation whose
uniformity is the initial uniformity generated by the extended responses is
uniquely uniformly isomorphic to the response completion; equivalently, no
second complete geometry can realize the same calibrated profile faithfully.
This is the deterministic uniqueness theorem
\Cref{thm:canonical-response-completion}.
\item Suppose in addition that a probabilistic implementation carries a
$\cP$-causal state $Z$ with stable-causal joint encoder
$\Phi:\mathsf Z\to\mathsf R$ whose value $\Phi(Z)$ is the declared joint
response under every $P\in\cP$, and a global stable-causal decoder
$D_{\mathfrak R}:\mathsf R\to\mathsf Z$ satisfying
$D_{\mathfrak R}\Phi=I_{\mathsf Z}$.  Then, for every $\cP$-causal state $S$,
joint realization of the completed package is equivalent to $Z\preceqsc S$,
and a joint readout $\Psi$ has the factor
\[
 R_S=D_{\mathfrak R}\Psi.
\]
If the decoder factors through one distinguished response,
$D_{\mathfrak R}=D_\star\Pi_\star$, and that response is
$\Pi_\star\Phi(Z)$, then a separate realization $\Psi_\star$ of it already
yields the factor $D_\star\Psi_\star$.
Thus $Z$ is the unique least sufficient realized state up to stable-causal
equivalence; the factor is unique on the realized source state.
\end{enumerate}

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Each operator $T\in B(H)$ has an adjoint $T^*\in B(H)$, given by: 
$$<Tx,y>=<x,T^*y>$$
The operation $T\to T^*$ is antilinear, antimultiplicative, involutive, and satisfies:
$$||T||=||T^*||\quad,\quad ||TT^*||=||T||^2$$
When $H$ comes with a basis $\{e_i\}_{i\in I}$, the operation $T\to T^*$ corresponds to
$$(M^*)_{ij}=\overline{M}_{ji}$$ 
at the level of the associated matrices $M\in M_I(\mathbb C)$.

	There exist $C,c > 0$ such that, for any $\varrho \geq 40$, $x,\xi \in \mathbb{R}$, $T \in (0,1)$ and $\delta>0$ satisfying $T \geq 20/ \varrho$ and $\varrho (1-T)^{1-\kappa} \geq 10$,
	we have
	\begin{align*}
	& \abs{\exp \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft( \lambda_0 \varrho \int_0^T \frac{\mathop{}\mathopen{}\mathrm{d} s}{(1-s)^{\kappa}} \aftergroup\egroup\originalright) g(0,\xi;T,x) 
		- \varphi_{0}(\xi) \cdot (1-T)^{-\kappa/4} \varphi_{0}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft( (1-T)^{-\kappa/2} x \aftergroup\egroup\originalright)} \\
	& \leq C \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft( \frac{1}{\varrho (1-T)^{1-\kappa}} + e^{-c\varrho T} \aftergroup\egroup\originalright)
	(1-T)^{-\kappa/4}
	e^{-c \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\lvert\xi\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\rvert^\alpha}

	\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, Every geodesic spanning tree of a Cayley graph has branching number equal to the growth rate (October 2026), proves that if T is a spanning tree of an infinite, connected, locally finite, quasi-transitive graph G, rooted at o and geodesic (every vertex is at the same distance from o in T as in G), then the branching number of T equals the growth rate of G. For Cayley graphs this answers Question 3.12 of Lyons and Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks, where it was known for lexicographically constructed trees (Lyons and Peres; Liu and Xiang, arXiv:2010.01530). As a consequence, Bernoulli percolation on any such tree has critical probability equal to one over the growth rate. Paper: https://github.com/yspennstate/geodesic-tree-branching (commit c8e96497f0ad). Not refereed.
title: Every geodesic spanning tree of a quasi-transitive graph has branching number equal to the growth rate, answering Lyons-Peres Question 3.12 (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/geodesic-tree-branching)

Unreviewed bridge checklist. For a finite nonempty family of real path log costs f_p(y), beta>0 and K paths, define H(y)=min_p f_p(y) and F_beta(y)=-(1/beta)log sum_p exp(-beta f_p(y)). Then 0<=H(y)-F_beta(y)<=log K/beta for every y. For growing families, L_n->infinity and log K_n/(beta_n L_n)->0 therefore suffice for normalized expected endpoint differences to agree whenever the hard endpoint limits exist and the costs are integrable. A sharper effective-entropy estimate may replace this sufficient condition. The finite Gaussian response identity also requires retaining the negative beta times covariance of path gradients; its two nonnegative pieces cannot be separated or discarded just because one route wins almost surely. Neither the entropy bound nor concentration evaluates the actual planar-LFPP normalization exponent.
Finite nonempty path families
Positive beta and normalization L_n
Integrable endpoint log costs
Uniform entropy error tends to zero for the stated transfer

Own-work draft; proof (unaudited); D0007-C007 v1; audits w667:PASS. Let r>=1 be finite, p_j>0 with sum p_j=1, and a_j<b_j finite. Then F=sum p_j Uniform[a_j,b_j] is n-CM for every sufficiently large integer n, with overlapping or disconnected intervals and arbitrary centers. Put ell_j=b_j-a_j, c_j=(a_j+b_j)/2, mu=sum p_j c_j, D=sum |c_j-mu|, ell_max=max ell_j, ell_bar=sum p_j ell_j. A sufficient threshold is ceil(max(2, max_j[(1+6D/(r*ell_j))/p_j], [2D+2*ell_max+sum ell_j]/ell_bar)). Rounded counts K_j have mean np_j and discrepancy at most one; conditional tilt slopes 6*delta/(r*K_j*ell_j), delta=n*mu-sum K_j*c_j, share a sign and restore exact uniform marginals because E[delta]=0. The established joint monotone-density criterion applies in each state. The threshold may diverge along approximations to a general density; no full D0007 solution is claimed.
r finite >=1
p_j>0 and sum p_j=1
a_j<b_j finite
Wang-Wang joint monotone-density criterion

Status: proof (unaudited). Special case of D0007 using the established Wang-Wang joint monotone-density criterion. Novelty not asserted.

Statement. Let r>=1 be finite, p_j>0 with sum p_j=1, and a_j<b_j finite. Then F=sum_{j=1}^r p_j Uniform[a_j,b_j] is n-CM for every sufficiently large integer n. The intervals may overlap or be disconnected; their centers need not agree.

An explicit sufficient threshold is as follows. Put ell_j=b_j-a_j>0, c_j=(a_j+b_j)/2, mu=sum p_j c_j, D=sum |c_j-mu|, ell_max=max ell_j, and ell_bar=sum p_j ell_j. Every integer n at least

 N=ceil(max(2, max_j[(1+6D/(r ell_j))/p_j],
                   [2D+2 ell_max+sum ell_j]/ell_bar))

is an admissible complete-mixability order.

External theorem used: If all n univariate laws have increasing densities (or all have decreasing densities) on finite essential intervals [A_i,B_i], then they are jointly mixable iff sum A_i+max(B_i-A_i)<=sum means<=sum B_i-max(B_i-A_i). Source: Wang-Wang, Joint Mixability, doi:10.1287/moor.2015.0755, as stated in Wang arXiv:1411.6190v3 Section 2.2(e), equation (7), p.9. This theorem is cited, not reproved.

1. Random counts. There is a finite random vector K=(K_1,...,K_r) of integers satisfying sum K_j=n, E[K_j]=n p_j, and |K_j-np_j|<=1, with each K_j either floor(np_j) or ceil(np_j). Here is a direct construction. Let z_j be the fractional parts of np_j. Their sum s=n-sum floor(np_j) is an integer. If two z coordinates are strictly between zero and one, move along the direction e_i-e_j to the first boundary in each direction, and choose between those two endpoint vectors with probabilities making their expectation the original vector. Every such step preserves the sum s and each conditional coordinate expectation and reduces the number of fractional coordinates by at least one. A vector with exactly one fractional coordinate cannot have integer sum. After finitely many steps all coordinates are zero or one. The resulting random Z has sum s and E Z_j=z_j. Put K_j=floor(np_j)+Z_j. Only finitely many count states occur.

The threshold on n ensures K_j>=np_j-1>=6D/(r ell_j), and also K_j>=1: when D>0 the first bound is strictly positive, while when D=0 the threshold gives np_j>=1 and floor(np_j)>=1.

2. Center discrepancies. For a count state K define

 delta(K)=n mu-sum_j K_j c_j.

Its expectation is zero. Since sum (np_j-K_j)=0,

 delta=sum_j (np_j-K_j)(c_j-mu),

so |delta|<=D.

3. Conditional tilted marginals. For each component j and state K, put

 t_j(K)=6 delta(K)/(r K_j ell_j),
 q_{j,K}(x)=(1/ell_j)[1+t_j(K)*2(x-c_j)/ell_j]
           for a_j<=x<=b_j, and zero outside.

The positivity bound from Step 1 gives |t_j|<=1, so q is nonnegative and integrates to one. Its essential support is the whole [a_j,b_j], even when one endpoint density is zero. A direct affine integral gives mean c_j+t_j ell_j/6=c_j+delta/(r K_j). For any fixed K, all t_j have the same sign. Thus all q_{j,K} densities are increasing when delta>0, decreasing when delta<0, and constant when delta=0. Form a list of n conditional laws by taking K_j copies of each q_{j,K}. Their means sum to

 sum K_j c_j + sum_j K_j*delta/(r K_j)
       =sum K_j c_j+delta=n mu.

4. Check the monotone-density mean condition. Let W(K)=sum_j K_j ell_j. The sum of left endpoints is sum K_j c_j-W/2, and the sum of right endpoints is sum K_j c_j+W/2. Also max interval width is at most ell_max. Since K_j>=np_j-1,

 W>=n ell_bar-sum ell_j>=2D+2 ell_max.

Hence W/2-|delta|>=ell_max, which places n mu between the left-endpoint sum plus the maximal width and the right-endpoint sum minus it. All hypotheses of the cited theorem hold. Therefore the n conditional laws admit a joint coupling with sum exactly n mu for each count state K. Only finitely many states occur, so selecting one coupling for each requires no measurable-selection argument.

5. Restore the original full marginals. Select K according to Step 1, use its constant-sum coupling, and uniformly permute coordinates. A fixed coordinate has marginal density

 sum_j E[(K_j/n)q_{j,K}(x)].

For each j its constant part is (E K_j/n)/ell_j=p_j/ell_j. Its linear perturbation has coefficient E[K_j t_j]/(n ell_j), and

 E[K_j t_j]=6 E delta/(r ell_j)=0.

Thus the full density is exactly sum p_j 1_[a_j,b_j]/ell_j, the density of F. Overlapping component intervals do not affect this identity. The sum is n mu in every selected coupling and remains so after permutation. This proves the statement and threshold.

Hardest remaining D0007 piece: approximate a general density by such mixtures at one fixed sufficiently large n with thresholds controlled uniformly. The displayed N depends on the smallest component weights and widths. Along increasingly fine approximations it may diverge, so weak approximation alone does not extend this theorem to every absolutely continuous law. [Own-work draft: T407-GD-006 v2, proof (unaudited); independent audit pending; priority unestablished. Extends the continuous-flow result in bundle_003 to finite discrete updates.] Candidate finite joint-GD regime: the shared square CNN with h=p(p+1)/2 spanning filters and patch-specific trainable readout reaches any positive population squared error from n=k h noiseless Gaussian samples in finitely many simultaneous full-batch gradient updates almost surely. Both layer steps are explicit strictly positive functions of observed data and initialization. Together with the unit-sphere rank lower bound, this gives order kp^2 versus (kp)^2 sample separation at risk 1/4 and confidence 15/16 for local CNN versus equivariant learners. Moreover a finite dyadic rescaling W_0=s W_base, a_0=s^-2 a_base preserves the initial function and makes the proved filter/readout step ratio exactly one. Hence one common positive constant GD step suffices from this explicit data-dependent scaled initialization. Scope: p,k>=1; independent standard Gaussian patches; arbitrary symmetric local quadratic targets; spanning shared filter initialization (Gaussian almost surely), arbitrary finite readout; sample-dependent two-timescale steps; exact real arithmetic; no uniform runtime, finite-precision or equal-rate claim. Lower bounds use unit L2 target class. Equal-rate corollary changes initialization by a data-dependent scaling; it is not IID standard Gaussian initialization or a universal fixed scale.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:3a80596b772f05118f111ea7ea2d0bb9581b1cb3119aa85901a44e31fee559f2","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/3a/3a80596b772f05118f111ea7ea2d0bb9581b1cb3119aa85901a44e31fee559f2.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:e22491e4bdddc0d064bc201be7de66cb6ca9ae5fabc1ee859530feeca7b603f9","bundle_entry_key":"draft-discrete-shared-quadratic-cnn","bundle_id":"population.t407-draft-discrete-joint-quadratic-cnn","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"statistical learning theory","draft":"w693/bundle_004.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:learning.sample_complexity:draft-finite-joint-gd-shared-quadratic-cnn-scaled-initialization","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Target 3: finite joint gradient descent for a shared quadratic CNN

Status: proof (unaudited), T407-GD-006 v2. This is a specified algorithm with sample-dependent positive step sizes. Priority is unestablished; the proof uses standard local conditioning and descent ideas. It extends the continuous-flow candidate T407-JOINT-005, without changing its version.

## Statement and model

Let p,k>=1, d=kp, h=p(p+1)/2, D=kh. For independent standard Gaussian patches x_j in R^p, targets are arbitrary f_star(X)=sum_j x_j^T M_j x_j, M_j symmetric. The shared-filter square CNN is
  f_(W,a)(X)=sum_j sum_r a_(r,j)(w_r^T x_j)^2,
with h shared filters and a separate trained coefficient for each filter/patch pair. Initialize with rank-one filter matrices spanning Sym(p), and any finite readout. Independent Gaussian filters have this spanning property almost surely, and Gaussian readout initialization is allowed.

From n>=D noiseless IID Gaussian examples, simultaneous full-batch gradient descent on BOTH parameter blocks with the explicit positive constant steps below attains any prescribed population squared error epsilon>0 after finitely many iterations almost surely. There is no target-coefficient oracle, continuous-flow computation, stochastic-gradient assumption, or claimed uniform running-time bound. The algorithm uses the empirical design and its singular values. This is not a theorem about fixed equal steps, noisy labels, or degree q>2.

The lower bounds from Section 5 of proofs/target3_joint_quadratic_flow.md apply unchanged: for the unit-L2 local target class at risk epsilon and confidence 1-delta, arbitrary local learners need n>=D(1-epsilon-4delta) when positive, while orthogonally equivariant learners need n>=[d(d+1)/2](1-epsilon-4delta). At epsilon=1/4, delta=1/16 these are D/2 and d(d+1)/4. Thus the discrete algorithm also yields the specified order kp^2 versus (kp)^2 separation. These are noiseless statistical sample bounds; computational constants can depend very badly on the realized sample.

## 1. Design and initialization

Use an orthonormal symmetric vectorization svec, Phi with rows concatenating svec(x_j x_j^T), and B(W) whose columns are svec(w_r w_r^T). Stack a by patch and put b(W)=I_k tensor B(W). Then theta=b(W)a and e=Phi theta-y. Gaussian full design rank for n>=D follows from a nonzero determinant polynomial: place e_i and e_i+e_l successively in one patch at a time, setting other patches zero. This gives a block-diagonal invertible evaluation witness. The same p(p+1)/2 witness vectors yield a spanning initial filter bank. Gaussian absolute continuity makes both rank failures null. Consequently sigma=sigma_min(Phi)>0, S=||Phi||op>0, gamma=sigma_min(B(W_0))>0.

Set M=||W_0||F, R=M+1, L=2M+1,
  rho=min(1,gamma/(2L)), beta=gamma/2, lambda=beta^2 sigma^2.
For ||W-W_0||F<=rho we have ||B(W)-B(W_0)||op<=L||W-W_0||F<=gamma/2; hence sigma_min(B(W))>=beta, ||B(W)||op<=R^2, and ||W||F<=R. These follow from ||ww^T-vv^T||F<=(||w||+||v||)||w-v||. In particular e always lies in range(Phi), because labels are realizable in this coefficient space.

Let E=||e_0||. If E=0, output the initialized function, which equals the target since Phi is injective. The gradients vanish, so any positive steps would preserve it. Assume E>0 henceforth. Define
  A=||a_0||+4 R^2 S E/lambda+1,
  eta=min(1, rho lambda/(16 S R A E)),
  Jbar=S(R^2+2 R A), Ebar=S R^2 A+||y||,
  H=Jbar^2+Ebar S(2 A+4 R),
  tau=min(1/H,1/(2lambda)).
All denominators are strictly positive. Fix these constants for the whole run. Write loss ell(W,a)=||e||^2/2. The simultaneous update is
  a_(t+1)=a_t-tau gradient_a ell(W_t,a_t),
  W_(t+1)=W_t-tau eta gradient_W ell(W_t,a_t).
Both gradients are evaluated at the same old iterate. Both learning rates are strictly positive and depend only on initialization and observed inputs/labels.

## 2. Derivative bounds on a convex safe set

Let K={||W-W_0||F<=rho, ||a||<=A}, a convex subset of Euclidean parameter space z=(W,a). Its output Jacobians obey
  ||J_a||op<=S R^2, ||J_W||op<=2 S R A,
so ||J_z||op<=Jbar. Indeed the coefficient derivative satisfies
  ||D_W theta[Delta W]||<=2||W||F ||a|| ||Delta W||F.
For two joint parameter perturbations u=(u_W,u_a), v=(v_W,v_a), expansion of theta, quadratic in W and linear in a, gives
  ||D^2 theta[u,v]||
  <=2 A ||u_W||F ||v_W||F
     +2R(||u_W||F ||v_a||+||v_W||F ||u_a||)
  <=(2 A+4R)||u|| ||v||.
This follows directly from Cauchy-Schwarz on the filter and patch indices; there is no dimension-dependent hidden constant. Since ||e||<=Ebar on K,
  ||D^2 ell||op <=||J_z||op^2+||e|| S(2 A+4R)<=H.
Also the readout block alone gives a local PL inequality on K:
  ||gradient_a ell||^2=||b(W)^T Phi^T e||^2
  >=beta^2||Phi^T e||^2>=lambda||e||^2.
The last inequality uses e in range(Phi), not an untrue minimum-singular-value inequality for arbitrary vectors in R^n.

## 3. Induction handles step segments before invoking descent

Put P=diag(eta I_W,I_a), so z_next=z-tau P gradient ell. As eta<=1, ||P g||^2<=g^T P g. On any update segment contained in K, Taylor's theorem with the Hessian bound yields
  ell(z_next)<=ell(z)-tau g^T P g+(H tau^2/2)||P g||^2
              <=ell(z)-(tau/2)g^T P g
              <=(1-tau lambda)ell(z).
This is not yet a justification that iterates stay in K. We prove both conclusions inductively.

Let q=sqrt(1-tau lambda), so 0<q<1 since 0<tau lambda<=1/2. Assume all iterates through t are in K and ||e_j||<=E q^j through t. Their update formulas and the derivative bounds give the CANDIDATE next iterate, before using any descent on its segment,
  ||a_(t+1)-a_0|| <=tau S R^2 E sum_(j=0)^t q^j
                  <=2 S R^2 E/lambda,
  ||W_(t+1)-W_0||F <=tau eta 2 S R A E sum_(j=0)^t q^j
                    <=4 eta S R A E/lambda<=rho/4.
Here tau/(1-q)=(1+q)/lambda<=2/lambda. In particular ||a_(t+1)||<A and the new filter bank is strictly inside the rho ball. The old and new iterates are both in the convex set K, so their entire segment lies in K. The preceding descent inequality is now justified, proving ||e_(t+1)||<=E q^(t+1). Initialization supplies the base case. This resolves the possible circularity in an informal discrete first-exit argument.

Thus all iterates stay bounded, B(W_t) stays invertible, and
  ||e_t||^2<=E^2(1-tau lambda)^t<=E^2 exp(-tau lambda t).
All updates are finite algebraic operations on real parameters at every finite t; this is a mathematical exact-arithmetic algorithm, not a finite-precision guarantee.

## 4. Population risk and finite stopping

For the block-diagonal symmetric coefficient error Delta M,
  R_pop=E(X^T Delta M X)^2=2||Delta M||F^2+(tr Delta M)^2
       <=(d+2)||Delta theta||^2<=(d+2)||e_t||^2/sigma^2.
Therefore stop when the computed residual squared is <=epsilon sigma^2/(d+2). A sufficient iteration count when E>0 is
  t>=max(0,ceil(log((d+2)E^2/(sigma^2 epsilon))/(tau lambda))).
The design is fixed and no new examples are used in these iterations. Although n=D suffices with probability one, the conditioning, steps and iteration count need not be uniform over samples or initializations. If the displayed logarithm is negative, t=0 suffices.

## Prior-art scope and hardest audit point

Primary sources checked: Li-Ma-Zhang arXiv:1712.09203v5, Theorem 1.2 and its teacher/factorization context (PSD quadratic teacher); Sarao Mannelli-Vanden-Eijnden-Zdeborova arXiv:2006.15459v3, Section 2 Equation (1) (fixed positive readout); Jin-Montufar arXiv:2006.07356v5, Theorem 1 (wide univariate ReLU implicit bias; all parameters trained). The last source is explicitly about joint gradient descent and illustrates that local conditioning/near-initialization analysis is established methodology. Its inspected theorem is not the finite shared quadratic bank and n=D statement here. These searches are incomplete and establish no novelty.

The hardest audit point is the combined uniform Hessian bound and the discrete induction: the candidate next iterate must be proved inside the safe set before invoking Taylor descent on its segment. The proof above orders these steps explicitly. No stochastic conditional bounds or floating-point estimates are used. The full discrete result is not Lean-certified.


## 5. Equal learning rates after an explicit initialization rescaling

This corollary removes the two-timescale UPDATE restriction by changing the initialization. It does not claim equal-rate convergence from every fixed initialization. Take any base spanning bank W_base and finite readout a_base. For s>=1 set
  W_(0,s)=s W_base, a_(0,s)=s^(-2) a_base.
Since B(s W_base)=s^2 B(W_base), the initial represented function and initial residual E are independent of s. The finite-design sigma and S are also independent of s. If E=0, the base function is already correct and no optimization is needed. Assume E>0.

Let M_base=||W_base||F, gamma_base=sigma_min B(W_base)>0,
  R_base=M_base+1, L_base=2M_base+1,
  lambda_base=gamma_base^2 sigma^2/4,
  A_bound=1+||a_base||+4 R_base^2 S E/lambda_base.
At scale s, gamma_s=s^2 gamma_base and lambda_s=s^4 lambda_base exactly, while R_s=s M_base+1<=s R_base and L_s<=s L_base. Therefore if
  s>=max(1,2 L_base/gamma_base),
the safe radius rho_s=min(1,gamma_s/(2L_s)) equals one. The Section 1 readout bound obeys
  A_s=||a_base||/s^2+4 R_s^2 S E/(s^4 lambda_base)+1<=A_bound.
Consequently
  rho_s lambda_s/(16 S R_s A_s E)
  >=s^3 lambda_base/(16 S R_base A_bound E).
Choose s by doubling 1,2,4,... until BOTH preceding radius condition and
  s^3 lambda_base>=16 S R_base A_bound E
hold. They hold at a finite scale because their right sides are finite constants. This is a terminating initialization procedure using only observed data and the base bank/readout; it never calls the unknown target coefficients. It can also be specified by choosing the first dyadic scale above the explicit maximum of the displayed thresholds.

For this chosen scaled initialization, Section 1's eta is exactly one. Thus the same proof gives ordinary simultaneous gradient descent
  (W_(t+1),a_(t+1))=(W_t,a_t)-tau gradient ell(W_t,a_t)
with ONE common strictly positive sample-dependent constant step tau. The n=D almost-sure sample guarantee and the finite stopping rule remain valid, as do the stated local-versus-equivariant lower bounds.

One may take the deterministic base bank e_i,e_i+e_l and a_base=0. Alternatively Gaussian base filters span almost surely. After data-dependent common rescaling their distribution is not IID standard Gaussian: do not present this corollary as a claim about standard Gaussian initialization or a universal sample-independent scale. Its statistical sample count is uniform over targets; its scale and running time are not bounded uniformly. No numerical simulation is used to choose the scale in this proof.


Supporting normalized rank lower proof:


For any finite-dimensional quadratic function space V of dimension q, equipped with its L2(Gaussian) inner product, choose an orthonormal basis psi_1,...,psi_q. For the local space q=D; for all homogeneous symmetric quadratics q=Q=d(d+1)/2. The covariance of the unwhitened symmetric coefficients is positive definite, because
  E (X^T M X)^2=2||M||_F^2+(tr M)^2>0 for M!=0,
so this orthonormal basis exists and all target coefficients below are valid quadratics.

Put a uniform prior on coefficient xi in the unit sphere S^(q-1). Every target f_xi=sum xi_i psi_i has L2 norm exactly one. Conditional on the input sample, its n noiseless labels reveal only the projection of xi on the row span of the evaluation matrix. That row span has rank r<=n and is independent of xi before seeing labels. By reflection symmetry on its orthogonal complement, the posterior mean is precisely the observed projection. Among arbitrary output functions, the posterior mean target minimizes squared prediction risk. Its Bayes risk, averaged over labels and inputs, is E||xi-P_row xi||^2=1-r/q>=1-n/q (and zero is the trivial bound for n>=q). This gives minimax expected squared risk >=(1-n/q)_+; it is a known spherical-prior dimension argument, not a new statistical principle.

For confidence bounds, postprocess any learner by projecting its output into V in L2 and then clipping its coefficient norm to the unit ball. This does not increase squared error against any unit-norm target and bounds that error by four. If an output is not in L2, map it to zero: it could not have finite error against a target in V on a successful event. A uniform guarantee risk<=epsilon with probability >=1-delta would thus imply average risk <=epsilon+4delta. Therefore n>=q(1-epsilon-4delta), whenever the factor is positive. This is an inequality for real n, so the actual integer sample requirement is its ceiling.

The local class includes all diagonal quadratics. Every full homogeneous quadratic is an orthogonal rotation of a diagonal one, and its L2 norm is preserved by Gaussian rotation. For an equivariant learner, a uniform guarantee on the normalized local class therefore implies the same guarantee on the entire normalized full quadratic class. Apply the preceding q=Q Bayes lower bound. For an arbitrary local learner use q=D. body:
[Theorem 19 (The models are EFIIDs) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] All three models alluded to above are EFIIDs.
    More precisely, we obtain the following results.
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[\emph{\textbf{XY}}] Consider the XY model in dimension $d\in\Z_{\geq 2}$
        at inverse temperature $\beta\in[0,\beta_c(d))$.
        Then the infinite-volume Gibbs measure $\mu_{\XY,\beta}^{+1}$
        is an EFIID.
        \item[\emph{\textbf{SWM}}] Consider the SWM in dimension $d\in\Z_{\geq 2}$
        at inverse temperature $\beta\in\R_{\geq 0}$.
        Then the infinite-volume Gibbs measure $\mu_{\SWM,\beta}^0$
        is an EFIID.
        \item[\emph{\textbf{Coulomb}}] Consider the two-dimensional Coulomb gas at $\beta\in[0,\beta_{\BKT}(\Villain))$.
        Then the sequence $(\mu_{\Coulomb,\Lambda_n,\beta}^\free)_n$
        tends to some infinite-volume measure $\mu_{\Coulomb,\beta}^\free$ on $\Z^{F(\Z^2)}$ as $n\to\infty$ in the local convergence topology,
        and this limit is an EFIID.
    \end{itemize}
    In the case of the Coulomb gas, we are careful not to call this measure a Gibbs measure, as the Hamiltonian of the model is non-local and therefore it is not so clear what it means exactly to be a Gibbs measure.

    In particular, these results imply that for any of the three models,
    correlations between bounded observables decay exponentially fast in the distance at which they are measured. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: The models are EFIIDs

body:
[Definition Dual-KMP of arXiv:2507.19222, 'Convergence of the KMP model to the KPZ equation'] The Dual-KMP model $(\xi(t,x)_{x\in\mathbb{Z}})_{t \geqslant 0}$ is a continuous-time Markov process defined on the state space $\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}^{\mathbb{Z}}$, where $\xi(t,x)$ represents a number of particles on site $x$ at time $t$. At rate $1$, on each bond $(x,x+1)$, the total  number of particles $\xi(x)+\xi(x+1)$ is redistributed according to a random variable  $R \sim  \mathrm{BetaBinomial}(n, \alpha, \alpha)$ random variable with  $n=\xi(x)+\xi(x+1)$, such that at every Poisson time $T$,  $(\xi(T^-,x), \xi(T^-,x+1))$ becomes
    $$ (R, \xi(T^-,x)+ \xi(T^-,x+1)-R)\,. $$
    We recall that a random variable $R\sim \text{BetaBinomial}(n,\alpha,\beta)$, if it has density given by $$ \mathbb{P}(R=k)=\binom{n}{k}\int_{0}^{1}p^{\alpha+k-1}(1-p)^{\beta+n-k-1}dp\,.$$
title: Dual-KMP

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2606.15630, 'Excursion Fluctuations and Spectral Universality in Gaussian Fields'] Fix $d\geq2$ and $u>0$. As $R\to\infty$,
\[
    R^{-(d+1)/2}
    \big(A^{(d)}_{R,u}-\bE[A^{(d)}_{R,u}]\big)
    \Rightarrow
    c_{d,u}h_d
    \qquad \text{in } \mathcal S'(\bR^d),
\]
where
\[
    c_{d,u}
    =
    u\gamma(u)
    \left(
        2^{d-2}\pi^{(d-1)/2}
        \frac{\Gamma(d/2)^2}{\Gamma((d-1)/2)}
    \right)^{1/2},
    \qquad
    \gamma(u)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-u^2/2}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: A random variable X with mean mu = E[X] is sub-exponential with parameters (nu, b), nu > 0 and b > 0, if E[exp(t(X - mu))] <= exp(nu^2 t^2 / 2) for all |t| < 1/b. Equivalently, up to absolute constants, the tails satisfy P(|X - mu| > s) <= 2 exp(-s^2 / (2 nu^2)) for 0 <= s <= nu^2/b and P(|X - mu| > s) <= 2 exp(-s/(2b)) for s > nu^2/b. Every sub-Gaussian random variable is sub-exponential, but sub-exponential variables such as squares of Gaussians or exponential random variables may have heavier tails than any sub-Gaussian. [standard, e.g. Wainwright, High-Dimensional Statistics]
title: Sub-Exponential Random Variable

        h_\xi(t)^{1/2}
        \le

    \right\}
\]
is contained in the union of at most \(C_\gamma\) intervals of total length at

[Lemma lem:psa_duality of arXiv:2609.01697, 'Unique ergodicity of projective cocycles over the 2D stochastic Navier--Stokes equations'] The following hold:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item Let $v, \varphi \colon \mathbf{T}^2 \to \mathbf{R}$ be $C^1$. Then, for every $k \in \mathbf{Z}^2_*$,
      \begin{equation}
        \langle v, H^k \varphi\rangle
        = -\frac{1}{|k|^2}\, \widehat{\operatorname{curl}\, (v \nabla \varphi)}(-k) ,
        \qquad
        \operatorname{curl}\, (v\nabla \varphi) = -\nabla^\perp v \cdot \nabla \varphi .
      \end{equation}
    \item Let $\zeta, v \in H^s(\mathbf{T}^2)$ for $s > 4$. Under the
      hypothesis of Proposition~(prop:transitivity_PSA of the paper) it holds that
      \begin{equation}
        \nabla^\perp v \cdot \nabla \zeta = 0
        \qquad\text{and}\qquad
        \nabla^2 \zeta\ \nabla^\perp v = 0
        \qquad \text{on } \mathbf{T}^2 .
      \end{equation}
  \end{enumerate}

[Mtheorem 2 of arXiv:2609.00254, 'On the geometry and cohomology of almost abelian solvmanifolds'] Let $G_A$ be a $2n$-dimensional almost abelian Lie group with $A$ diagonal. Then $G_A$ admits a
left-invariant generalized complex structure of type $k$ if and only if the eigenvalues of $A$, listed
with multiplicity, can be reordered as
$$\{\underbrace{\lambda_1,\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{k},\lambda_{k}}_{k\text{ identical pairs}},\ \mu,\
\underbrace{\zeta_1,-\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_{n-k-1},-\zeta_{n-k-1}}_{n-k-1\text{ opposite pairs}}\},
\qquad k\le n-1,$$
or as
$$\{\underbrace{\lambda_1,\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{k-1},\lambda_{k-1}}_{k-1\text{ identical pairs}},\
\mu,\ \underbrace{\zeta_1,-\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_{n-k},-\zeta_{n-k}}_{n-k\text{ opposite pairs}}\},
\qquad k\ge 1 .$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Corollary 24 (\textsc{VarDE--MCTS} root error probability) of arXiv:2608.21995, '2608.21995'] Assume the conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm:VarDE-mcts-root} hold.  
Suppose the optimal root action
\[
a^* \;=\; \arg\max_{a} Q^*(s_0,a)
\]
is unique, and define the optimality gap
\[
\Delta_{\min}
\;:=\;
\min_{a \neq a^*}
\bigl( Q^*(s_0,a^*) - Q^*(s_0,a) \bigr)
\;>\; 0 .
\]
Let $\hat a_T = \arg\max_a \hat Q_T(s_0,a)$ be the action recommended by
\textsc{VarDE--MCTS} after $T$ simulations.  
Then there exist constants $c,C>0$ such that
\[
\Pr\!\left( \hat a_T \neq a^* \right)
\;\le\;
C \exp(-cT).
\]

then $X\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}} Y$.

body: [Definition 5 (Distances) of arXiv:1710.10644, 'Percolation without FKG'] Let Q be a quad, and let x and y be two vertices belonging to Q. (1) The ambient distance between x and y, denoted by d(x, y), is the graph distance in Λ between x and y, i.e. the length of the shortest path from x to y. It does not depend on Q. (2) The intrinsic distance between x and y in Qo ∪∂Q, denoted by dQ(x, y), is the length of the shortest path γ from x to y satisfying ˚γ ⊆Qo (or +∞if no such path exists).

body:
[Lem 109 (regularity for spatially smoothed coefficients) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] The coefficients from Definition~\ref{d:sp.smooth} are continuously differentiable in the space coordinate, and satisfy the bounds
	\[
	\Big(
	\|\sB^N\|_\infty
    +
    \|\partial_y\sB^N\|_\infty\Big)^2
	+ \max\bigg\{
    \|\tilde{A}\|_\infty
    +\|\partial_y\tilde{A}\|_\infty
    : \tilde{A}\in\{ \sV,\sU,\srrr,\swww\}^N
    \bigg\}
	\le 
	\bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2\,,
	\]
with $\MAX_N$ as in \eqref{e:MAX.N} and Proposition~\ref{p:Y.kolmogorov}.

\begin{proof}
We continue to use the abbreviations introduced above. To simplify notation, we mostly suppress the dependence on $N$ inside the proof. Consider
	\[
	\sB(t,y)
	=\frac{\overline{\varrho_{D,t}*\sphi}(y)}
		{\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)}
	\equiv \frac{\Num(t,y)}{\Den(t,y)}\,.
	\]
We first aim to lower bound the denominator $\Den$.
Recall from Definition~\ref{d:sp.smooth} that $\sphi$ has support $[-\sep,\sep]^3$, and is $\ge \Omega(1)/\sep^3$ on $[-\sep/2,\sep/2]^3$. 
From the construction of $\vX^\frozen$ and $\vY^\frozen$
(Definitions \ref{d:trunc}--\ref{d:rerand.Ising}), we see that $\varrho_t$ gives measure at least $\Omega( \sep^3 /\trK^{O(1)} )$ to any box of side length $\sep$ contained in $[-2\trK,2\trK]^3$. It follows that, for all $\vy\in[-2\trK+1,2\trK-1]^3$,
	\[
	\varrho_t*\sphi(\vy)
	\ge \int_{[-\sep/2,\sep/2]^3}
		\sphi(\vy-\vx)\,\varrho_t(d\vx)
	\ge \frac{1}{\trK^{O(1)}}\,.
	\]
Integrating over $\vy\in H(y)$ (as defined by \eqref{e:hspace.y}) gives
	\beq
	\Den(t,y)
	= \overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)
	\ge \frac{1}{\trK^{O(1)}}
	\eeq
for all $y\in[-5\trK,5\trK]$. Next note that since particles outside $[-\trK,\trK]^3$ are frozen (see Definition~\ref{d:trunc}), the numerator $\Num(t,y)$ must be zero for $y\notin[-3\trK-1,3\trK+1]$. For $y\in[-3\trK-1,3\trK+1]$, we bound
	\begin{align*}
	|\Num(t,y)|
	&=\Big|\overline{\varrho_{D,t}*\sphi}(y)\Big|
	=\bigg| \int_{H(y)}
	\int_{\R^3} \sphi(\vy-\vx)B(t,\vx)\,\varrho_t(d\vx) \,d\vy\bigg|\\
	&=\bigg| \int_{\R^3}
	B(t,\vx) \overline{\sphi}(y-(\underline{1},\vx))\,\varrho_t(d\vx)\bigg|
	\le \|\overline{\sphi}\|_\infty \cdot \int_{\R^3}
	|B(t,\vx)|\,\varrho_t(d\vx)
	\le  \bigg(\frac{L}
		{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)}
		\MAX_N\,,
	\end{align*}
where the last step uses the quenched moment bound on $\bbb$ from Lemma~\ref{l:barD.I.second.quenched}, together with the bound $(p^N)' \le  L^2$ from \eqref{e:sdelimits.pprime}. Combining with \eqref{e:denominator.lbd} gives
	\[\|\sB\|_\infty 
	\le \bigg(\frac{\trK L}
		{\sep}
		\bigg)^{O(1)}
		\MAX_N\,.
	\]
We can also apply \eqref{e:denominator.lbd} to obtain
	\beq
	\Big|\partial_y \tilde{B}(t,y)\Big|
	\le \trK^{O(1)}
	\bigg|
	\frac{\partial}{\partial y} \Num(t,y)
	- \tilde{B}(t,y)
	\frac{\partial}{\partial y} \Den(t,y)
	\bigg|\,.\eeq
The first term on the right-hand side of \eqref{e:sB.quotient.rule} can be bounded by
	\begin{align*}
	\bigg|\frac{\partial}{\partial y} \Num(t,y)\bigg|
	&=\bigg|\frac{\partial}{\partial y}
	\overline{\varrho_{D,t}*\sphi}(y)\bigg|
	=\bigg| 
	\int_{\R^3} B(t,\vx)
	\overline{\sphi}' (y-(\vec{1},\vx))
	\,\varrho_t(d\vx)
	\bigg|\\
	&\le
	\|\overline{\sphi}' \|_\infty
	\int_{\R^3} | B(t,\vx) | \,\varrho_t(d\vx)
	\le \bigg(\frac{L}
		{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} \MAX_N\,.
	\end{align*}
The second term on the right-hand side of \eqref{e:sB.quotient.rule} can be controlled using the preceding bound on $\tilde{B}$, together with a similar  calculation as above:
	\[
	\bigg|\frac{\partial}{\partial y}
		\Den(t,y) \bigg|
	=\bigg|\frac{\partial}{\partial y}
	\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)\bigg|
	\le  \| \overline{\sphi}' \|_\infty \cdot
	\int_{\R^3} \varrho_t(d\vx)
	\le \frac{1}{\sep^{O(1)} }\,.
	\]
Combining the above gives the claimed bound on $\partial_y \sB$.
The bounds on $\sV$, $\sU$, $\srrr$, and $\swww$ follow by the same argument, using the quenched moment bounds from Lemma~\ref{l:tQ.first.quenched}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: regularity for spatially smoothed coefficients

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.22693, 'Uniformity of extremal behaviour along geodesics in Liouville quantum gravity'] Fix $\gamma \in (0,2)$ and $\alpha \in [-2,2]$, and let $h$ be a whole-plane GFF. 
Then, there exist deterministic constants $\Delta^{\mathrm{Euc}}, \Delta_{\alpha}^{\mathrm{Euc}}, \Delta_{\alpha}^{\mathrm{LQG}}, \chi, \chi', \alpha_{\mathrm{min}}$, and $\alpha_{\mathrm{max}}$, such that the following holds almost surely. For any $D_h$-geodesic $P\colon [0,T]\rightarrow \CC$ parametrised by $D_h$-length and any $[s,t]\subseteq (0,T)$, we have
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item  $\dim_{\mathrm{Euc}}(P\lvert_{[s,t]})=\Delta^{\mathrm{Euc}}$.
  \item $\dim_{\mathrm{Euc}}(P\lvert_{[s,t]}\cap \cT_h^{\alpha})= \Delta^{\mathrm{Euc}}_{\alpha}$ and $\dim_{\mathrm{LQG}}(P\lvert_{[s,t]}\cap \cT^\alpha_h)= \Delta^{\mathrm{LQG}}_{\alpha}$.
  \item  $\chi(P\lvert_{[s,t]})=\chi$ and $\chi'(P\lvert_{[s,t]})=\chi'$.
  \item  $\alpha_{\mathrm{max}}(P|_{[s,t]})=\alpha_{\mathrm{max}}$ and $\alpha_{\mathrm{min}}(P|_{[s,t]})=\alpha_{\mathrm{min}}$.
 \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.22693

[Prop 10 of arXiv:2606.14812, 'Joint convergence in Wiener chaos via transport hierarchy and Malliavin covariances'] Consider two integers $p, q\geq 2$ and let
		\[
		X_N = I_p(f_N), \qquad Y_N = I_q(g_N),
		\]
		where $f_N\in H^{\odot p}$, $g_N\in H^{\odot q}$, and assume that $X_N$ 
		satisfies \eqref{c1} and $Y_N$ is bounded in $L^2(\Omega)$. Write 
		$q = ap + r'$ with $a\geq 1$ and $0\leq r' < p$. For $r\geq 1$, let 
		$Y_{r,N}$ be given by \eqref{yr}. Then the following hold.
		
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item For every integer $r\geq 1$ with $rp\leq q$,
			\begin{equation}
				Y_{r,N} = C_{r,p,q}\,
				I_{q-rp}\!\left(f_N\widetilde\otimes_p^{(r)} g_N\right)
				+ R_{r,N},
			\end{equation}
			where $f_N\widetilde\otimes_p^{(r)} g_N$ denotes the 
			$r$-fold iterated contraction of $f_N$ with $g_N$, 
			defined recursively by $f_N\widetilde\otimes_p^{(1)} g_N 
			= f_N\widetilde\otimes_p g_N\in H^{\odot(q-p)}$ and
			\begin{equation*}
				f_N\widetilde\otimes_p^{(r)} g_N 
				:= f_N\widetilde\otimes_p 
				\left(f_N\widetilde\otimes_p^{(r-1)} g_N\right)
				\in H^{\odot(q-rp)},
				\quad r=2,\ldots,a,
			\end{equation*}
			i.e.\ at each step the $p$ variables of $f_N$ are 
			fully contracted with $p$ of the remaining variables 
			of the kernel from the previous step. Also,  $C_{r,p,q} = (p!)^r\frac{q!}{(q-rp)!}$ and 
			$R_{r,N}\to 0$ in $L^2(\Omega)$ as $N\to\infty$.
			
			\item \textbf{Non-critical case} $ap < q < (a+1)p$: 
			\begin{equation}
				Y_{a+1,N} \to _{N \to \infty}0 \quad \text{in } L^2(\Omega).
			\end{equation}
			
			\item \textbf{Critical case} $q = ap$: taking $r=a$ in \eqref{14m-2b} gives
			\begin{equation*}
				Y_{a,N} - \mathbf{E}[Y_{a,N}] \to  _{N \to \infty}0 \quad \text{in } L^2(\Omega).
			\end{equation*}
			In particular, if $\mathbf{E}[Y_{a,N}]\to _{N \to \infty}\rho_a$ for some $\rho_a\in\mathbb{R}$, 
			then $Y_{a,N}\to _{N \to \infty}\rho_a$ in $L^2(\Omega)$. Moreover,
			\begin{equation}
				Y_{a+1,N} \to_{N \to \infty}  0 \quad \text{in } L^2(\Omega).
			\end{equation}
		\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop 10 of arXiv:2606.14812

[Lemma 46 of arXiv:2608.03575, '2608.03575'] Let a stationary random rooted graph be equipped with a compatible family
of metrics, and suppose that its random walk converges almost surely to the
resulting boundary. Then the exit measure is almost surely either
non-atomic or a single atom of mass \(1\).

\[
    h_\xi(v):=\mathbb P_v^G(\Xi=\xi),
\]
and let
\[
    M(G,v):=\sup_{\xi}h_\xi(v)
\]
be the maximal atomic mass. By Lévy's zero--one law,
\[
    h_\xi(X_n)
    \longrightarrow
    \mathbf 1_{\{\Xi=\xi\}}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
    M(G,X_n)
    \longrightarrow
    \mathbf 1_{\{\Xi\text{ is an atom}\}}.
\]

[Theorem 99 (Projective/inverse limits) of arXiv:2604.01685, 'Probability with Measure\footnote{Lecture notes. University of Ljubljana.}'] Let $F$ be a set on which is defined a partial (reflexive, transitive, antisymmetric) order $\leq$, directed upwards in the sense that for arbitrary $\{\alpha,\beta\}\subset F$ there is $\gamma\in F$ such that $\gamma\geq\alpha$ and $\gamma\geq\beta$. For each $\alpha\in F$ let there be given a probability space $(\Omega_\alpha,\FF_\alpha,\mu_\alpha)$, $\Omega_\alpha$ being a Hausdorff\footnote{or, more generally, one in which every compact subset is closed} topological space, $\FF_\alpha$ including all the compact sets of $\Omega_\alpha$, $\mu_\alpha$ being inner regular w.r.t. the compact sets in the sense that $$\mu_\alpha(A)=\sup\{\mu(K):K\text{ a compact subset of }A\},\quad A\in \FF_\alpha.$$

Let maps $\pr_{\beta\downarrow \alpha}$ as $(\alpha,\beta)$ runs over $\leq$ verify the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
 \item  $\pr_{\alpha\downarrow \alpha}=\mathrm{id}_{\Omega_\alpha}$ for all $\alpha\in F$;
 \item $\pr_{\beta\downarrow \alpha}\circ \pr_{\gamma\downarrow \beta}=\pr_{\gamma\downarrow \alpha}$ for all $\alpha\leq\beta\leq \gamma$ from $F$;
 \item $\pr_{\beta\downarrow \alpha}:\Omega_\beta\to \Omega_\alpha$ is continuous, also measurable in the sense that $\pr_{\beta\downarrow \alpha}\in \FF_\beta/\FF_\alpha$ for all $\alpha\leq \beta$ from $F$;
 \item $\pr_{\beta\downarrow \alpha}$ maps onto $\Omega_\alpha$ for all $\alpha\leq \beta$ from $F$.
 \end{enumerate}
 Suppose furthermore the consistency condition
\begin{enumerate}[(e)]
\item  $(\pr_{\beta\downarrow \alpha})_\star \mu_\beta=\mu_\alpha\text{ for all $\alpha\leq \beta$ from $F$}$
\end{enumerate} holds true. 

Next, set $$\Omega:=\left\{\omega\in \prod_{\gamma\in F}\Omega_\gamma: \pr_{\beta\downarrow \alpha}\omega_\beta=\omega_\alpha\text{ for all }\alpha\leq \beta\text{ from }F\right\},$$ introduce $\pr_\alpha:=(\Omega\ni\omega\mapsto \omega_\alpha)$ for $ \alpha\in F$, and assume 
\begin{enumerate}[(f)]
\item $\pr_\alpha$ maps $\Omega$ onto $\Omega_\alpha$ for each $\alpha\in F $. 
\end{enumerate}
Suppose finally that 
 \begin{enumerate}[(g)]
 \item for each non-empty countable $F'\subset F$ that is not bounded above (no $\gamma\in F$ such that $\alpha\leq\gamma$ for all $\alpha\in F'$) admitting an enumeration in increasing order (there is a $\uparrow$ map from $\mathbb{N}$ onto $F'$): if $\omega'\in \prod_{\alpha\in F'}\Omega_\alpha$ is such that $\pr_{\beta\downarrow \alpha}\omega_\beta'=\omega'_\alpha\text{ for all }\alpha\leq \beta\text{ from }F'$, then there is $\omega\in \Omega$ such that $\omega'=\omega\vert_{F'}$.
 \end{enumerate}
Then there exists a unique probability $\mu$ on $(\Omega,\lor_{\alpha\in F}(\pr_\alpha)^{-1}(\FF_\alpha))$ satisfying ${\pr_\alpha}_\star\mu=\mu_\alpha$ for all $\alpha\in F$.

[Corollary 33 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] There exists a universal constant such that for any martingale difference sequence $D_i$ adapted to a filtration $\mathcal{F}_i$---so $D_i$ is $\mathcal{F}_i$ measurable and $\E[D_i \mid \mathcal{F}_{i-1}] =0$---we have for all $p \geq 2, n \geq 1$, the bounds
    \begin{equation}
        
        \Big\|\sum_{i=1}^n D_i\Big\|_{L^p_\omega} \leq C \sup_{ 2  \lor \frac{p}{n} \leq q \leq p} \frac{p}{q} \Big(\frac{n}{p}\Big)^{1/q} \max_{1 \leq i \leq n} \big\|\E[|D_i|^q \mid \mathcal{F}_{i-1}]^{1/q}\big\|_{L^\infty_\omega}.
    \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary 33 of arXiv:2608.05931

then $h=\alpha^+\circ\beta^-$ is TT, and
\begin{equation}
    \cE_g h=-\frac{s}{2}h-2\sum_a(\nabla_a\alpha^+)\circ(\nabla_a\beta^-),

which implies from $\big\langle(\nabla_a\alpha^+)\circ(\nabla_a\beta^-),
 \alpha^+\circ\beta^-\big\rangle
 =\langle\nabla_a\alpha^+,\alpha^+\rangle

[Definition Def: reduction steps of arXiv:2607.18635, 'Remainders of generalised Taylor expansions and a priori bounds for rough differential equ'] Given $\rho\in{\mathcal T}_b^{I_k}$ we fix a reduction chain $(\rho^0,\rho^1,\ldots,\rho^k)$ of $\rho$ as in Definition (Def: reduction chain of the paper).
		Then we set 
		\begin{itemize}
			\item $r^i$ as the maximum decoration of the leaves of $\rho^i$
			(note that $k=r^0\ge r^1\ge\cdots\ge r^k=0$),
			\item $q^{m_L(\rho)+1}:=0$,
			\item For $a\in\{1,\ldots,m_L(\rho)\}$, we define $q^a:=\min\{i>q^{a+1}: r^{i}<r^{i-1}\}$, 
			namely the smallest $i>q^{a+1}$ such that the maximum decoration of $\rho^i$ is strictly less than the maximum decoration of $\rho^{i-1}$,
			\item for $a\in\{1,\ldots,m_L(\rho)\}$, $p^a:=k-q^a$,
		\end{itemize}
		Finally, for $\boldsymbol{j}_{m_L(\rho)}\in\{0,1,\ldots,k-1\}^{m_L(\rho)}_<$, 
		define $H_{\rho}(\,\boldsymbol{j}_{m_L(\rho)})$ as the number of 
	reduction chains $(\rho,\rho^1,\ldots,\rho^{k})$ of $\rho\in{\mathcal T}_b^{I_k}$ such that
	$\boldsymbol{j}_{m_L(\rho)} = (p^1,\ldots,p^{m_L(\rho)})$.
title: Definition Def: reduction steps of arXiv:2607.18635

[Lemma lem:expconv of arXiv:2604.24389, '``True" self-avoiding walks on general trees'] The unique stationary distribution of $(\eta_n)$ is 
\[
\varrho(x) := \frac{e^{-\beta(x+1)^2}}{\sum_{z \in \mathbb{Z}} e^{-\beta(z+1)^2}}, \quad x \in \mathbb{Z},
\]
whose variance is
\[
\varsigma^2_{\beta} := \frac{\sum_{z \in \mathbb{Z}} z^2 e^{-\beta z^2}}{\sum_{z \in \mathbb{Z}} e^{-\beta z^2}}. 
\] 
Furthermore, there exist positive constants $C$ and $c$ such that: 
\begin{itemize}
    \item[a.] For all \(n \ge 0\),
\[
\sum_{y \in \mathbb{Z}} |P^n(0,y) - \varrho(y)| \le C  e^{-c n}. 
\]
Consequently, $|\mathbb{E}[\eta_{n}\mid\eta_0=0]+1|\le C e^{-c n}$ and $|\mathbb{E}[\eta_{n}^2\mid\eta_0=0]-\varsigma^2_{\beta}|\le C e^{-cn}.$
\item[b.] For all $n\ge0$ and $x\ge0$, \[ P^n(0,x+1)\le C e^{-\beta x}P^n(0,x). \] 
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 1 and Lemma 2 in \cite{Toth1995}

DRAFT, proof (unaudited), T411-w740-C004 v1. For n>=128, D=n+n^2, a smooth prior with LSI at most 21 and a linear Gaussian observation ratio at most 420000 has posterior Poincare and LSI constants at least n*exp(n/16)/128 with probability at least 1-5*exp(-n/16) over observations. Thus prior LSI and the proposed small-ratio condition cannot alone supply a polynomial posterior-LSI bound, even for typical observations. This does not establish sampling hardness. No novelty or independent-check claim. No independent review or novelty claim; no efficient-score representation is asserted for this family. Twenty-four exact checks pass. {"artifact_digest":"sha256:933c1414c688812f0168e6dd597a45252591c27120045874f479e9d03cbd1738","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/93/933c1414c688812f0168e6dd597a45252591c27120045874f479e9d03cbd1738.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:dd45cc5a37eb2bdf6ee694037d47cb625d9da2c201909daabff05ac8adbb64c5","bundle_entry_key":"draft-typical-observation-posterior-lsi-obstruction","bundle_id":"population.w740-t411-polynomial-lsi-hardness-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"posterior sampling and functional inequalities","draft":"w740/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.sampling:draft-typical-observation-posterior-lsi-obstruction","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Typical observations can destroy a constant prior LSI

Status: proof draft, unaudited. Pending: frontier-check output, source comparison, and exact arithmetic checks. This is a functional-inequality obstruction, not a computational sampling lower bound. No novelty claim is made.

## Statement

For each integer n>=128, put D=n+n^2 and eta^2=sigma^2=1/20000. There is an explicitly samplable, everywhere positive smooth prior mu_n on R^D with C_LS(mu_n)<=21, and a norm-one linear observation selector A:R^D->R^(n^2), such that for Y=AX+sigma E, X~mu_n and E standard Gaussian, with probability at least

1-5 exp(-n/16)

over Y, the posterior satisfies

C_P(mu_n(.|Y)) >= (n/128) exp(n/16),
C_LS(mu_n(.|Y)) >= (n/128) exp(n/16).

The LSI convention is Ent(f^2)<=2 C_LS E||grad f||^2. The observation ratio is at most 420000, independent of n. In particular it is <=c log D for every fixed c>0 and all sufficiently large n, while the typical posterior constants grow faster than every polynomial in D.

The conclusion rules out the proposed high-probability polynomial posterior-LSI inheritance route based only on prior LSI and the observation ratio. It does not rule out a polynomial sampler, an annealing method that handles the two modes, or a method using their exact sign symmetry. It does not supply an efficient neural-network representation of every forward score. All prior scores exist and exact score oracles may be considered abstractly.

## 1. A Gaussian Lipschitz prior

Identify R^D with a vector block R^n and a matrix block R^(n by n), using the Frobenius norm on matrices. For z in R^n let

u(z)=2 projection_{closed ball of radius sqrt(n)/2}(z).

This map is 2-Lipschitz and ||u(z)||<=sqrt(n). Euclidean projection onto a ball is nonexpansive: inside it is the identity, outside its derivative has radial eigenvalue 0 and tangential eigenvalue r/||z||<=1; integrating along line segments, or using the convex projection inequality, gives the global bound.

For ||u||<=sqrt(n) define F(u)=(u,uu^T/sqrt(n)). For two such vectors u,v,

||uu^T-vv^T||_F <= (||u||+||v||)||u-v|| <=2 sqrt(n)||u-v||.

Therefore F is sqrt(5)-Lipschitz. If Z is a standard Gaussian vector in R^n and W an independent standard Gaussian vector in R^D, set

X=F(u(Z))+eta W.

The map (Z,W)->X is sqrt(20+eta^2)-Lipschitz, by Cauchy--Schwarz applied to sqrt(20)||Delta Z||+eta||Delta W||. Gaussian LSI and composition with test functions give C_LS(mu_n)<=20+eta^2<21. Gaussian convolution gives an everywhere positive C-infinity density. Also ||F(u)||^2<=2n, so E||X||^2<=2n+eta^2 D. All the construction's inputs and operations are explicit; unconditional sampling costs polynomial time in D.

Let A select the matrix block. Then ||A||=1 and ||A||^2 C_LS/sigma^2<=21*20000=420000.

## 2. A spherical reference and a rigorous coupling

Define U_s=sqrt(n) Z/||Z|| (the value at Z=0 is immaterial). It is uniform on the sphere of radius sqrt(n). Define a reference prior S_n as the law of X_s=F(U_s)+eta W, using the same Z,W as above. If ||Z||>=sqrt(n)/2, then u(Z)=U_s, so X=X_s.

Write delta=Pr(||Z||<sqrt(n)/2). Gaussian integration gives E exp(-||Z||^2/2)=2^(-n/2). Markov's inequality gives

delta <= exp(n/8)2^(-n/2) <= exp(-n/8),

where log 2>=1/2 follows from integrating 1/x on [1,2]. Thus TV(mu_n,S_n)<=delta. The same coupling, with the same observation noise, bounds by delta both the joint laws of (X,Y) and the Y marginals.

This reference prior is used only to compute the posterior; no LSI assertion for the sphere is needed.

## 3. The Gaussian matrix event

Under S_n, the observed matrix has the form

Y=U_s U_s^T/sqrt(n)+(1/100)G,

where G has independent standard Gaussian entries, since eta^2+sigma^2=1/10000.

A 1/4-net N of the unit sphere can be chosen with |N|<=9^n. To see the bound, take a maximal separated set and compare volumes of disjoint radius-1/8 balls with the containing radius-9/8 ball; maximality supplies the covering property. For every real matrix G,

||G||op <=2 max_{a,b in N}|a^T G b|,

because approximating both unit vectors in a bilinear form produces error at most (1/2)||G||op. Each fixed a^T G b is standard Gaussian. A union bound therefore gives

Pr(||G||op>8 sqrt(n)) <=2*9^(2n) exp(-8n) <=2 exp(-3n),

using log 9<5/2. The latter inequality follows, for example, because the fourth-degree Taylor lower bound for exp(5/2) exceeds 9.

Put H=(Y+Y^T)/2. On the displayed matrix event, its eigenvalues satisfy

lambda_1>= (23/25)sqrt(n),
lambda_2<= (2/25)sqrt(n),
lambda_n>=-(2/25)sqrt(n).

Indeed the noiseless matrix has one eigenvalue sqrt(n) and the rest zero; the symmetric noise has norm at most (2/25)sqrt(n). The first and last bounds follow directly from Rayleigh quotients. For the second, any two-dimensional subspace contains a nonzero vector perpendicular to U_s, whose signal Rayleigh quotient is zero; the eigenvector span for the two largest eigenvalues then proves the bound. In particular the top eigenvalue is simple. Choose a measurable top unit eigenvector v(H); its sign will not matter.

Let E be the event that these three eigenvalue inequalities hold. They depend only on the observation and S_n(Y in E)>=1-2 exp(-3n).

## 4. The reference posterior has an exponentially small equatorial belt

Conditional on U_s=u, Y has independent Gaussian entries with means uu^T/sqrt(n) and variance 1/10000. Since ||u||=sqrt(n), the squared Frobenius norm of uu^T/sqrt(n) is the constant n. Bayes' formula therefore gives the reference latent posterior density, relative to uniform spherical measure, proportional to

exp(theta u^T H u),  theta=10000/sqrt(n).

This is the standard Bingham form. The identity follows by expanding the Gaussian likelihood; the antisymmetric part of Y has zero inner product with uu^T.

Fix Y in E. Let B={|u.v|<=sqrt(n)/2} and C={|u.v|>=sqrt(3n)/2}. On B, the energy theta u^T H u is at most

theta n(lambda_1/4+3 lambda_2/4).

On C it is at least

theta n(3 lambda_1/4+lambda_n/4).

The second minus the first is at least

theta n(lambda_1/2+lambda_n/4-3 lambda_2/4) >=3800 n.

The spherical measure of C is at least exp(-3n). For completeness, use polar angle around v: the two caps of angle pi/6 have measure

2 integral_0^(pi/6) sin(t)^(n-2) dt / integral_0^pi sin(t)^(n-2) dt.

Restrict the numerator integral to [pi/12,pi/6], where sin(t)>1/4, and bound the denominator by pi. The result is at least (1/6)4^(-(n-2)), which is greater than exp(-3n) for n>=2 (use log 6<2 and log 4<2). Consequently

Pr_{S_n}(|U_s.v|<=sqrt(n)/2 |Y) <=exp(-3797 n).

The vector block X_s,vec=U_s+eta W_vec contains Gaussian noise independent of Y and U_s. Even though v depends on Y, conditional on Y its projection of W_vec is still a standard Gaussian independent of U_s. Hence

Pr_{S_n}(|X_s,vec.v|<sqrt(n)/4 |Y)
 <=exp(-3797n)+2 exp(-n/(32 eta^2))
 <=3 exp(-625n).

All probabilities here concern the actual noisy vector block, not a latent variable to which the posterior sampler has no access.

## 5. Transfer to the constant-LSI prior under its own observation law

For any two priors P,Q and a common observation channel, the elementary triangle inequality for their joint and marginal densities gives

E_{Y~Q_Y} TV(P(.|Y),Q(.|Y)) <=2 TV(P,Q).

The proof is included in C002: add and subtract Q_Y(y)P(dx|y), integrate, and use contraction of TV under marginalization. Positive Gaussian observation densities ensure these conditional densities are well-defined throughout.

Apply this with P=mu_n, Q=S_n and epsilon=exp(-n/16). Markov's inequality gives a set J of observations on which the conditional TV distance is at most epsilon, with

S_n(Y notin J) <=2 delta/epsilon <=2 exp(-n/16).

The observation marginals differ in TV by at most delta. Therefore, under the actual prior mu_n,

Pr(Y in E intersect J)
 >=1-2 exp(-3n)-2 exp(-n/16)-exp(-n/8)
 >=1-5 exp(-n/16).

For every Y in this set, its actual posterior belt probability satisfies

Pr_{mu_n}(|X_vec.v|<sqrt(n)/4 |Y) <=3 exp(-625n)+epsilon <=4 epsilon.

The reference measure in the conditional-TV averaging inequality is important: the final extra delta is what changes the observation law from S_n to mu_n.

## 6. A posterior Poincare test

The actual prior is invariant under the transformation that negates the vector block and leaves the matrix block fixed: send Z->-Z, W_vec->-W_vec, and leave W_matrix fixed. The observation depends only on the matrix block, so every posterior has the same symmetry. Thus, for each good observation, the posterior masses of X_vec.v<=-sqrt(n)/4 and X_vec.v>=sqrt(n)/4 are equal and at least (1-4epsilon)/2.

For n>=128, epsilon<=exp(-8)<1/20; the quadratic Taylor lower bound for exp(8) is 41>20. Both masses are therefore at least 2/5.

For this fixed Y choose f_Y(X) that is 0 when X_vec.v<=-sqrt(n)/4, 1 when X_vec.v>=sqrt(n)/4, and linear between them. Its Euclidean gradient has squared norm 4/n in the belt and 0 elsewhere. Therefore

E[||grad f_Y||^2 |Y] <=16 epsilon/n.

Two independent posterior copies show Var(f_Y|Y) is at least the product of the two plateau masses, hence at least 4/25>1/8. The Poincare variational inequality gives

C_P(mu_n(.|Y)) >= (n/128)exp(n/16).

The test function may depend on the fixed observation: C_P of each conditional law is a supremum over its test functions. This dependence is permitted by the quantifiers. Linearizing LSI at a constant gives C_P<=C_LS, proving the same posterior LSI lower bound.

## What this does and does not settle

The ambient dimension is D=n+n^2, so exp(n/16) is superpolynomial in D. The prior LSI and dimensionless observation ratio are bounded by absolute constants. The failure of posterior-LSI inheritance occurs with probability tending to one under the actual observations, rather than on a rare tail event.

This eliminates a proposed proof architecture for Target 1; it does not eliminate all posterior samplers. In particular exact sign symmetry can allow a sampler to assign the two modes correct masses without crossing a low-density belt. No mixing lower bound for a particular initialization, no cryptographic reduction, no efficient score-network construction, and no full resolution of either T411 target is claimed.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:7ab9e28c856e2293467a5e36ef14790c8a81e7db0b438eb38951cbab6bdbf181","revision_digest":"sha256:fa4e94378b30cd280124ab5ca647e8499b935dc6cf60738002a67bc6c3fb783c","source_id":"owner:T411:w740:C004-v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1-unaudited","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body:
Let G = PSL(2,R) and let Gamma be a LATTICE in G: a discrete subgroup such that the quotient M = Gamma\G carries a G-invariant Borel probability measure m (finite covolume, normalised). Gamma is not assumed torsion free, cocompact, or arithmetic. For real t let u_t denote the image in G of the unipotent matrix with rows (1, t) and (0, 1), and define the horocycle flow on M by h_t(Gamma g) = Gamma g u_t. Then: (1) each h_t preserves m; (2) HEDLUND: the flow is ergodic with respect to m; (3) PARRY: the flow is strongly mixing, that is for all F1, F2 in L^2(M, m) the inner product of F1 composed with h_t against F2 converges, as |t| -> infinity, to the product of the integral of F1 and the conjugate of the integral of F2; equivalently m(A intersect h_{-t}B) -> m(A) m(B) for all Borel A, B. Moreover the flow is mixing of all orders. WHERE THE HYPOTHESES BITE: (i) finite covolume is essential. Mixing as stated is a statement about a probability measure; for a discrete subgroup of infinite covolume the correct statements concern Burger-Roblin and Patterson-Sullivan measures and carry extra hypotheses (for instance on the critical exponent), so (3) must not be quoted there. (ii) Ergodicity and mixing hold for EVERY lattice, but MINIMALITY (every orbit dense), Hedlund's other theorem, needs Gamma cocompact: a noncompact finite-volume quotient has closed horocycle orbits encircling each cusp, so the flow there is mixing yet neither minimal nor uniquely ergodic. Confusing the two Hedlund statements is the usual error. (iii) The result concerns the unipotent direction. The geodesic flow a_s is also mixing but has positive entropy and a huge simplex of invariant measures, whereas the horocycle flow has zero entropy and (in the cocompact case) is uniquely ergodic; rigidity statements do not transfer between them. (iv) Nothing here gives a RATE; quantitative mixing needs a spectral gap input and the rate depends on the lattice.
G = PSL(2,R) and Gamma < G is discrete with finite covolume (a lattice)
m is the G-invariant probability measure on Gamma\G
the flow is right translation by the one-parameter unipotent subgroup u_t
no cocompactness, torsion freeness or arithmeticity is assumed for (1)-(3); cocompactness is needed only for minimality and unique ergodicity, which are NOT claimed here
mixing is understood with respect to the normalised invariant probability measure

[Prop geods-stability of arXiv:2604.12963, 'Shocks, instability, and the twenty networks\\ of infinite geodesics in the Directed Lands'] Let $\omega \in \Omega_0$ and $\theta \in \Theta^\omega$.  
Suppose $(x,s) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \IG\theta$.  
Then the following are the only possible configurations of $\theta$-directed geodesics emanating from $(x,s)$. 
Each of the configurations occurs for a dense set of such starting points $(x,s)$. See the last four configurations on the first row in Figure (fig:geodesics of the paper).    
\begin{enumerate}[label={\rm(\alph*)}, ref={\rm\alph*}] \itemsep=1pt
        \item $(x,s)\not\in{\mathrm{NU}}_1^{\theta+}\cup{\mathrm{NU}}_1^{\theta-}$. There exists $t>s$ such that 
        \begin{align*}
            &\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{L}{\theta}{-}\big|_{[s,t]} = \Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{R}{\theta}{+}\big|_{[s,t]}\quad\text{and}\quad
            \Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{L}{\theta}{-}(t) = \Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{R}{\theta}{+}(t)\in\IGpns\theta.
        \end{align*}
 
        \item $(x,s)\in{\mathrm{NU}}_1^{\theta+}\cap{\mathrm{NU}}_1^{\theta-}$. There exist times $t>t'>s'>s$ such that $t' = s+{\mathfrak a}^{\theta-}(x,s) = s+{\mathfrak a}^{\theta+}(x,s)$, 
        \begin{align*}
        &\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{L}{\theta}{-}\big|_{(s,t')} = \Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{L}{\theta}{+}\big|_{(s,t')}\prec\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{R}{\theta}{-}\big|_{(s,t')} = \Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{R}{\theta}{+}\big|_{(s,t')},\\
        &\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{L}{\theta}{-}\big|_{[t',t]} = \Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{R}{\theta}{+}\big|_{[t',t]},\quad
        \Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{L}{\theta}{-}(t) = \Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{R}{\theta}{+}(t)\in\IGpns\theta,
        \end{align*}
        and exactly one of the following occurs:
        \vspace{5pt}
              
        \begin{enumerate}[label={{\rm(}(prop:geods-stability.b of the paper).\rm\roman*)}, ref={(prop:geods-stability.b of the paper).\rm\roman*}] \itemsep=1pt
            \item   $\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{M}{\theta}{-}=\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{L}{\theta}{-}$ and $\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{M}{\theta}{+}=\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{R}{\theta}{+}$, or

            \item $\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{M}{\theta}{-}\bigl|_{[s,t]}=\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{M}{\theta}{+}\big|_{[s,t]}$, $\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{L}{\theta}{-}\big|_{(s,s')}\prec\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{M}{\theta}{-}\big|_{(s,s')}=\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{M}{\theta}{+}\big|_{(s,s')}\prec\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{R}{\theta}{+}\big|_{(s,s')}$, and the matching middle geodesics intersect exactly one of $\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{L}{\theta}{-}$ or $\Gamma_{{(x,s)}}\dir{R}{\theta}{+}$ at time $s'$, proceeding with said geodesic until time $t'$. Each of the two configurations occurs for a dense set of starting points $(x,s)\in\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\IG\theta$.
        \end{enumerate}       
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Own work draft, proof (unaudited), not independently checked and not Lean-certified. Fix 0<b<infinity and alpha in (0,infinity); n/(d-1)->alpha. The noiseless teacher is e1, the probe is independently specified and perfect, and iid kept rows are obtained by thresholding |x_1|<=b in Gaussian data. Let T have the positive half-normal law conditional on T<=b and H be an independent standard Gaussian. The draft identifies the limiting unit-norm max-margin teacher coordinate a* as the unique pair (a*,s*) maximizing k>=0 subject to a,s>=0, a^2+s^2<=1 and sqrt(alpha E[(k-aT-sH)_+^2])<=s. The maximum k is positive, its pair has unit norm and s*>0; the proposed test-error limit on fresh unconditioned Gaussian inputs is arccos(a*)/pi. The written proof transfers fixed-slice CGMT limits via uniform scalar empirical laws and concavity of the primary margin profile. It does not optimize the kept fraction for fixed original-pool budget, cover a slab width vanishing with dimension, or treat theta>0. Exact-count order-statistic pruning requires additional arguments. Full proof is saved in the cited owner-work file; reviewer PASS is still absent.

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2604.04267, 'On Sharpest Tail Bounds for Functions \\ of Tail Bounded Random Variables'] Let $\mathcalorig{F}_j$ be a $\sigma$-algebra for $\Omega_j$ with $\sigma$-finite measure $\mu_j$ for $j=1,...,n$. Then there is a unique measure $\mu$ on the product $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcalorig{F}$ of $\Omega=\Omega_1\times \cdots \times \Omega_n$
such that for any $A_j \in \mathcalorig{F}_j$, for $j=1,...,n$, $\mu(A_1 \times \cdots \times A_n) = \mu_1(A_1) \times \cdots \times \mu_n(A_n)$, or $0$ if any $\mu_j(A_j) = 0$, even if another is $+\infty$. If $f$ is non-negative and jointly measurable on $\Omega$, or if $f \in \mathcalorig{L}^1(\Omega,\mathcalorig{F},\mu)$, then 
$$
\int f \ d \mu = \int \cdots \int f(x_1,...,x_n) d\mu_1(x_1)\cdots d \mu_n(x_n)
$$
where for $f \in \mathcalorig{L}^1(\Omega,\mathcalorig{F},\mu)$, the iterated integral is defined recursively, ``from the outside" in the sense that for $\mu_n$-almost all $x_n$, the iterated integral with respect to the other variables is defined and finite, so that except on a set of $\mu_{n-1}$ measure $0$ (possibly depending on $x_n$) the iterated integral for the first $n-2$ variables is defined and finite, and so on. The same holds if integrations are done in any order. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

			:=\frac12\int_s^1\xi''(r)
			\left(\mathbb{E}[(M_r^\mu)^2]-r\right)\,\mathrm{d} r,
			\qquad s\in[q,1].
		\end{equation}
		The unique minimizer $\zeta_\mu$ of $V_\zeta(q,\mu)$ over $\mathcal P([q,1])$ is characterized by
		\begin{equation}
			\mathrm{supp}(\zeta_\mu)
			\subset
			\operatorname*{argmin}_{s\in[q,1]}H_{\zeta_\mu}^\mu(s).
		\end{equation}
		Moreover, $\zeta_\mu(\{1\})=0$. At every interior contact point
		$s\in\mathrm{supp}(\zeta_\mu)\cap[q,1)$, and at $s=q$ by the law matching when
		$\int a^2\mu(\mathrm{d} a)=q$,
		\begin{equation}
			\mathbb{E}[(M_s^\mu)^2]=s .
		\end{equation}
		For $q=0$ and $\mu=\delta_0$, this reduces to the usual first-variation and contact equations for the Parisi functional $P_\zeta$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

$

$

    \big|
        f(x)

    \big|
    \le
    \varepsilon
.
\end{equation}

[Definition Decoupled processes of arXiv:2607.22908, 'Epidemic Phase Transitions in the Zero-Range Process'] Consider the slot-priority dynamics with the priority partition of
  (def:priority_partition of the paper). Define two auxiliary processes.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item $\hat\eta^L_t$ is the zero-range process on $V_1$ with an absorbing boundary condition at $M_1$ (particles that jump to $M_1$ are removed), started from
      \[
        \hat\eta^L_0(x) = \eta^{(1)}_0(x) \text{ for } x \in V_1.
      \]

    \item $\hat\eta^R_t$ is the zero-range process on $V_2$ with an absorbing boundary condition at $M_2$, started from
      \[
        \hat\eta^R_0(x) = \eta^{(2)}_0(x) \text{ for } x \in V_2.
      \]
  \end{enumerate}
  Both processes are driven by the same Poisson clocks as the original process, restricted to their respective regions.

For Weyl polynomials sum_k b_k z^k / sqrt(k!) with i.i.d. standard Gaussian b_k, prove that the empirical distribution of roots tends to the uniform law on a disc and that in the real Gaussian case there are about (2/pi) sqrt n real roots. Resolution: Kabluchko-Zaporozhets 2014; Edelman-Kostlan; Tao-Vu 2015. Notes: Kabluchko and Zaporozhets ('Asymptotic distribution of complex zeros of random analytic functions', Ann. [Lem 19 of arXiv:2608.26698, 'Mapping class groups of simply connected closed spin 5-manifolds with no 2- and 3-torsion '] Let $S : S^2 \times D^3 \hookrightarrow M$ be an embedding in a closed 5-manifold $M$, and let $\beta \in \pi_3(\mathrm{SO}(3))$. Let $\mathbf{t}_{S, \beta}$ be the Dehn twist about $S$ and $\beta$. Choose an embedding $\ell : I \hookrightarrow S^1$ and identity $S^2 \times D^4$ with the image of the embedding $S \times \ell : S^2 \times D^3 \times I \hookrightarrow M \times S^1$. Then:
      	\begin{itemize}
      		\item[(1)] We have \[M_{\mathbf{t}_{S, \beta}} = (M \times S^1 \setminus S^2 \times D^4) \cup_{\varphi} (S^2 \times D^4)\] where $\varphi : S^2 \times S^3 \rightarrow S^2 \times S^3$ is given by $(x, y) \mapsto (\beta(y) \cdot x, y)$.
      		
      		\item[(2)] Let $\xi_{\beta}$ be the 3-dimensional vector bundle over $S^4$ with clutching function $\beta$. Let $D(\xi_{\beta})$ denotes the total space of the associated unit disc bundle, and $\partial D(\xi_{\beta})$ denotes the total space of the associated unit sphere bundle. Then $\partial D(\xi_{\beta}) = (S^2 \times D^4) \cup_{\varphi} (S^2 \times D^4)$ and $M_{\mathbf{t}_{S, \beta}} = \partial ((M \times D^2) \cup_{S^2 \times D^4} D(\xi_{\beta}))$.
      	\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 19 of arXiv:2608.26698

[Proposition prop:minimax-implies-composite-ville of arXiv:2512.21026, 'Minimax Duality in Game-Theoretic Probability\thanks{Work in progress: mistakes are likely'] Let $(\mathcal{Y},\hat\mathcal{Z},T)$ be a disintegrable sequential gamble space which is sequentially scalable and arbitrage free.
  Let $\mathcal{P} = \Delta_0^T(\hat\mathcal{Z})$.
  If $\overline{\mathbb{E}}^* X = \overline{\textsf{\textbf{E}}} X$ for all bounded measurable $X:\mathcal{Y}^T\to\mathbb{R}$, or all indicators $X = \mathds{1}_A$ for measurable $A\subseteq \mathcal{Y}^T$, then we have
  \begin{align*}
    \sup_{P\in\mathcal{P}} P(A)
    &= \inf\left\{ \alpha > 0 : \{X_t \geq 0\}_t \; \mathcal{P}\text{-supermartingale}, X_0 = 1, X_T \geq \frac 1 \alpha \text{ on } A\right\}~.
  \end{align*}
title: Proposition prop:minimax-implies-composite-ville of arXiv:2512.21026
