[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2608.22342, 'Completely Positive Entropy and Fourier Central Limit Theorems for Stationary Random Measu'] Let $A,B\subset\bR^d$ be bounded Borel sets with
$\lambda_d(\partial A)=\lambda_d(\partial B)=0$. Then
\begin{equation}

    \Cov_\eta\bigl(\mathbb S\ind_A,\mathbb S\ind_B\bigr)
    =\int_{\bR^d}\widehat{\ind}_A(\xi)
       \overline{\widehat{\ind}_B(\xi)}\,d\sigma_\eta(\xi).
\end{equation}
In particular, $\Var_\eta(\mathbb S\ind_A)$ is obtained by taking $A=B$.
For every $g\in\mathcal S(\bR^d)$, one also has the mixed identity
\begin{equation}

    \Cov_\eta\bigl(\mathbb S\ind_A,\mathbb S g\bigr)
    =\int_{\bR^d}\widehat{\ind}_A(\xi)
      \overline{\hat g(\xi)}\,d\sigma_\eta(\xi).
\end{equation}
Consequently, the Bartlett covariance identity holds on the linear span of
Schwartz functions and indicators of bounded Borel sets with boundary of
Lebesgue measure zero. Moreover, for every $\xi\in\bR^d$, the centered statistic
$M(\ind_A\chi_\xi)$ has Koopman spectral measure
\begin{equation}

    d\varsigma_{M(\ind_A\chi_\xi)}(\lambda)
    =\bigl|\widehat{\ind}_A(\lambda-\xi)\bigr|^2
      \,d\sigma_\eta(\lambda).
\end{equation}

body:
[Definition 12 of arXiv:2607.02434, 'A Topological Formula for \\ Potts Lattice Gauge Theory Correlations'] The $i$-dimensional \textbf{plaquette random cluster model (PRCM)} with free boundary conditions on a finite cell complex $X$ with parameters $p\in\brac{0,1}$ and $q\in\N_{\geq 2}$ is the random $i$-complex $P$ with the following distribution:
$$\mu^{\mathbf{f}}_{X}\paren{P} = \mu^{\mathbf{f}}_{X,p,q}\paren{P} \propto p^{\abs{P}}\paren{1-p}^{\abs{X^{i}} - \abs{P}}\abs{H^{i-1}\paren{P;\Z_q}}$$
where $\abs{X^{\paren{i}}}$ and $\abs{P}$ denote the number of $i$-faces $X$ and $P.$

Moreover, if $\Lambda=\brac{-N,N}^d\subset \Z^d$ is a box, the PRCM with wired boundary conditions on $\Lambda$ is the measure
$$\mu^{\mathbf{w}}_{\Lambda}\paren{P} = \mu^{\mathbf{w}}_{\Lambda,p,q}\paren{P} \propto p^{\abs{P}}\paren{1-p}^{\abs{\Lambda^{\paren{i}}} - \abs{P}}\abs{H^{i-1}\paren{P\cup \partial \Lambda;\Z_q}}\,.$$
The weak limits of these measures as $\Lambda\nearrow \Z^d$ exist by standard stochastic monotonicity arguments and are denoted by $\mu^{\mathbf{f}}_{\Z^d,p,q}$ and $\mu^{\mathbf{w}}_{\Z^d,p,q}.$
title: Definition 12 of arXiv:2607.02434

body: [Lemma lem:FKG-CLE of arXiv:2609.04140, 'The conformally invariant metric on $\CLE_4$ III:\\ uniqueness'] Let $U \subsetneq \BC$ be a deterministic simply connected domain and let $\Gamma_U$ be a non-nested $\CLE_4$ in $U$. Let $F, G \colon \BR^{U_\BQ \times U_\BQ} \to \BR_{\ge 0}$ be non-negative measurable mappings. Suppose that $F(d) \ge F(d^\prime)$ and $G(d) \ge G(d^\prime)$ for all $d, d^\prime \in \BR^{U_\BQ \times U_\BQ}$ with $d(x, y) \ge d^\prime(x, y)$ for all $x, y \in U_\BQ$. Then $\BE\lbrack F(D_{\Gamma_U}^U) G(D_{\Gamma_U}^U)\rbrack \ge \BE\lbrack F(D_{\Gamma_U}^U)\rbrack \BE\lbrack G(D_{\Gamma_U}^U)\rbrack$. The same is true for any pair of non-negative measurable functionals of $(\Gamma_U, D_{\Gamma_U}^U)$ which are a.s.\ non-increasing under the merging operation of (lem:monotonicity of the paper), and in particular for the indicator functions of the events $\{D_{\Gamma_U}^U(A, B) > \varepsilon\}$, where $A, B \subseteq \overline U$ are deterministic and $\varepsilon > 0$.

body:
[Thm 43 of arXiv:2609.03836, 'Koszul Orlik--Solomon Algebras from Non-supersolvable Arrangements'] Let $M$ be a matroid. Suppose $F$ is a flat of $M$ minimal for the property that $M$ is a non-trivial modular join over $F$. Choose flats $F_0, F_1$ with $F = F_0 \cap F_1$ such that $M = P_F(F_0, F_1)$. 
Then $M$ is supersolvable if and only if $M_0 \deq M|_{F_0}$ and $M_1 \deq M|_{F_1}$ are both supersolvable and at least one of them has a full modular flag passing through $F$.

[Lemma 53 (minimal five-factor extension) of arXiv:2609.03593, '\textbf{New Homogeneous Einstein Metrics from Detection}'] Suppose that the primitive simple enlargements of the four original
$\mathfrak h$-ideals have been excluded.  If a connected compact transitive
isometry algebra $\mathfrak i$ properly contains
\[
 \mathfrak g=\mathfrak h^4,
\]
then the connected isometry group contains a transitive subgroup $J$ with
\[
 \Lie(J)\simeq\mathfrak h^5
\]
which contains the original $\mathfrak h^4$ action.

[Theorem thm:main of arXiv:2505.14012, 'Ergodicity for stochastic neural field equations'] \phantom{ }
\begin{enumerate}
\item
Under Assumptions (assu:space of the paper) and (assu:noise of the paper), for any $p\ge 2$, any $T>0$, and for any initial datum $u_0\in L^p(\Omega,\mathcal{F}_0,\mathbb{P};L^2(U,\rho))$, there exists a unique $\mathbb{P}$-a.s. continuous and $\{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t\in [0,T]}$-adapted
$L^2(U,\rho)$-valued strong solution $u(t)$, $t\in [0,T]$ of (equation eq:gen_model of the paper), and there exists a constant $C_{p,T}>0$, such that
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}(\|u(t)\|^p_{L^2(U,\rho)})\leq C_{p,T}\left(1+\mathbb{E}\|u_0\|^p_{L^2(U,\rho)}\right),\quad t\in[0,T].
\end{align*} 
\item
Under Assumptions (assu:space of the paper), (assu:noise of the paper), (assu:hat of the paper), and (assu:inv of the paper), there exists a non-trivial compactly embedded linear subspace $H_1\subset L^2(U,\rho)$, such that for every initial datum $v\in H_1$, there exists a sequence of real numbers $T_n\ge 1$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$ with $T_n\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$, and a probability measure $\mu^v$ on the Borel sets of $(L^2(U,\rho))$ which is invariant for the semigroup $\{P_t\}_{t\ge 0}$, and the following convergence holds
\[\frac{1}{T_n}\int_0^{T_n}\mu_{u}(t,v)\,dt\rightharpoonup \mu^v\quad\text{as}\;\;n\to\infty,\]
in the sense of weak convergence of probability measures.
\item Under Assumptions (assu:space of the paper), (assu:noise of the paper), (assu:hat of the paper), (assu:inv of the paper), and (assu:ergo of the paper), there exists a unique probability measure $\mu$ on the Borel sets of $(L^2(U,\rho))$ with second moments which is invariant for the exponentially ergodic and exponentially mixing semigroup $\{P_t\}_{t\ge 0}$, and, in particular,
\[\mu_{u}(t,v)\rightharpoonup \mu\quad\text{as}\;\;t\to\infty,\]
for every $v\in L^2(U,\rho)$ in the sense of weak convergence of probability measures.
In particular, there exist constants $\hat{C}\ge 0$ and $\lambda\in (0,2\alpha)$, such that for any $v\in H$, and any $t\ge 0$,
\[\left|\mathbb{E}[\varphi(u(t,v))] - \int_{L^2(U,\rho)}\varphi(z)\, \mu(dz) \right|\le 2\operatorname{Lip}(\varphi)\left(\|v\|^2_{L^2(U,\rho)}+\hat{C}\right)e^{-(2\alpha-\lambda)t},\]
for any bounded and Lipschitz continuous function $\varphi:L^2(U,\rho)\to\mathbb{R}$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:main of arXiv:2505.14012

body: Let mu and nu be probability measures on a measurable space (S, S), and let (X, Y) be any coupling of mu and nu, meaning X and Y are random variables defined on a common probability space with X distributed as mu and Y distributed as nu. DRAFT proof-audit material, independent referee check pending. On the path o--a2--b--a1 with three independent Bernoulli(1/2) bonds, order A=(a1,a2). Let F2 mean that a2 is the first member of A connected to o in this order. Then P(F2)=3/8 and P(F2 and a2 connects to b)=1/8, so P(a2 connects to b | F2)=1/3, whereas min_(a in A)P(a connects to b)=1/2. The first-reached event contains a decreasing exclusion, so FKG does not justify the pointwise conditional lower bound. The Kozma--Nitzan global inequality P(o connects to b)>=P(o connects to A)min_(a in A)P(a connects to b) is nevertheless an equality here (both sides 1/4). This refutes the conditional proof premise, not the global conjecture.

Can the advantage function
\[
g_{A,B}(p):=\Pr(A\!>\!B)-\tfrac12
\]

More generally, for fixed lengths $(L_1,L_2)$, what is the largest possible number of winner flips
(i.e.\ the largest possible number of sign changes of $g_{A,B}(p)$ on $(0,1)$)
over all pairs with $|A|=L_1$, $|B|=L_2$? (Stated as a question by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)

body: Let (mu_n) be a sequence of probability measures and mu a probability measure on a metric space S with its Borel sigma-algebra. [Thm 5 (Stability of compensated jump functionals under quadratic variation convergence) of arXiv:2605.11783, 'Stability of Compensated Jump Integrals under Quadratic Variation Convergence'] Let \(X\) and \(\{X^n\}_{n\ge 1}\) be real-valued càdlàg processes on
\([0,t]\), with jump measures \(\mu\) and \(\mu^n\), and predictable
compensators \(\nu\) and \(\nu^n\), respectively. Assume that 
\[
        [X^n-X]_t \longrightarrow 0
        \quad\text{in probability.}
\]

Let \(f\) and \(f_n\), \(n\ge 1\), be predictable functions on
\(\Omega\times[0,t]\times\mathbb R\), 
such that the compensated jump integrals
\[
        M_t
        :=
        \int_0^t\int_{\mathbb R}
        f(s,x,\omega)(\mu-\nu)(ds,dx),
\]
and
\[
        M^n_t
        :=
        \int_0^t\int_{\mathbb R}
        f_n(s,x,\omega)(\mu^n-\nu^n)(ds,dx)
\]
are well-defined purely discontinuous local martingales.
Assume that $\P\left(\exists s\le t: \Delta X_s(\omega)\in \mathrm{disc}(f(s,.,\omega))\right)=0$.
Assume moreover that, for every \(a>0\), there exists a nonnegative
predictable process \(C^a\), locally bounded on \([0,t]\), such that, for
all \(n\ge1\),
\[
|f_n(s,x,\omega)|+|f(s,x,\omega)|
\le C^a_s(\omega)|x|,
\qquad s\le t,\ |x|\le a .
\]
Assume also that there exists a set \(\Omega_0\in\mathcal F\) with
\(\mathbb P(\Omega_0)=1\) such that, for every \(\omega\in\Omega_0\), every
\(s\leq t\), and every compact set \(K\subset\mathbb R\),
\[
        \sup_{x\in K}|f_n(s,x,\omega)-f(s,x,\omega)|\longrightarrow 0 .
\]

Then
\[
        M^n \longrightarrow M
        \quad\text{ucp on }[0,t].
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Stability of compensated jump functionals under quadratic variation convergence

[Definition def:graph-matrix-for-shape of arXiv:2608.12415, 'Sharp Phase Transition for Ellipsoid Fitting'] Given a shape \(\tau\), its graph matrix \(M_\tau\) is indexed by boundary labelings.
For boundary labelings \(S\) of \(U_\tau\) and \(T\) of \(V_\tau\), define
\[
    \mathsf{M} _{\tau}[S,T]
    =
    \sum_{\substack{
        \sigma:\,V(\tau)\to \mathbb N \\
        \sigma \text{ is a mapping of } \tau \\
        \sigma(U_\tau)=S,\ \sigma(V_\tau)=T
    }}
    \prod_{e\in E(\tau)}
    \chi_{t(e)}\bigl(G[\sigma(e)]\bigr).
\]
Here, if \(e=\{x,y\}\) is an edge between a square vertex and a circle vertex, then
\(G[\sigma(e)]\) denotes the corresponding entry \(G[\sigma(x),\sigma(y)]\).

[Proposition 13 of arXiv:2608.17509, '2608.17509'] Let \((T_L)_{L\geq1}\) be positive trace-class contractions on a Hilbert space. Assume that
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item \(\sup_{L\geq1}L^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(T_L)<\infty\);
\item there is a measurable \(r:(0,\infty)\to[0,1]\) with \(r\in L^1(0,\infty)\) such that, for every \(m\geq1\),
\[
\lim_{L\to\infty}
\frac{1}{L}\operatorname{tr}(T_L^m)
=
\frac{1}{2\pi}
\int_0^\infty r(\xi)^m\,\mathrm{d}\xi.
\]
\end{enumerate}
Then, for each \(t>-1\),
\[
\lim_{L\to\infty}
\frac{1}{L}\log\det(\operatorname{Id}+tT_L)
=
\frac{1}{2\pi}
\int_0^\infty \log\bigl(1+t\,r(\xi)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}\xi,
\]
locally uniformly for \(t\) in compact subsets of \((-1,\infty)\).

[Corollary 70 (Projective observability without finite truncation) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] Assume $H$ is infinite dimensional and let $(\Pi_n)$ be finite-rank orthogonal
projections with $\Pi_n\to I_H$ strongly.  Then the map
\[
 z\longmapsto\bigl((\Pi_n)_\sharp z\bigr)_{n\ge1}
\]
is injective on $\mathsf Z_{\eta;\mathfrak I,1}(H)$, and every state is
recovered by the state-topology limit
\[
 z=\lim_{n\to\infty}(\Pi_n)_\sharp z.
\]
No single finite-rank compression $(\Pi_n)_\sharp$ is injective on the full
operational state space, hence no fixed finite truncation is lossless.  On the
common stochastic domain the same assertions hold for the canonical state
$\mathcal A_2$.

  We call $\tau$ a \textit{functor} on $\mathfrak{M}_{c}$ if it satisfies the following.
  \begin{enumerate} [label = (\roman*)]
    \item 
      For every $ (S, d^{S}, \rho_{S}) \in \mathfrak{M}_{c}$,
      one has a metric space $(\tau(S, d^{S}, \rho_{S}), d_{\tau}^{S, \rho_{S}})$
      where $\tau(S, d^{S}, \rho_{S})$ is a set and $d_{\tau}^{S, \rho_{S}}$ is a metric on it.
      We simply write $\tau(S) \coloneqq \tau(S, d^{S}, \rho_{S})$.
    \item 
      For every $(S_{i}, d^{S_{i}}, \rho_{S_{i}}),\, i=1,2$ 
      and root-and-distance-preserving map $f: S_{1} \to S_{2}$, 
      one has a distance-preserving map $\tau_{f}: \tau(S_{1}) \to \tau(S_{2})$.
    \item 
      For any two root-and-distance-preserving maps $f :S_{1} \to S_{2},\, g : S_{2} \to S_{3}$,
      it holds that $\tau_{g \circ f} = \tau_{g} \circ \tau_{f}$.
    \item 
      For any $(S, d^{S}, \rho_{S}) \in \mathfrak{M}_{c}$, 
      it holds that $\tau_{\id_{S}} = \id_{\tau(S)}$.
  \end{enumerate}
  Similarly, we call $\tau$ a functor on $\mathfrak{M}$ if it satisfies the same conditions 
  not for $\mathfrak{M}_{c}$ but for $\mathfrak{M}$.

body:
[Theorem thm:singularity of arXiv:2607.24705, 'Derangetropy Operators'] Let $f \in \mathcal{D}_{+}\cap C^{3}$ have a regularly varying right
		tail in the smooth sense:
		$f^{(j)}(x) = (-1)^{j}(p)_{j}\,c_{0}\,x^{-p-j}(1+o(1))$ for
		$j = 0, 1, 2$, with $p > 1$. If $p \neq 2$, then
		\begin{equation}
			R \;\sim\; \frac{p(2-p)}{2c_{0}^{2}}\,x^{2p-2}:
			
		\end{equation}
		the curvature at the boundary of the support diverges to $+\infty$
		for $1<p<2$ and to $-\infty$ for $p>2$; for exponential or faster
		tails, again in the smooth sense, $R \to -\infty$. At $p = 2$ the
		leading divergence cancels and regularity is decided at second
		order: if
		\begin{equation}
			f(x) = c_{0}x^{-2}\big(1 + b\,x^{-\alpha} + o(x^{-\alpha})\big),
			\qquad 0 < \alpha < 2,\ \alpha \neq 1,\ b \neq 0,
			
		\end{equation}
		in the smooth sense, then
		\begin{equation}
			R \;\sim\; \frac{\alpha b(\alpha - 1)}{c_{0}^{2}}\,x^{2-\alpha},
			
		\end{equation}
		which still diverges. Hence a quadratic leading tail is necessary
		for the curvature to remain bounded at the boundary of rank, but
		not sufficient: every second-order correction of order $x^{-\alpha}$
		with $0 < \alpha < 2$, $\alpha \neq 1$, forces divergence, while
		corrections of order two and faster, again in the smooth sense,
		leave the curvature bounded. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Singularity theorem

Every set can be well-ordered: for every set X there exists a total (linear) order on X in which every nonempty subset of X has a least element. Over ZF the well-ordering theorem is equivalent to the axiom of choice and to Zorn's lemma.

Consider the set P of pairs (W, r) where W is a subset of X and r is a well-ordering of W. Order P by end-extension: (W_1, r_1) <= (W_2, r_2) when W_1 is an initial segment of (W_2, r_2) and r_2 restricted to W_1 equals r_1. P is nonempty (the empty set with the empty order, or any singleton). Every chain in P has an upper bound: take the union of the domains with the union of the orders; end-extension makes this a well-defined linear order, and it is a well-order because any nonempty subset meets some member W of the chain, and its least element within that W remains least overall, since later members of the chain only add elements above all of W. By Zorn's lemma P has a maximal element (W*, r*). If W* were not all of X, pick x in X outside W* and place it above every element of W*: this yields a well-ordering of W* union {x} that properly end-extends (W*, r*), contradicting maximality. Hence W* = X and X is well-ordered. [Proposition 8 (Gradient and Hessian) of arXiv:2608.20337, 'Information on trajectories:\\ martingales and random times'] Assume differentiation under the integral is justified.
Set $\Phi_T(\alpha) := \log Z_T(\alpha)$.
Then $\Phi_T$ is convex on its domain, and
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\partial \Phi_T}{\partial \alpha_i}(\alpha)
  = \E_{Q_T^\alpha}[\log \Pi_{i,T}],
  \qquad
  \frac{\partial^2 \Phi_T}{\partial \alpha_i \partial \alpha_j}(\alpha)
  = \Cov_{Q_T^\alpha}(\log \Pi_{i,T}, \log \Pi_{j,T}).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem6.3 of arXiv:2411.03528, '\textbf{On a boundary of the central limit theorem for strictly stationary, reversible Mar'] Suppose $(y_1, y_2, y_3, \dots)$ and $(z_1, z_2, z_3, \dots)$
are each a sequence of elements of the set $\{-1,0,1\}$.
Suppose that (i) there exists $m \in \mathbb N$ such that
$y_k = z_k = 0$ for all $k > m$, and
(ii) there exists $k \in \mathbb N$ such that $y_k \neq z_k$.

   Suppose $r_1, r_2, r_3, \dots$ is a sequence of positive numbers 
such that $r_{k+1}/r_k \geq 3$ for every $k \in \mathbb N$.

   Then each of the sums $\sum_{k=1}^\infty r_ky_k$ and 
$\sum_{k=1}^\infty r_kz_k$ has at most finitely many non-zero summands 
(and therefore trivially converges absolutely); and these sums satisfy 
$\sum_{k=1}^\infty r_ky_k \neq \sum_{k=1}^\infty r_kz_k$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem6.3 of arXiv:2411.03528

[Dfn 37 (Sub-exponential class) of arXiv:2609.02398, '\textbf{Convex Order Comparisons for Sub-Gamma Random Variables}'] Let $\sigma, \alpha > 0$. A random variable $X$ belongs to the class
$\SE(\sigma^2, \alpha)$ if
\begin{align}
    \E\left[e^{\lambda X}\right]
    \leq \exp\left(\frac{\sigma^2\lambda^2}{2}\right)
    \qquad \text{for all } |\lambda| \leq \frac{1}{\alpha} \, .
    
\end{align}
title: Sub-exponential class

There exists a $O(n^2 + \log^2(1/\varepsilon))$-time embedded root finding algorithm that returns $H(\varepsilon, n)$ of size satisfying $|H(\varepsilon, n)|\log |H(\varepsilon, n)| \leq c_1 \log(1/\varepsilon)$. body:
[Prop discretize of arXiv:2608.06500, 'Free energy of Ising models under a spectral condition'] Given a strong solution $t\mapsto \text{\boldmath $x$}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}^N$ to the SDE

    \begin{align*}
{\rm d}\text{\boldmath $x$}^{(t)}=\text{\boldmath $a$}(\text{\boldmath $x$}^{(t)}){\rm d} t+\sigma{\rm d}\text{\boldmath $w$}^{(t)}
\end{align*}

    on $\mathbb{R}^N$ for some function $\text{\boldmath $a$}:\mathbb{R}^N\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^N$ and constant diffusion coefficient $\sigma$, along with a step
    size $\delta\in(0,1)$, consider the Euler-Maruyama scheme
    $\text{\boldmath $y$}^{(0)},\text{\boldmath $y$}^{(1)},\text{\boldmath $y$}^{(2)},\ldots$ defined recursively by
    $\text{\boldmath $y$}^{(0)}=\text{\boldmath $x$}^{(0)}$ and

    \begin{align*}
\text{\boldmath $y$}^{(n+1)}=\text{\boldmath $y$}^{(n)}+\delta
\text{\boldmath $a$}(\text{\boldmath $y$}^{(n)})+\sigma(\text{\boldmath $w$}^{(\delta(n+1))}-\text{\boldmath $w$}^{(\delta n)}).
\end{align*}

    Suppose that, for some positive constants $K_1,K_2,K_3$, we have that
    $\mathbb{E}[\|\text{\boldmath $x$}^{(0)}\|^2]\le K_1N$, $\| \text{\boldmath $a$}({\boldsymbol 0})\|^2\le K_2N$, and
    $\| \text{\boldmath $a$}(\text{\boldmath $u$})-\text{\boldmath $a$}(\text{\boldmath $v$})\|\le K_3\|\text{\boldmath $u$}-\text{\boldmath $v$}\|$ for all $\text{\boldmath $u$},\text{\boldmath $v$}\in\mathbb{R}^N$,
    i.e. the initial condition is bounded in $L^2$ and the drift
    coefficient is Lipschitz and bounded at the origin. Then there
    exists a constant $L$ depending only on $K_1,K_2,K_3$ such that
    for all $\delta>0$ and $T\in\delta\mathbb{N}$, we have that

    \begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}[\|\text{\boldmath $x$}^{(T)}-\text{\boldmath $y$}^{(T/\delta)}\|^2]\le Le^{LT}\delta N.
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop discretize of arXiv:2608.06500

body:
[Theorem 7 of arXiv:2607.25645, 'Estimates of the total variation distance between laws of Sobolev mappings on Gaussian spa'] Let $k\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\ge 2k$, let
\[
q:=\frac{p}{p-2k+1},
\]
let $\varkappa\in(0,q)$, and let $a,b>0$. For $r\in\mathbb{N}$, set
\[
\beta_r:=
\frac{p\varkappa}{p(r+\varkappa)+\varkappa r(2k-1)}.
\]
Then, for every pair of mappings $f=(f_1,\ldots,f_k)$ and $g=(g_1,\ldots,g_k)$ with
$f_j,g_j\in W^{2,p}(\gamma)$,
\[
\max_{1\le j\le k}\|f_j\|_{\dot W^{2,p}(\gamma)}\le b,
\quad
\max_{1\le j\le k}\|g_j\|_{\dot W^{2,p}(\gamma)}\le b,
\]
and
\[
\gamma(\Delta_f\le \varepsilon)\le a\varepsilon^\varkappa,
\quad
\gamma(\Delta_g\le \varepsilon)\le a\varepsilon^\varkappa
\quad \forall\, \varepsilon>0,
\]
one has
\[
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(f,g)
\le
2^{14}k^{7/2}(q-\varkappa)^{-1}(a+b^p+1)\,
d_{\mathrm{KR}}(f,g)^{\beta_1}.
\]
More generally, for every $r\in\mathbb{N}$,
\[
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(f,g)
\le
C(r,k)(q-\varkappa)^{-1}(a+b^p+1)\,
d_r(f,g)^{\beta_r},
\]
where
$C(r,k)>0$ depends only on $r$ and $k$.

\begin{align*}

= & \sup_{t\in [a,b]} |f(t) - g(\la(t))|.

[Lemma lem:descent_curves of arXiv:2605.03896, 'Dimer models on astroidal zig-zag graphs'] Let~$(x,y)\in \mathcal D_c^\circ$ lie in a phase region, and let~$\zeta_0=\zeta_*(x,y)$. If~$(x,y)\in \mathcal F_{(\alpha,\beta)}$, where~$(\alpha,\beta)\subset A_0$ is the interval between consecutive angles~$\alpha,\beta$, assume that~$(x,y)\notin \bm l_{e(\alpha)}\cup \bm l_{e(\beta)}$. Then we may choose orientations of~$C_{(x,y),\mathrm{desc}}$ and~$C_{(x,y),\mathrm{asc}}$ such that, for all sufficiently large~$n$ and all
\(
\mathsf b_n\in B(\mathsf C_n),
\mathsf w_n\in W(\mathsf C_n),
\)
the curve~$C_{(x,y),\mathrm{desc}}$ is {homologous} to~$C(I_{\mathsf b_n})$ in

\]
and the curve~$C_{(x,y),\mathrm{asc}}$ is {homologous} to~$C(I_{\mathsf w_n})$ in
\[
\Sigma\setminus \bigcup_{e\in I_{\mathsf w_n,+}} \bm\alpha_e.
\]

[Theo Approximation of arXiv:2411.19543, 'Feller property and convergence for semigroups of time-changed processes'] Let $F_n,\, F$ be the fine supports of $\mu_n,\mu_\infty$, respectively. Assume that $F_n,\, F,\, n\in\mathbb{N}$ are closed. Let $\Pi_n : C_0(F)\to C_0(F_n),\;\, u\mapsto (P_F u)|_{F_n}$. Then for all $u\in C_0(F)$ it holds
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\rm(1)] 
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{x\in F_n} \left|\check{T}_t^n \Pi_n u(x) - \Pi_n \check{T}_t^\infty u(x) \right| = 0
\]
locally uniformly in $t\in [0,\infty)$.
\item[\rm(2)] For all $\alpha>0$
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{x\in F_n} \left|V_\alpha^n \Pi_n u(x) - \Pi_n V_\alpha^\infty u(x) \right| = 0.
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2609.01996, 'Baumslag--Solitar Subgroups Obstruct Model Companions for Fields with Group Actions'] Let \(H\leq G\), let \(K\) be a \(G\)-field, and let \(\chi:H\to K^\times\) satisfy the \(1\)-cocycle condition
  \[
    \chi(h_1h_2)=\chi(h_1)\,h_1\bigl(\chi(h_2)\bigr)\quad(h_1,h_2\in H).
  \]
  Choose a section
  \[
    \rho:G/H\longrightarrow G,\quad \rho(H)=1,
  \]
  and put
  \[
    \alpha(\gamma,\lambda):=\rho(\gamma\lambda)^{-1}\gamma\rho(\lambda)\quad(\gamma\in G,\ \lambda\in G/H).
  \]
  If the elements \(z_\lambda\), \(\lambda\in G/H\), are algebraically independent over \(K\), then the formulas
  \begin{equation}
    \gamma(z_\lambda):=\rho(\gamma\lambda)\bigl(\chi(\alpha(\gamma,\lambda))\bigr)z_{\gamma\lambda}
  \end{equation}
  extend the given action on \(K\) to a \(G\)-field structure on the purely transcendental extension
  \[
    E:=K\bigl(z_\lambda:\lambda\in G/H\bigr).
  \]
  In particular,
  \[
    h(z_H)=\chi(h)z_H\quad(h\in H).
  \]

  Moreover, let \(D\trianglelefteq G\) satisfy \(D\subseteq H\) and \(\chi|_D=1\).
  If \(D\) acts trivially on \(K\), then it acts trivially on \(E\).

body:
[Proposition 126 (Obstruction to a flattening-only bound at
\texorpdfstring{$r=\infty$}{r=infinity}) of arXiv:2606.29292, 'Intrinsic Gaussian Tensor Geometry and Random Operator Spectra'] Let $K_{\boldsymbol 1,N}$ be the equal-weight diagonal kernel from
Proposition~\ref{prop:r-growth-sharpness}.  Then
\begin{equation}

  \Prof_{m,\infty}(K_{\boldsymbol 1,N})=1,
  \qquad
  \max_{S\subset[m]}\rank\Flat_S(K_{\boldsymbol 1,N})=N.
\end{equation}
For either the real or the circular complex Gaussian model, there are
constants $0<c_m\le C_m<\infty$ such that, for every $N\ge1$ and $p\ge2$,
\begin{equation}

  c_m\bigl(p+\log(eN)\bigr)^{m/2}
  \le
  \|\cT_{K_{\boldsymbol 1,N}}^{(m)}\|_{L^p(\Omega;\cL)}
  \le
  C_m\bigl(p+\log(eN)\bigr)^{m/2}.
\end{equation}
Taking $r$ comparable to $\log(eN)$ in
Theorem~\ref{thm:m-finite} gives the matching logarithmic upper order.
Consequently, an operator-norm estimate based only on the max-cut profile must
retain effective-rank information; in particular, no bound of the form
\[
  \E\|\cT_K^{(m)}\|_{\cL}
  \le C_m\Prof_{m,\infty}(K)
\]
can hold uniformly over finite dimensions.

[Proposition 21 of arXiv:2607.22470, 'A Logarithmic Fluctuation Hierarchy for Sequential Interacting Diffusions'] Let \(n_1,\ldots,n_q,k_1,\ldots,k_r\ge0\), and let
\(\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_q,\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_r\in
C_c^\infty(\R^d)\). Then, as \(N\to\infty\), the following convergences hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] The initial vector
\[
\bigl(\langle Y_0^{N,n_a},\varphi_a\rangle\bigr)_{a=1}^q
\]
converges weakly in \(\R^q\) to the centered Gaussian vector with covariance
\eqref{eq:limit-initial-covariance}.

\item[(ii)] The martingale vector
\[
\bigl(M^{N,k_b}(\psi_b)\bigr)_{b=1}^r
\]
converges weakly in \(C([0,T];\R)^r\) to the centered continuous Gaussian
martingale with covariations \eqref{eq:limit-martingale-covariance}.

body:
[Cor daffodil of arXiv:2411.07609, 'Activated Random Walks on $\bZ$ with Critical Particle Density'] Let $n$ be a positive integer. Consider activated random walk on $\mathbb{Z}$ with sleep rate $\lambda > 0$. Let $\sigma$ be an initial configuration with at least one active particle on the interval $[a, a + n - 1]$ for some integer $a$.

Let $b$ be an integer and $\gamma \in (0,1]$ such that $I_{b,\gamma} = [b, b +  n\gamma - 1]\cap \mathbb Z \subseteq I$. Let $U$ be a stable odometer on $I_{b,\gamma}$ that satisfies $U(b) = u_0$ and $U(x) > 0$ for every site $x \in I_{b,\gamma}$ containing a particle in $\sigma$. Define $Y_{I_{b,\gamma}}(u_0)$ to be the number of sleeping particles remaining in $I_{b,\gamma}$ after applying $U$. Then, for any $\rho > \rho_*(\lambda)$,
$$\mathbb{P}_\sigma\left[ Y_{I_{b,\gamma}}(u_0) \geq \rho  n\gamma  \right] \leq C e^{-c n}$$
for some constants $C$ and $c$, depending only on $\lambda$ and $\rho$.

body:
[Proposition cor:minibatch-variable-range-eb of arXiv:2608.25551, 'Beyond Optimal Rates in Stochastic Optimization: Trajectory-Adaptive Stopping Rules'] Fix deterministic integers $t_0 \ge 1$ and $b \ge 1$, and let $\{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t \ge t_0-1}$ be a filtration. For every $t \ge t_0$, let $H_t^{(1)}, \ldots, H_t^{(b)}$ be integrable, $\mathcal{F}_t$-measurable random variables that are conditionally independent given $\mathcal{F}_{t-1}$ and have a common conditional mean $m_t \coloneqq \mathbb{E}\left[H_t^{(i)} \mid \mathcal{F}_{t-1}\right]$, for $i = 1, \ldots, b$. Let $\{c_t\}_{t \ge t_0}$ be an almost surely finite,\footnote{As in Theorem~(thm:variable-range-eb of the paper), no uniform upper bound on the process $\{c_t\}_{t \ge t_0}$ is assumed.} nonnegative predictable process such that $\left|H_t^{(i)}\right| \le c_t$ almost surely for every $t \ge t_0$ and $i = 1, \ldots, b$. Define
\[
    \overline H_{t_0-1}^{\mathrm{MB}}
    \coloneqq
    0,
    \qquad
    \overline H_t^{\mathrm{MB}}
    \coloneqq
    \sum_{s=t_0}^t
    \left(
        \frac{1}{b}
        \sum_{i=1}^b
        H_s^{(i)}
        -
        m_s
    \right),
\]
and
\[
    W_{t_0-1}^{\mathrm{MB}}
    \coloneqq
    0,
    \qquad
    W_t^{\mathrm{MB}}
    \coloneqq
    \sum_{s=t_0}^t
    \sum_{i=1}^b
    \left(H_s^{(i)}\right)^2,
    \qquad
    C_t
    \coloneqq
    \max_{t_0 \le s \le t}
    c_s.
\]
Then, for every $\alpha \in (0,1)$,
\begin{equation}

    \mathbb{P}\left(
        \forall t \ge t_0:\
        \overline H_t^{\mathrm{MB}}
        \le
        \frac{1}{b}
        \mathfrak B_\alpha\left(
            W_t^{\mathrm{MB}},
            C_t
        \right)
    \right)
    \ge
    1-\alpha.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Minibatch empirical Bernstein bound with a growing predictable range

body:
[Lemma lem_1 of arXiv:2607.11469, 'Breuer-Major-Donsker invariance principle'] Let $\{ G_k \}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ be a centered stationary Gaussian sequence 
with $\rho_G(0)=1$. Let $\mathcal{F}_k = \sigma\{ G_j: j\leq k \}$,
 $Y_k = \mathbb{E}[ G_k | \mathcal{F}_{k-1}]$, and $\varepsilon_k = G_k - Y_k$ for $k\in\mathbb{Z}$.
Then the following results hold. 

\smallskip

\noindent
{\rm (i)}  $\{ Y_k \}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ is a  centered stationary Gaussian sequence 
with $\rho_Y(0)  = 1 -\nu^2$ with $\nu = \| G_0 - Y_0\|_2$.
Moreover, $\varepsilon_k$, $k\in\mathbb{Z}$, are i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}(0, \nu^2)$.
 
\smallskip

\noindent
{\rm (ii)}  If $\rho_G\in\ell^d(\mathbb{Z})$ for some $d\geq 2$, then $\rho_Y\in\ell^d(\mathbb{Z})$ as well. 

\smallskip

\noindent
{\rm (iii)} Suppose $\nu^2 < 1$ and define 
$
Z_k:=\frac{Y_k}{\sqrt{1-\nu^2}}.
$
Then, 
for each $k\in\mathbb{Z}$,
\begin{equation}
\qquad\qquad\qquad
\mathbb{E}[\varphi(G_k)\mid\mathcal{F}_{k-1}]
=
P_\tau\varphi(Z_k)
\quad\text{with  
$e^{-\tau}=\sqrt{1-\nu^2}
$.}
\end{equation}
title: Lemma lem_1 of arXiv:2607.11469

body: Let tau be a stopping time with respect to a filtration (F_t)_{t in T} (that is, {tau <= t} is in F_t for every t). The sigma-algebra of events prior to tau, denoted F_tau, is defined as the collection of all A in F such that A intersect {tau <= t} is in F_t for every t in T. F_tau is itself a sigma-algebra, tau is F_tau-measurable, and if sigma and tau are stopping times with sigma <= tau almost surely then F_sigma is a subset of F_tau. [standard, e.g. Karatzas and Shreve, Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus]
title: The Stopping-Time Sigma-Algebra F_tau

[Lemma lem:shape-monotonicity of arXiv:2604.25108, 'Terminal Defects, Growing Multiplicity, and Variance Extremality\\in the Double Dixie Cup '] Let $X_\theta\ge0$ have CDF $G_\theta$ and density $g_\theta$.  Put
\[
        W(\theta)=\operatorname{Var}(X_\theta)-\mathbb E X_\theta,
        \qquad
        \mu_\theta=\mathbb E X_\theta.
\]
Assume that $\operatorname{Var}(X_\theta)\ge \mathbb E X_\theta$ and that
\[
        w_\theta(x):=-\partial_\theta G_\theta(x)
\]
is nonnegative, locally integrable, and satisfies
$0<\int_0^\infty w_\theta(x)\,d x<\infty$.  Assume also that differentiation under the tail integrals below is justified.  If
\begin{equation}
        \frac{w_\theta(x)}{xg_\theta(x)}
\end{equation}
is increasing in $x$, then $W'(\theta)>0$.

body: [Definition def:crossing_cluster of arXiv:2506.07158, 'The diffusivity of supercritical Bernoulli percolation is infinitely differentiable'] We say that a cube ${\scaleobj{1}{\square}}$ is crossable if each of the $d$ pairs of opposite $(d-1)$-dimensional faces of the cube ${\scaleobj{1}{\square}}$ is joined by an open path in ${\scaleobj{1}{\square}}$. We say that a cluster $\mathscr{C}\subseteq {\scaleobj{1}{\square}}$ is a crossing cluster for ${\scaleobj{1}{\square}}$ if $\mathscr{C}$ intersects each of the $(d-1)$-dimensional faces of ${\scaleobj{1}{\square}}$.

[Thm 228 (\textbf{main result for symmetrized projection pursuit}) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] The following holds in the Ising (resp. spherical) cases.
    \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
        \item 
        
        If $\mu \in \ocM^{\Ising,\sym}(\alpha)$ (resp. $\ocM^{\sph,\sym}(\alpha)$), for any $\iota > 0$ there exist $L$ large enough and $c$ small enough such that for sufficiently large $N$, there exists an $L$-Lipschitz algorithm that $(\iota,1-e^{-cN})$-symmetrically attains $\mu$.
        \item 
        
        For any $\fq \in [1,2)$ and $\iotamsr > 0$, there exists small $\iotasol > 0$ such that the following holds.

[Proposition prop:energy_enstrophy of arXiv:2609.01697, 'Unique ergodicity of projective cocycles over the 2D stochastic Navier--Stokes equations'] Fix $T > 0$. Then for $V_\rho$ as in~(equation eq:lyapunov_S4 of the paper), the following hold:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item There exists a $q \geqslant 1$ such that for every $p \geqslant 1$ and every $\beta \in (1, \alpha_\star) \setminus \mathbf{N}$
      there exists a $C = C(p, \beta, T) > 0$ with
      \begin{equation}
        \mathbb{E}\Big[ \sup_{t \in [0,T]} \|w_t\|_{\mathcal{C}^{\beta}}^p \Big] \leqslant C(1 + \| w_0 \|_{\mathcal{C}^{\beta}})^{pq} .
      \end{equation}
    \item For every $p \geqslant 1$ and
      $0 \leqslant s \leqslant t$ there exists $C = C(p, t) > 0$ such that, at $\rho = p$,

        \mathbb{E}\big[ \|\pi_t\|_{H^1}^p \big]
        \leqslant C \mathbb{E}\big[ \|\pi_s\|_{H^1}^{2p} + 1 \big]^{1/2} V_\rho(u_0)^{1/2} .

For f(u)=1-exp(-u), P_s the semigroup of dV=(2V+a)ds+sqrt(2)VdW, a=1/(3pi), and Q_n the global hybrid ReLU reciprocal kernel, let g_k=P_(v_k)f with arbitrary deterministic v_k in[0,T]. Along its chain from U0=1/(n theta0), fixed theta0 in(0,pi], N<=Tn, sum_(k=0)^(N-1) E|(Q_n-P_(1/n))g_k(U_k)-Cg_k(U_k)/n^2|<=C_(theta0,T)/n. Here C=(8u+a/5+b/u)D+(4u^2-3au/5)D^2, b=1/(6pi^2). Assumptions: Independent Gaussian zero-bias ReLU rows/layers, hybrid normalized/ordinary Gram self-loop kernel of C039, n sufficiently large, fixed T. Semigroup tests have bounded polynomially weighted positive-order derivatives of every fixed order, proved from the affine SDE solution. The angle transition uses n independent row pairs x=max(g,0), y=max(cos(theta)g+sin(theta)h,0), g,h iid standard Gaussians, independent across layers, and the angle between the resulting vectors. Kill at zero norm or zero angle. For the hybrid kernel use a fixed small concentration box for (mean(x^2+y^2),mean((x-y)^2)/theta^2,mean(x^2-y^2)/theta) at small theta, and ordinary Gram averages at larger theta, each centered at its expectation; self-loop on failure. Limit: New proof of all-state uniformity and accumulation awaits independent audit. This is an accumulated local-defect statement, with finite-moment calculations confined to the hybrid chain. P_s g(u)=E[g(V_s^u)] for dV=(2V+a)ds+sqrt(2)VdW,V0=u,a=1/(3pi). The semigroup sensitivity D_t=D P_t f(0)=E[exp(t+sqrt(2)W_t-V_t^0)], f(u)=1-exp(-u).

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:4fa172f7326b7cf343a5dab2ef18c188e23a118bb2655d2c8fd721ca7b379026","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/4f/4fa172f7326b7cf343a5dab2ef18c188e23a118bb2655d2c8fd721ca7b379026.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:98724c8e7c4c4475db5c666bd81d25ff0417c42dc077cf1ae14f24f3ad7d26fa","bundle_entry_key":"relu-all-state-weak-defect","bundle_id":"population.t244-logarithmic-bounded-weak-rate-015","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability; random neural networks","draft":"w691/bundle_015.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.randomnetworks:t244-relu-all-state-weak-defect","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C042-C043: bounded-observable logarithmic finite-width bias

Version 1, 20 October 2026. Target 1, kind moved. Proofs (unaudited).
All claims below depend on the preceding unaudited C032-C041 calculations
as specified. They require the reviewer's independent check. This is a
bounded-observable result, not an expansion of the infinite raw exact
reciprocal mean. Literature novelty is not asserted.

Let a=1/(3pi), b=1/(6pi^2), and

    A=(2u+a)D+u^2 D^2,
    B=(10u+6a/5+b/u)D+(11u^2+12au/5+a^2/2)D^2
                                +(4u^3+au^2)D^3+(u^4/2)D^4,
    C=B-A^2/2=(8u+a/5+b/u)D+(4u^2-3au/5)D^2.

Let P_s be the semigroup of dV=(2V+a)ds+sqrt(2)V dW, and f(u)=1-exp(-u).
Use C039's global hybrid Gaussian/ReLU kernel Q_n for the reciprocal
U=1/(n theta). Fix theta0 in (0,pi], T<infinity.

## C042: accumulated local weak defect, with no reciprocal upper cutoff

For any deterministic v_k in [0,T], put g_k=P_(v_k)f. Uniformly in
N<=Tn, with U_k the hybrid chain started at U0=1/(n theta0),

    sum_(k=0)^(N-1) E| (Q_n-P_(1/n))g_k(U_k)
                                          -Cg_k(U_k)/n^2 |
                                             <=C_(theta0,T)/n. (1)

The v_k need not be monotone. This is a local-defect estimate along the
chain, sufficient for telescoping bounded tests. It contains no stopping
boundary correction and uses no finite raw reciprocal moment of the exact
network.

### Weighted semigroup derivative bounds

The affine solution V_v^u=V_v^0+uJ_v, J_v=exp(v+sqrt(2)W_v), gives

    D^j g_v(u)=(-1)^(j+1) E[J_v^j exp(-V_v^0-uJ_v)], j>=1.

For every nonnegative integer r and positive integer j,

    sup_(0<=v<=T,u>=0) u^r |D^j g_v(u)| < infinity.             (2)

For r=0 use E J_v^j. For r>0 use (uJ_v)^r exp(-uJ_v)<=r^r exp(-r)
and the finite lognormal moment E J_v^(j-r), uniform for v in [0,T].
Also 0<=g_v<=1. These are uniform all-state bounds, stronger than merely
bounded unweighted derivatives on fixed reciprocal compacts.

### The small-angle expansion with constants uniform in u

Fix the small-angle threshold epsilon of the hybrid kernel and set
theta=1/(nu)<=epsilon, allowing arbitrarily large u. In C032's normalized
concentration box, T_theta(z)=theta/output_angle is between fixed positive
constants, with uniformly bounded coordinate derivatives of every fixed
order needed below. By the chain rule and (2),

    |D_z^ell [g_v(uT_theta(z))]|<=C_T min(u,1), 1<=ell<=5.     (3)

For u<=1 every term contains u^j with j>=1 and a bounded derivative.
For u>=1 use (2) with r=j and the positive lower bound on T_theta.
The same bounds apply to the further finitely many weighted derivatives
needed for the theta-expansion coefficients and their mean-coordinate
variation. No derivative of g_v of order zero is asserted to decay.

Repeat C032's fourth-order centered sample-average expansion, retaining
(3). Its scaled Taylor remainder is C_T min(u,1)n^(-3/2). Freezing the
third- and fourth-moment coefficient at theta=0 costs at most
C_T min(u,1)sqrt(theta)/n. The covariance and coordinate multiplier
second-order theta remainders cost C_T min(u,1)theta^2. Deleted bounded
test terms cost C_T n exp(-cn), uniformly in u. Their polynomial Taylor
terms have the same exponential control by uniform row moments and (3).

The baseline zero-angle coefficients remain precisely C030's terms,
uniformly in u, by the same Taylor expansion and (3). The deterministic
map has displacement

    u theta/F(theta)-u=a/n+b/(n^2 u)+O(1/(n^3 u^2)),

which is O(1/n) uniformly for theta<=epsilon. Its scalar test Taylor
remainder after scaling is bounded by C_T(1+1/u+1/u^2)/n^2, exactly as
in C036. Thus the identical explicit operators A,B satisfy

    | n(Q_n-I)g_v(u)-Ag_v(u)-Bg_v(u)/n |
      <=C_T[n^(-3/2)+(1+1/u+1/u^2)/n^2+n exp(-cn)],
                                      theta=1/(nu)<=epsilon.  (4)

In simplifying, min(u,1)/sqrt(u)<=1 and
min(u,1)theta^2<=C(1+1/u+1/u^2)/n^2 were used. The constants in (4)
are independent of any upper cutoff on u. This uniformity is the new
step beyond C036; it is justified by the derivative decay in (2).

### The diffusion step and the large-angle step

The functions Ag_v,A^2g_v,A^3g_v are uniformly bounded by (2), since
their coefficients are polynomials multiplying positive-order derivatives.
Their Ito martingale coefficients are bounded as well, using the bounds
on u times their first derivatives. Iterated Dynkin identities therefore
give, with h=1/n,

    P_h g_v=g_v+hAg_v+h^2 A^2g_v/2+O_T(h^3),                 (5)

uniformly for all u>=0. One can first localize the nonexplosive linear SDE
and then remove the localization by boundedness; no assertion of a
globally analytic semigroup is needed. Combining (4)-(5) proves the
pointwise small-angle defect bound

    |(Q_n-P_h)g_v-Cg_v/n^2|
       <=C_T[n^(-5/2)+(1+1/u+1/u^2)/n^3+exp(-cn)].           (6)

If theta>epsilon, then u<=1/(n epsilon). The hybrid ratio U_next/u is
bounded, so |Q_n g_v-g_v|<=C_T u<=C_T/n by the bounded first derivative.
Also |P_hg_v-g_v|<=h||Ag_v||_infinity<=C_T/n. From the displayed formula
for C and 1/u=n theta<=n pi, |Cg_v(u)|/n^2<=C_T/n on this range.
Consequently the defect is at most C_T/n for large angles.              (7)

### Sum the defects

C039 gives E theta_k^p<=C_(p,T)/(k+1)^p, and on every hybrid state
1/U_k=n theta_k. Sum (6) at the small-angle states, using the full
positive moment bounds as upper bounds. The resulting terms are

    C_T n^(-3/2), C_T/n^2,
    (C_T/n^2)sum_(k<N)1/(k+1)<=C_T log(n+1)/n^2,
    (C_T/n)sum_(k<N)1/(k+1)^2<=C_T/n,
    C_T n exp(-cn).

For (7), C039 at p=2 bounds the expected number of large-angle visits
by epsilon^(-2)sum E theta_k^2<=C_T. Its total contribution is C_T/n.
All displayed smaller terms are O(1/n), proving (1).

## C043: the terminal bounded-observable rate

For fixed t>0, N=floor(nt), let theta_N be the exact width-n Gaussian
zero-bias ReLU angle with fixed theta0 in (0,pi]. Define its observable
to be f(1/(n theta_N)) on nondegenerate paths and zero after killing.
Then, as n tends to infinity,

    E[f(1/(n theta_N));alive]
       =E[f(V_t^0)] + (D_t/(2pi))log(n)/n+O_(theta0,t)(1/n),   (8)

where

    D_t=D P_t f(0)=E[exp(t+sqrt(2)W_t-V_t^0)]>0.

Any other fixed bounded cemetery value changes (8) only exponentially
through time N, by the same hybrid coupling. In particular the leading
bounded-observable bias is positive and is of order log(n)/n, rather
than a pure c(t)/n expansion. The O(1/n) coefficient is not identified.

Proof. Set t_n=N/n and G_k=P_((N-k)/n)f. The exact semigroup relation
G_k=P_(1/n)G_(k+1) and the Markov property of the hybrid chain give

    E f(U_N)-P_(t_n)f(U0)
      =sum_(k=0)^(N-1) E[(Q_n-P_(1/n))G_(k+1)(U_k)].          (9)

All tests are bounded. Apply (1) to conclude that (9) equals

    (1/n^2)sum_(k=0)^(N-1) E[(C G_(k+1))(U_k)]+O(1/n).      (10)

The k=0 term is O_(theta0,t)(1/n): its singular part is bounded by
C/(n^2 U0)=C theta0/n, and the other terms are smaller. For k>=1,
C041's proof applies also to the one-step shifted test G_(k+1).
Explicitly, its first derivative differs from D_t by at most
C_t[(k+1)/n+u], because |t_n-t|<=1/n. Multiplying by theta_k and
using theta_k U_k=1/n and E theta_k<=C/(k+1) shows a bounded total
weighted error after summation. C040 gives

    sum_(k=1)^(N-1) E theta_k=(1/a)log(n)+O_(theta0,t)(1).

Thus the singular part of (10) is
(b/a)D_t log(n)/n+O(1/n). The remaining parts of C contribute O(1/n),
by bounded first and second test derivatives and the hybrid reciprocal
moment bounds (4) in C040. Since b/a=1/(2pi), this identifies (10).

Finally U0=1/(n theta0). Bounded D P_s f and bounded Af imply

    |P_(t_n)f(U0)-P_t f(0)|<=C_(theta0,t)/n.

This includes the initial-angle and fractional-layer effects at the
remainder order. The global hybrid coupling through N steps fails with
probability at most C_t n exp(-cn). Since f and its cemetery value are
bounded, transfer to the exact chain changes the expectation by that
order, which is smaller than 1/n. This proves (8).

## Scope and review priority

No exact-chain raw reciprocal moment is claimed or used. The proof
performs its martingale estimates on a finite-moment regularization,
then transfers bounded observables. The estimate is for the specified
smooth bounded test, not a total-variation, Wasserstein, joint-output or
full-path quantitative rate. Independent review should check (4)'s
uniformity in unbounded u, the hybrid coupling, and the covariance
calculation underlying B before accepting (8).","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:48d5412d05f2566420246d906fe5e2cb5ea63da0a7aee9e2d7460ec5d88ae3f3","revision_digest":"sha256:fe4020fda7ee8bb5bc64e7c9222149cf2937451449a472e5282436a82c485792","source_id":"own-work:T244-w691-C042:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body:
Fix 0<rho<1 and independent standard normal Z_0,...,Z_m. Let X_i=sqrt(rho)*Z_0+sqrt(1-rho)*Z_i and M_m=max_i X_i. Coordinates have variance one and distinct covariance rho. Var(M_m)>=rho, so the field is not superconcentrated. Nevertheless the number of coordinates at deficit at most delta_m=(log m)^(-1/4) from M_m tends to infinity in probability. Thus growing near-peaks with pairwise covariance merely bounded away from one, even at vanishing absolute deficit, are insufficient for superconcentration. This does not refute a criterion requiring overlaps to tend to zero.
Independent standard Gaussian coordinates
Fixed positive common covariance rho
Candidate uses overlap bounded away from one, not overlap tending to zero

Each X_i has variance one; distinct coordinates have covariance rho, bounded away from one. Put M_m=max_i X_i. Independence gives

    Var(M_m)=rho+(1-rho)*Var(max_i Z_i)>=rho.

Thus these maxima are not superconcentrated relative to the unit coordinate variance. Any two selected coordinates have covariance at least rho, including maximisers before and after Gaussian noise, so an overlap-to-zero chaos criterion also fails.

Nevertheless, for delta_m=(log m)^(-1/4), the number K_m of coordinates within delta_m of M_m tends to infinity in probability. To prove this, let b_m=sqrt(2 log m), d_m=delta_m/(2 sqrt(1-rho)), and x_m=b_m-d_m. A Gaussian Chernoff bound gives

    P(max_i Z_i > b_m+d_m) <= exp(-b_m*d_m-d_m^2/2) -> 0.

Let N_m count Z_i>=x_m. It is binomial with mean mu_m=m*barPhi(x_m). For x>=1, integrating the Gaussian density on [x,x+1/x] gives barPhi(x)>=exp(-3/2)*exp(-x^2/2)/(sqrt(2*pi)*x). Therefore

    log mu_m >= b_m*d_m-d_m^2/2-log(x_m)-3/2-log(2*pi)/2 -> infinity.

Here b_m*d_m is a positive constant times (log m)^(1/4), which dominates log(x_m)=O(log log m). Since Var(N_m)<=mu_m, Chebyshev gives N_m->infinity in probability. On the high-probability maximum event, each of these N_m coordinates is within 2*d_m of max Z, hence within delta_m of M_m. Thus K_m>=N_m with probability tending to one.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:1deb4aa843187c9d450435c7fc0c1afa910014777011d895e2234fe041a99ea0","revision_digest":"sha256:fe420d9fc175ada9a72336a114086a30af388936503c5c1ef368ae6195b38abd","source_id":"owner-work:w335:c0127-common-factor-peaks","source_revision":"author-checked-20261010-pending-independent-w347","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body:
[Lem 60 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] The set $\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,1)$, as defined by \eqref{e:sM.Lip.q0}, is a singleton set consisting of the standard gaussian measure:
$\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,1)=\{\cN(0,1)\}$.
\begin{proof}
    Consider any $\mu \in \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,1)$. By the definition \eqref{e:sM.Lip.q0}, this means that for any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $L>0$ and a sequence of $L$-Lipschitz algorithms $(\cA_{N_j})_{j\ge 1}$ such that
    \begin{align*}
        &\WERR(\cA_{N_j}, \mu)
        =\max\bigg\{
            \bbW_2\Big( \mu(\cA_{N_j}), \mu \Big),
            \bbW_2\Big(\mu^{\Ising}(\cA_{N_j}), \cP(\{\pm 1\}) \Big)
        \bigg\} \le \epsilon\,, \\
        &q_0(j) \equiv \chi_{\cA_{N_j}}(0) 
        = \frac{\|\bbE \bsig_j\|_2^2}{N_j} 
        \stackrel{j\to\infty}{\longrightarrow} 1
        \,,
    \end{align*}
where we abbreviate $\bsig_j\equiv \cA_{N_j}(\bG,\bg^\aux)$. 
    Define the perturbed (deterministic) algorithm $\tilde\cA_{N_j}$ by setting 
    \[
        \tilde{\bsig}_j
        \equiv \tilde\cA_{N_j}(\bG,\bg^\aux) 
        = \frac{\bbE\bsig_j}{q_0(j)^{1/2}} \,.
    \]
This clearly satisfies $\bbE[\|\tilde{\bsig}_j\|_2^2]  = N_j$, so $\tilde\cA_{N_j}$ is a $0$-Lipschitz algorithm in the sense of Definition~\ref{d:Lip}.
Since $\tilde{\bsig}_j$ is a deterministic vector in $N_j$ dimensions of norm $(N_j)^{1/2}$, we have $\mu(\tilde \cA_{N_j}) = \cN(0,1)$.
    Note that
    \begin{align*}
        \frac{\bbE[
            \|\bsig_j - \tilde{\bsig}_j\|^2]}{N_j} 
        &= \frac{1}{N_j} \bbE\bigg[ \bigg\|
            \bigg(\frac{1}{q_0(j)^{1/2}} - 1 \bigg) 
            	(\bbE\bsig_j)
            - (\bsig_j - \bbE\bsig_j)
        \bigg\|^2 \bigg] \\
        &= \Big(1 - q_0(j)^{1/2}\Big)^2 + \Big(1 - q_0(j)\Big)
        \le 2\Big(1-q_0(j)\Big)\,,
    \end{align*}  
again using that inequality $|x^{1/2}-y^{1/2}| \le |x-y|^{1/2}$ for $x,y\ge0$.
    Then, by Lemma~\ref{l:control.problems.approx}, with constants $c_0$, $C_1(\alpha)$, $C_2(\alpha,L)$ as defined therein, we have
    \[
        \bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_{N_j}),
        	\mu(\tilde \cA_{N_j}) = \cN(0,1) 
	\Big)
        \le \bigg\{
        C_1(\alpha) 2(1-q_0(j)) + C_2(\alpha,L) e^{-c_0N_j} \bigg\}^{1/2}\,.
    \]
Combined with the assumption that $\bbW_2(\mu(\cA_{N_j}), \mu) \le \epsilon$ for all $j$, we find $\bbW_2(\mu,\cN(0,1)) \le \epsilon$.
    Since this holds for all $\epsilon > 0$, we conclude $\mu = \cN(0,1)$.
    We have thus shown $\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,1) \subseteq \{\cN(0,1)\}$.
    The reverse inclusion $\cN(0,1) \in \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,1)$ is witnessed by the (sequence of) deterministic algorithms
    \[
        \cA_N(\bG,\bg^{\aux}) = (1,\ldots,1) \in \bbR^N\,, 
    \]
    which are $0$-Lipschitz with $\mu(\cA_N) = \cN(0,1)$, $\mu^{\Ising}(\cA_N) = \delta_1 \in \cP(\{\pm 1\})$, and $\chi_{\cA_N}(0) = 1$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 60 of arXiv:2608.29416

[Prop 4 of arXiv:2506.17979, '\large\bf A remark on subharmonicity for symmetric Dirichlet forms'] Let $L(x,{\d} y)$ be a kernel on $E\times\mathscr{B}(E)$. Suppose that the jumping measure $J$ satisfies $J({\d} x{\d} y)\leq D_2L(x,{\d} y)\m({\d} x)$ for some $D_2>0$.
Let ${\sf d}$ be a distance function on $E$ consistent with the given topology. Assume that there exists $\beta\in]0,+\infty[$ such that 
\begin{align*}
M_{\beta}:={\m}\text{\rm-ess-sup}_{x\in E}\int_E(1\land {\sf d}(x,y)^{\beta})L(x,{\d} y)<\infty.
\end{align*} 
Then, for $p\in[1,+\infty]$, {\rm(}resp.~$p\in[2,+\infty]${\rm)}, 
we have 
 $D(\mathscr{E})_{\loc}\cap L^p(E;{\m})\subset D(\mathscr{E})_{\loc}^{\diamond}$ 
and $D(\mathscr{E})_{e,\loc}\cap L^p(E;{\m})\subset D(\mathscr{E})_{e,\loc}^{\diamond}$ {\rm(}resp.~$D(\mathscr{E})_{\loc}\cap L^p(E;{\m})\subset D(\mathscr{E})_{\loc}^{\dag}$ 
and $D(\mathscr{E})_{e,\loc}\cap L^p(E;{\m})\subset D(\mathscr{E})_{e,\loc}^{\dag}${\rm)}.

For a continuous curve gamma:[0,1]->C and r>=0,q>0, E(r,q) is the event that there exist s<t with |gamma(s)-gamma(t)|<=r and diameter(gamma([s,t]))>=q. A nonconstant self-return is equality gamma(s)=gamma(t) with a positive-diameter intervening subcurve. Constant waiting intervals are not nonconstant self-returns.
gamma is continuous on the compact interval [0,1]

body: [Lemma lem:gff_independence_across_scales of arXiv:2507.15589, 'Tightness of approximations to metrics on non-simple conformal loop ensemble gaskets'] Suppose that $h$ is a GFF on $D$ with some bounded boundary values.  For every $b>0$ and $q \in (0,1)$ there exists $M > 0$ so that the following is true. [Theorem thm:relu_samples of arXiv:2512.04371, 'Constructive Approximation under Carleman's Condition, \\ with Applications to Smoothed An'] Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and $\delta\in(0,1)$. 
Let $\ell(y,y') = (y-y')^2$ be the quadratic loss function.
Suppose that the $y$-marginal of $\mu$ has a finite fourth moment, i.e., $\EE[|y|^4] <\infty$. 
Then there exists an algorithm that agnostically learns $\cH_\mathsf{ReLU}$ with accuracy $\varepsilon$ and confidence $1-\delta$ using i.i.d. samples of size 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \(\tilde{O}\left(\varepsilon^{-3} d^{O((1/\varepsilon)^r)} \log(1/\delta)\right)\) under \(r\)-strictly sub-exponential input $\mu_x$;
    \item \(\tilde{O}\left(\varepsilon^{-3} d^{O(\exp{O(\varepsilon^{-1})})} \log(1/\delta)\right)\) under sub-exponential input $\mu_x$. lip
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition def:random_length_worms_model of arXiv:2505.07145, 'Nonamenable Poisson zoo'] Let us consider a probability mass function $\eta: \mathbb{N}_{>0} \to [0,1] $ and an $\mathbb{N}_{>0}$-valued random variable $\mathcal{L}$ satisfying $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{L}=\ell)=\eta(\ell), \, \ell \in \mathbb{N}_{>0}$. 
	We call the distribution of $\mathcal{L}$ the length distribution of the worms. Let us also consider a nearest neighbour simple random walk $(X(t))_{t \in \mathbb{N}}$ on the vertices of $G$ starting from $X(0)=o$, independent of $\mathcal{L}$.
	Let us define the probability measure $\nu^{\text{worm;}{\eta}}$ on $\mathcal{H}_{o}$ by 
	\begin{equation}
		
		\nu^{\text{worm;}{\eta}}(H) := P_{o}( \{ X(0), X(1), \ldots, X(\mathcal{L} - 1) \} = H )
	\end{equation}
	for each $H \in \mathcal{H}_{o}$.
	Given any $\lambda >0$, the Poisson zoo $\mathcal{N}_{\eta}^{\lambda} := \mathcal{N}_{\nu^{\text{worm;}{\eta}}}^{\lambda}$ built upon this measure via Definition (def:poisson_zoo of the paper) is called the random length worms model at level $\lambda$, and the corresponding random set $\mathcal{S}_{\eta}^\lambda := \mathcal{S}_{\nu^{\text{worm;}{\eta}}}^\lambda$ is the random length worms set at level $\lambda$.

body:
[Definition def:RBGshell of arXiv:2510.13733, 'Internal Diffusion Limited Aggregation \\ with Critical Branching Random Walks'] Fix an initial (integer) radius $R_0$ and
an initial particle configuration $\eta_0$ with support on 
 $\partial B_{ R_0}$.
Let $N_0 := \sum_{x \in \mathbb{Z}^d} \eta_0(x)$ be the total number of particles at time zero. 
At each step $t \in \mathbb{Z}_+$,
given the step $t-1$, 
we set
$
R_t := R_{t-1} +   H_t,$
where 
\begin{equation}
H_{t}   : = \Big   \lceil  \,     \Big(  \kappa \,  N_{t-1}  \,   \big( \log (N_{t-1} + 1) \big)^{\beta}  \Big )^{ \frac{1}{d}}  \, \Big \rceil
\end{equation}
with $\beta= 1$ if $d=3$ and $\beta=0$ if $d > 3$. Here $\kappa>0$  is a large enough constant depending only on the dimension.
We start a RBG with radii $R_{t-1}$ and $R_t$ from the  particle configuration 
$\eta_{t-1}$ 
(which has support in $\partial B_{R_{t-1}})$
and let $\eta_t$ be the escaping particle configuration of such process 
(which has  support
in $\partial B_{R_t}$,  recall Definition (def:RBG of the paper)).
We then move to the next step $t+1$ and repeat the procedure. 
Define for any $\alpha >0$ the  stopping time (with the convention that $\inf \emptyset = + \infty$)
\begin{align}

T^{(\alpha)} & : = \inf \{ t  \geq 0  \, : \, N_t  > \alpha  N_0  \} . 
\end{align}
title: \textit{Random Barrier Growth through shells}

[Lemma 5 of arXiv:2607.17192, 'Geometric Regime--Switching Diffusions on Stratified Riemannian Spaces with an Application'] For
		\(f=(f_\alpha)_{\alpha\in I}\in C_0(\widetilde E)\), define
		\(
		(\widetilde P_t f)|_{S_\alpha}
		:=
		P_t^\alpha(f_\alpha).
		\)
		Then \((\widetilde P_t)_{t\geq0}: C_0(\widetilde E) \to C_0(\widetilde E)\) is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup.
		Its generator \(\widetilde L\) is given by
		\(
		\widetilde L f|_{S_\alpha}
		=
		L_\alpha(f_\alpha),
		\)
		with domain
		\[
		D(\widetilde L)
		=
		\left\{
		f\in C_0(\widetilde E):
		f_\alpha\in D( L_\alpha)\ \forall\alpha,
		\quad
		\bigl(L_\alpha f_\alpha\bigr)_\alpha
		\in C_0(\widetilde E)
		\right\}.
		\]
		Moreover, \(\cl D_0\) is a core for \(\widetilde L\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let M(X) be the essential supremum of the density of X (M = infinity if there is no bounded density). (Thm 1) For independent random vectors X_1,...,X_n in R^d: M(X_1+...+X_n)^{-2/d} >= (1/e) sum_k M(X_k)^{-2/d}. (Cor 2) If M(X_k) <= M for all k and sum a_k^2 = 1, then M(sum a_kX_k) <= e^{d/2} M. (Closing remark, from Rogozin's theorem and Ball's cube slicing) For real X_k: M(S_n)^{-2} >= (1/2) sum_k M(X_k)^{-2}, and 1/2 is best possible (two independent uniforms on intervals of equal length give equality). 1/e is the dimension-free constant; for fixed d >= 2 the sharp constant is Gamma(1+d/2)^{2/d}/(1+d/2) (Madiman-Melbourne-Xu), which decreases to 1/e as d -> infinity.

Assumes: independence; random vectors in R^d (Thm 1, Cor 2); real variables (the 1/2 remark)

body:
Author-proved reduction awaiting independent review. In a proper strictly positive weighted graph, if a bigeodesic gamma uses an edge e of weight t_e, replacing only that weight by s in (0,t_e) preserves the entire bigeodesic. A finite straddling segment decreases by Delta=t_e-s; a simple competitor decreases by either Delta if it uses e or zero if it avoids e. Thus every e-avoiding competitor has new excess cost at least Delta. A subsegment on one side stays minimizing because it sits inside a minimizing straddling segment. In iid nonatomic positive FPP, positive probability of a bigeodesic through e implies positive probability of such a uniformly pinned bigeodesic under the same iid law: choose a<b<c with F(b)>0 and P(A_e,t_e>=c)>0, where a is the essential infimum, then independently resample s with law F. The event has probability F(b)*P(A_e,t_e>=c)>0 and penalty at least c-b. This multiplication uses exactly the fresh independent coordinate. No planar exclusion of these pinned paths is proved.
proper strictly positive metric for deterministic preservation
iid positive nonatomic finite edge law for the probability reduction

body: [Lemma 52 of arXiv:2608.27630, 'Oriented planar maps and \\ annular mating of trees'] Let $\beta_1,\beta_2<Q$ and $\beta_3\in(-\infty,Q)\cup\{Q^-\}$. body: In mathematics, the Borel sets of a topological space are a particular class of "well-behaved" subsets of that space. Which sets are Borel can be specified in a number of equivalent ways. Borel sets are named after Émile Borel.

Own-work draft; proof (unaudited); D0007-C004 v1; audits w668:PASS. Every probability law F with bounded support, absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, and symmetric about its mean is n-completely mixable for all sufficiently large n. No density floor or unimodality is assumed. A positive-measure density level set A on the positive half-line supplies a bounded odd-order zero-sum reserve by convolving differences until they reach A; global sign and coordinate permutation give a symmetric dominated marginal. The residual is symmetric and pairs, so the odd-order reserve lemma applies. The threshold depends on F; the nonsymmetric case is not resolved.
F absolutely continuous
F has bounded support
F symmetric about its mean

Status: proof (unaudited). Special case of D0007; novelty not yet cleared.

Statement. Let F be an absolutely continuous probability law with bounded support, symmetric about its mean mu. Then there is a finite N(F) such that F is n-CM for every integer n>=N(F). No pointwise lower bound on its density, no support interval without gaps, and no unimodality are assumed.

We will construct one odd-order symmetric reserve H with bounded density dominated by a positive multiple of f, and apply D0007-C002. The main open piece of D0007 is the nonsymmetric case, for which the residual-pair argument is unavailable.

1. Normalize mu=0. Write f for a symmetric version of the density, so f(-x)=f(x) almost everywhere. Choose M>0 bounding the support. Since F is absolutely continuous, it has no atom at zero and its mass in (0,M] is 1/2. There are eps>0 and a measurable set A subset (0,M] of positive Lebesgue measure a such that f(x)>=eps almost everywhere on A and also on -A. For example some level set {x in (0,M]:f(x)>=1/j} has positive measure, since the union of these sets carries all positive-half mass. Put u(x)=1_A(x)/a. This is a bounded probability density.

2. Let v=u*tilde(u), with tilde(u)(x)=u(-x). It is the density of Y-Y' for independent Y,Y' with density u. It is continuous and v(0)=1/a>0. To justify continuity directly, v(t)=|A intersect (A+t)|/a^2, and the absolute difference of v(t) and v(s) is bounded by ||1_A(.-t)-1_A(.-s)||_1/a^2. Translations are continuous in L1 for every finite-measure measurable set: approximate 1_A in L1 by finite linear combinations of bounded-interval indicators, whose translation continuity follows from the interval symmetric-difference bound, and use the triangle inequality. Thus choose delta>0 and c>0 with v(t)>=c for |t|<=delta.

3. Choose an integer k>=1 with k delta>M. The k-fold convolution v^{*k} is strictly positive at every t in (-k delta,k delta). Indeed v>=c 1_{[-delta,delta]}, so v^{*k}>=c^k (1_{[-delta,delta]})^{*k}; the latter is strictly positive in that open interval. For k>=2 this follows by integrating over a small open neighborhood of the first k-1 coordinates equal to t/k, leaving the last also within (-delta,delta); k=1 is immediate. Consequently

    Z=integral_A u(y) v^{*k}(y) dy

is positive. It is finite since every convolution density here is bounded above by ||u||_infinity=1/a.

4. An exact zero-sum probability vector. Draw a vector (Y_1,...,Y_{2k}) with joint density

    [ product_{i=1}^{2k} u(y_i) ] u(s(y)) / Z,
    s(y)=sum_{i=1}^k y_i - sum_{i=k+1}^{2k} y_i.

It integrates to one because s under the unweighted product law has density v^{*k}, and E[u(s)]=Z. Set Y_0=s(Y). The weight u(s) forces Y_0 in A, while all Y_i are in A almost surely. Form the odd vector W of length m=2k+1 with entries

    (Y_1,...,Y_k, -Y_{k+1},...,-Y_{2k}, -Y_0).

Its sum is exactly zero.

    h(x)<=1/(2a^2 Z) almost everywhere on A union -A.

The factor 1/2 follows because A and -A are disjoint, and each globally randomized coordinate is a symmetric magnitude law with density q_i(|x|)/2. Averaging over coordinates preserves the bound. Hence H is symmetric and m-CM.

7. Set p=min(1/2,eps*a^2*Z)>0. Then p h<=eps/2<=f on A union -A, and p h=0 elsewhere. The residual density g=(f-ph)/(1-p) is a symmetric probability density with bounded support. Apply D0007-C002: F is n-CM for all even n and for every odd n with n>=m and np>=m. Thus N(F)=ceil(m/p) is a valid finite threshold. Translate all coordinates back by mu.

[Lemma 13 (Robust separated batch) of arXiv:2608.16701, 'Order-Sensitive Fast-Synapse Limits in Sparse Excitatory--Inhibitory Threshold--Reset Netw'] Suppose that for some $\eta>0$,
\begin{equation}
 \min\{\theta-x,\ x+a-\theta,\ \theta-(x+a-b)\}\ge\eta.
 
\end{equation}
Use the separated supports above, but let the actual initial left voltage
and aggregate input magnitudes be $x'$, $A\ge0$, and $B\ge0$.  Suppose that
under both orderings the continuous drift rate before a first hit has
magnitude at most $L_{\rm dr}$ and that
\begin{equation}
 |x'-x|+|A-a|+|B-b|+4L_{\rm dr}\varepsilon<\eta,
 \qquad 4\varepsilon<\rho.
 
\end{equation}
Then the target fires exactly once in the excitatory-first system and does
not fire in the inhibitory-first system on $[0,4\varepsilon]$.

[Definition Agnostic learning of arXiv:2512.04371, 'Constructive Approximation under Carleman's Condition, \\ with Applications to Smoothed An'] Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and $\delta\in (0,1)$. 
Let $\ell:\RR\times\RR\to \RR^+$ be a loss function.
Suppose that $\mu$ is a distribution over $\RR^d \times \RR$ and $\cH$ is a hypothesis class where each element $h\in \cH$ is a function from $\RR^d$ to $\RR$.  
And let $\cD = \{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i\in [n]}$ be a dataset with i.i.d. samples drawn from $\mu$. 
We say that an algorithm $\cA$ that takes $\cD$ as input and outputs a hypothesis $f:\RR^d\to \RR$ learns $\cH$ agnostically, if with probability at least $1-\delta$ over the draw of $\cD$, it holds that
\begin{align}
    \EE_{\mu}\big[\ell(y,h(x))\big] &\le \mathrm{opt}_{\cH} + \varepsilon, \text{ where } \mathrm{opt}_{\cH} = \inf_{f\in \cH} \EE_{\mu}\big[\ell(y,f(x))\big].  
\end{align}
title: Agnostic learning

[Prop eqn:qg of arXiv:2411.11415, 'The ballistic limit of the log-Sobolev constant equals the Polyak--\L{}ojasiewicz constant'] Suppose $h \in C^2(\R^d)$
with $h_\star  \deq  \inf_{x \in \R^d} h(x) > -\infty$,
and such that $C_{\msf{PL}}(h) < \infty$.
Let $S$ denote the set of minimizers of $f$.
Then, for all $x\in\R^d$,
\begin{equation}
   \frac{1}{2C_{\msf{PL}}(h)}\,d(x, S)^2 \leqslant h(x) - h_\star\,,
\end{equation}
where $d(x, S)  \deq  \inf_{y \in S} \|x - y\|$ is defined
as usual. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition of arXiv:2604.08462, 'Convergence of $k$-point functions in\\ high dimensional percolation'] For every $\omega\in \Gamma(x_0,\ldots,x_k)$, the connectivity tree $T(\omega)$ is a directed tree with leaves in the set $\{x_0,\ldots,x_k\}$. $T$ is also a tree when viewed as an undirected graph.
    \begin{proof}
    By construction, every vertex in $T$ except $x_0$ has a unique parent, so $\# E(T)=\#V(T)-1$ which implies that $T$ is a tree. Starting at any vertex of $v$ and applying the parent operation repeatedly, we obtain a path in $T$ ending at $x_0$. Since $m_{ij}$ appears on any path from $x_i$, only the vertices $x_j$, $0\le j\le k$ can have 0 children.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 57 (Sharp quadratic phase diagram on polynomial-growth groups) of arXiv:2607.16724, 'Algebraic Transfer for Operator-Valued Gaussian Chaoses: Oriented Schatten Profiles and Si'] Let $\Gamma$ be an infinite finitely generated group of polynomial growth
degree $D$.  Fix $1\le r<\infty$, $a,b\ge0$,
$0<\sigma\le D/2$, and $c_x=\langle x\rangle^{-\sigma}$.
Then $(T_{2,N}^{a,b}(c))_N$ is Cauchy in
$L^2(\Omega;\Sch_r)$ if and only if
\begin{equation}

 \frac D4<\sigma\le\frac D2
\end{equation}
and, with $\beta=D-2\sigma$,
\begin{equation}

 a>\beta,\qquad b>\beta,\qquad
 a+b>\beta+\frac Dr.
\end{equation}
Whenever these conditions hold, all the $L^p$-convergence, deviation,
almost-sure convergence, and quantitative cutoff-rate conclusions of
Theorem~\ref{thm:second-order-singular-transfer} hold.  At the logarithmic
endpoint $\sigma=D/2$, the three conditions become
\[
 a>0,\qquad b>0,\qquad a+b>\frac Dr.
\]
If $\sigma\le D/4$, no choice of $a,b\ge0$ yields
$L^2(\Omega;\Sch_r)$ convergence.

body:
[Defn Schottky double of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] Let $\Omega \subsetneq \mathbb{C}$ be a simply connected domain in $\mathbb{C}$ with $\Gamma=\partial \Omega$ consisting of prime ends. Take copy $\tilde{\Omega}$ of $\Omega$ and weld $\Omega$ and $\tilde{\Omega}$ together along $\Gamma$ so that a compact topological surface $\Omega^{Double}=\Omega \cup \Gamma \cup \tilde{\Omega}$ is obtained. If $z \in \Omega$ let $\tilde{z}$ denote the corresponding point on $\tilde{\Omega}$. Then an involution $j$ on $\Omega^{Double}$ is defined by
$$
\begin{array}{ll}
j(z)=\tilde{z} & \text { and } \\
j(\tilde{z})=z & \text { for } z \in \Omega, \\
j(z)=z & \text { for } z \in \Gamma .
\end{array}
$$

The conformal structure on $\tilde{\Omega}$ will be the opposite to that on $\Omega$, which means that the function $\tilde{z} \mapsto \overline{z}$ serves as a local variable on $\tilde{\Omega}$, and $j$ becomes anti-analytic. 

For $p\in \partial \Omega$, let $\phi:U\subset \overline{\Omega} \rightarrow \phi(U)$ be a local boundary chart at $p$, 
let $\tilde{U}$ be the corresponding subset in $\tilde{\Omega}$, 
then $\tilde{\phi}:\tilde{U} \subset \tilde{\Omega} \rightarrow \overline{\phi}(\tilde{U})$ is a local chart at $\tilde{p}$.
Then we can define a local chart $\tau$ for $\Omega^{Double}$ at boundary point $p$ by 
$$ \tau(z)=\left\{
\begin{aligned}
&\phi(z), z \in U \\
& \overline{\phi(z)}, z \in \tilde{U}.
\end{aligned}
\right.
$$

Thus, the conformal structure on $\Omega^{Double}$, inherited from $\mathbb{C}$, extends in a natural way across $\Gamma$ to a conformal structure on all of $\Omega^{Double}$. This makes $\Omega^{Double}$ into a symmetric Riemann sphere.

For example, we identify $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ with the Schottky double of $\mathbb{H}$ or that of $\mathbb{D}$. Then the corresponding involution $j$ is $j_{\mathbb{H}}: z \mapsto z^*=\bar{z}$ for $\Omega=\mathbb{H}$ and $j_{\mathbb{D}}: z \mapsto z^*=1 / \bar{z}$ for $\Omega=\mathbb{D}$.
title: Schottky double

[Theorem HALFGODHALFSOUVLAKI of arXiv:2412.09290, 'Asymptotics of Harish-Chandra transform and infinitesimal freeness'] Let $A$ be a random Hermitian matrix of size $N$
  and $0 < \theta < 1$. Assume that for every finite $r$ one has
  \begin{equation}
    \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{N^{\theta}} \log \mathbb{E} [H
    \text{} C (x_1, \ldots, x_r, 0^{N - r} ; \lambda_1 (A), \ldots, \lambda_N
    (A))] = \sum_{i = 1}^r \Psi (x_i), 
  \end{equation}
  where $\Psi$ is a smooth function in a complex neighborhood of $0$ and the above
  convergence is uniform in a complex neighborhood of $0^r$. Then, for every $k \in
  \mathbb{N}$, the $k$-th moment of the random measure $N^{- \theta} \sum_{i =
  1}^N \delta \left( N^{- 1} \lambda_i (A) \right)$ converges, as $N \rightarrow \infty$, in
  probability to $\Psi^{(k)} (0) / (k - 1) !$.
title: Theorem HALFGODHALFSOUVLAKI of arXiv:2412.09290

[Thm 5 (Crandall--Rabinowitz) of arXiv:2608.30796, 'Tumor boundary instability induced by pressure feedback'] Let \(W\) and \(Z\) be real Banach spaces, and let
\(\mathcal F:W\times\mathbb R\to Z\) be a \(C^k\) mapping,
\(k\geq3\), in a neighborhood of \((0,\mu_0)\). Assume that
\begin{enumerate}
\item \(\mathcal F(0,\mu)=0\) for \(\mu\) near \(\mu_0\);
\item
\(\ker \mathcal F_w(0,\mu_0)=\operatorname{span}\{w_0\}\);
\item \(\operatorname{Range}\mathcal F_w(0,\mu_0)\) is closed and has
codimension one in \(Z\);
\item
\(\mathcal F_{w\mu}(0,\mu_0)w_0\notin
\operatorname{Range}\mathcal F_w(0,\mu_0)\).
\end{enumerate}
Then the nontrivial solutions of \(\mathcal F(w,\mu)=0\) near
\((0,\mu_0)\), together with the bifurcation point, form a
\(C^{k-2}\) curve \((w(\epsilon),\mu(\epsilon))\) satisfying
\[
w(\epsilon)=\epsilon w_0+o(\epsilon),
\qquad
\mu(0)=\mu_0.
\]
Locally, every solution lies either on this curve or on the trivial
branch \((0,\mu)\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Crandall--Rabinowitz

[Theorem 49 of arXiv:2608.09700, 'A general paracontrolled ansatz for singular SPDEs'] Suppose that $\mcZ=(Z_\tau)$ is an admissible collection of stochastic fields and that $u$ can be be developed in the paracontrolled system up associated with \eqref{eq_gPAM} to order $\gamma$,.
For any smooth function $h$ depending on $v_* = (\partial^k_{*} u)_{k \in A}$ where $A$ is a finite subset of $\N^{d+1}$ such that $r_h<\gamma$ with $r_h =\sup \{ |k|,k\in A\} $, one has 
			$$
			h(v_*) = \sum_{n\geq 0}\sum_{\substack{\tau=  X^r \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mcI^+_{a_i}(\tau_i)^{\beta_i}\in\mcT^+ \\ |\tau|<\gamma-r_h}} \frac{1}{ r!}\P\Big( \partial^r \prod_{i=1}^n D_{a_i}^{\beta_i} h(v_*) \prod_{j=1}^{n} \frac{u_{\tau_j}^{\beta_j}}{\beta_j!} \, ,Z_\tau\Big)  + h(v)^\#,
			$$
			where the $ \mathcal{I}_{a_i}(\tau_i) $ are pairwise disjoint. One has $h(v)^\#\in C^{\gamma-r_h}$, and that $\bm{u}\in\mcD^\gamma_\P(\mcZ) \mapsto h(v_*)^\#\in C^{\gamma-r_h}$ is local Lipschitz.

[Lem 4 of arXiv:2605.07369, '2605.07369'] Let $\beta_{k}^n(c):=\prod_{j=k}^n \left(1+\frac{c}{j+1}\right)$, where $c<0$. We have
\begin{enumerate}[$(i)$]
\item For any $n\ge 1$ and $\left(-2c-1 \right)\vee 1 \le k\le n$, we have
\beq
\exp\left(-\frac{c^2}{\left(-2c-1 \right)\vee 1}\right) \left(\frac{n+1}{k}\right)^c\le \beta_{k}^n(c)\le\left(\frac{n}{k+1}\right)^c.
\deq

\item For $c<-1/2$, we have
\beq
\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \frac{\left(\sum_{k=0}^n (k+1)^{-2} \left(\beta_{k}^n(c)\right)^2\right)^{-1}}{(-2c-1)n}=1.
\deq

\end{enumerate}

[Lemma 5 (See \cite{Marcus2021,Marcus-Spielman-Srivastava2022,Arizmendi-Perales2018}) of arXiv:2506.08910, 'Critical points of random polynomials and finite free cumulants'] Let $p$ and $q$ be degree $N$ polynomials, and let $P$ and $Q$ be formal power series such that $P\left(\frac{\dd}{\dd x}\right)x^{N}=p(x)$ and $Q\left(\frac{\dd}{\dd x}\right)x^{N}=q(x)$. Then,     $p\boxplus_{N}q(x)=P\left(\frac{\dd}{\dd x}\right)Q\left(\frac{\dd}{\dd x}\right)x^N$.
     Moreover, the coefficients of $R_{p}$ are the finite free cumulants of $p$, i.e.\ \begin{equation}
        R_{p}(s)=\kappa_{1}^{N}(p)+\kappa_{2}^{N}(p)s+\cdots+\kappa_{N}^{N}(p)s^{N-1}.
    \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 31 (Filtered and strict response) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] A linear map $\mathcal R:M^*\to\mathcal Y$ is \emph{filtered} if
\[
 \mathcal R(\mathscr D_rM^*)\subseteq K_r\mathcal Y
 \quad\text{for every }r.
\]
It is \emph{strict} if
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal R^{-1}(K_r\mathcal Y)=\mathscr D_rM^*,
 \qquad -1\le r\le d.
 
\end{equation}
A filtered map induces
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{gr}_r\mathcal R:
 G_r^*\longrightarrow\partial_r\mathcal Y.
 
\end{equation}

body: [Lemma prop:bounded_cle_crossings of arXiv:2609.04140, 'The conformally invariant metric on $\CLE_4$ III:\\ uniqueness'] Let $\overline{\Gamma}$ be a nested $\CLE_4$ on $\BD$, let $F \subseteq \BD$ be a compact set,  and set $d \defeq \dist(F ,  \partial \BD)>0$.  Then,  there exists a universal constant $b_0 \in (0,1)$ such that the following is true.  For each $\epsilon \in (0,1)$,  there exists $\delta \in (0,1)$ depending only on $\epsilon$ and $d$ such that for all $z \in F$ and all $0 < r_1 < r_2 < d/2$ with $r_1 / r_2 \leq \delta$,  the probability that there are at least four crossings of $B_{r_2}(z) \setminus \overline{B_{r_1}(z)}$ made by loops in $\overline{\Gamma}$ is at most $(r_1 / r_2)^{2 - \epsilon}$.  Also,  the probability that there are more than four crossings of $B_{r_2}(z) \setminus \overline{B_{r_1}(z)}$ made by loops in $\overline{\Gamma}$ is at most $(r_1 / r_2)^{2 + b_0}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Corollary 34 of arXiv:2609.01826, 'An extension theory for fully fractional Schr\"odinger equations with memory'] The oscillatory Poisson lifting
$\mathcal P_s:\Sm\to L_a^2(\RN)$ extends uniquely to an isometry
\[
\mathcal P_s:\mathcal H^s\longrightarrow L_a^2(\RN).
\]
Indeed, if $u_0^{(k)}\to u_0$ in $\mathcal H^s$, then
$\mathcal P_su_0^{(k)}$ is Cauchy in $L_a^2(\RN)$ by Theorem~\ref{T:history}; its limit
is independent of the approximating sequence and satisfies
\[
\|\mathcal P_su_0\|_{L_a^2(\RN)}=\|u_0\|_{\mathcal H^s}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Theorem 6 of arXiv:2607.18201, 'Finding Adam in noisy trees'] Fix $\varepsilon>0$, and assume that $n$ is even. Let $G$ be a uniformly sampled perfect matching on the complete graph on $[n]$, independent of $\cT_n$. Then, observing the unlabeled graph $\cT_n(G)$, it is possible to construct a confidence set $K(\varepsilon)$, such that $\Prob{1\in K(\varepsilon)}\geq 1-\varepsilon$. body:
Let G be a finite group and let p be a prime dividing the order |G|. Then G contains an element of order exactly p; equivalently, G has a subgroup of order p. The number of such elements is a multiple of p - 1, and the number of subgroups of order p is congruent to 1 modulo p.
G finite
p prime with p | |G|

[Theorem thm:full HOMFLY complex of arXiv:2608.29986, 'Khovanov-Rozansky homology over $\F[U,V]$'] Let $K \subset S^3$ be a knot. There is a $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \oplus\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \oplus\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} $-graded finitely generated free chain complex $(\mathit{CH}(K), \partial)$ over $\ensuremath{\mathbb{F}} [U,V]$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
    \item the isomorphism type of $\mathit{CH}(K)$ is a knot invariant, and
    \item $H_*(\mathit{CH}(K) \otimes_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{F}} [U,V]} \ensuremath{\mathbb{F}} ) \cong \widehat{\mathit{H}}(K)$ as $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \oplus\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \oplus\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} $-graded vector spaces where $\widehat{\mathit{H}}(K)$ denotes the reduced Khovanov-Rozansky homology.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Then

Let alpha > 0. A random variable X is called sub-Weibull with parameter alpha (denoted Sub-Weibull(alpha)) if its Orlicz norm with Young function psi_alpha(x) = exp(x^alpha) - 1 is finite: ||X||_{psi_alpha} = inf { c > 0 : E[exp(|X| / c)^alpha] <= 2 } < infinity. Sub-Weibull(2) corresponds to sub-Gaussian, and Sub-Weibull(1) corresponds to sub-exponential.

body:
[Lemma 13 of arXiv:2607.10102, 'Dynamical mean-field limit and replica-symmetric free energy for the orthogonally-invarian'] Suppose Assumptions \ref{assump:X} and \ref{assump:dynamics} hold with $f=-U'$,
the lower bound $\alpha>0$ in \eqref{eq:Uconvexity} satisfies
$\alpha>\Lambda_{\max}$, and Assumption \ref{assump:convergence} holds. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item The Gibbs measure $\mu_\Gibbs$ is well-defined, and there exist deterministic almost sure limits
\begin{equation}
v_*=\lim_{n \to \infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle \|\btheta\|_2^2 \rangle,
\qquad q_*=\lim_{n \to \infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle \btheta^\top \btheta' \rangle.
\end{equation}
\item For each fixed $\tau \in \R$, there exists a limit
$c_\theta(\tau)=\lim_{s \to \infty} C_\theta(s+\tau,s)$. This defines a
symmetric positive-semidefinite function
$c_\theta:\R \to \R$ satisfying, for some $C,c>0$ and
all $s,t \geq 0$ and $\tau \in \R$,
\begin{equation}
\begin{gathered}
c_\theta(0)=v_*, \qquad \lim_{\tau \to \infty} c_\theta(\tau)=q_*,\\
|C_\theta(t,s)-c_\theta(t-s)|\leq Ce^{-c\min(s,t)},
\qquad |c_\theta(\tau)-q_*| \leq Ce^{-c|\tau|}.
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}
\item For each fixed $\tau \geq 0$, there exists a limit
$r_\theta(\tau)=\lim_{s \to \infty} R_\theta(s+\tau,s)$. This defines a
function $r_\theta:[0,\infty) \to \R$ satisfying, for some $C,c>0$
and all $t \geq s \geq 0$ and $\tau \geq 0$,
\begin{equation}
\begin{gathered}
|R_\theta(t,s)| \leq Ce^{-c(t-s)}, \qquad
|r_\theta(\tau)| \leq Ce^{-c\tau},\\
|R_\theta(t,s)-r_\theta(t-s)| \leq Ce^{-cs}, \qquad
\int_0^t |R_\theta(t,s)-r_\theta(t-s)| \d s \leq Ce^{-ct}.
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}
\item $c_\theta$ is continuous on $\R$, smooth on $(0,\infty)$,
and has a right derivative $c_\theta'(0^+)=\lim_{\tau \to 0^+} c_\theta'(\tau)$
at $\tau=0$. We have the fluctuation-dissipation relation
\begin{equation}
r_\theta(\tau)={-}c_\theta'(\tau) \text{ for } \tau>0,
\qquad r_\theta(0)={-}c_\theta'(0^+)=1.
\end{equation}
Furthermore, for all $\tau>0$, we have
\[c_\theta(\tau) \geq 0,
\qquad r_\theta(\tau) \geq 0, \qquad r_\theta'(\tau) \leq 0.\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 13 of arXiv:2607.10102
