body:
[Proposition t.randomfieldCLT-new of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Let $M=\{M(x)\}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}$ be a random field in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with values in a Polish space
$\mathbb {M} $ and $\zeta: \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb {M}  \to \mathbb{R}$ a  measurable function. 
Let $\mathcal{P}$ be a simple point process on $\mathbb{R}^d $,
independent of the random field $M$. 
Consider empirical random measures $(\hat{\sigma}_{n}^{\zeta(M)})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ as in (equation linearstatBsigma of the paper).
\begin{enumerate}[wide,label=(\roman*),labelindent=0pt]
\item 
Assume that $\mathcal{P}$ has fast mixing correlations 
as in Definition~(d.omegamixing of the paper)(i.mixing-ground-fast of the paper). Assume that either (a) the random field $M$ satisfies the fast $\mathbb{B} $-mixing condition of Definition~(d.omegatmixing-field of the paper)(i.B-mixing-field of the paper)-(i.mixing-field-fast of the paper) or (b) 
$M$  satisfies the fast \textnormal{BL}-mixing condition of Definition~(d.omegatmixing-field of the paper)(i.BL-mixing-field of the paper)-(i.mixing-field-fast of the paper)
and $\zeta(x,\cdot)$ is Lipschitz. If $\zeta$ satisfies the $p$-moment condition~(equation e:M-p-moment of the paper) with respect to $M$ for all $p>1$ then the central limit theorem holds for
    $(\hat\sigma_{n}^{\zeta(M)}(f))_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, i.e., as $n \to \infty$

\[   ({\rm Var} \, \hat\sigma_{n}^{\zeta(M)}(f) )^{-1/2}\Big( \hat\sigma_{n}^{\zeta(M)}(f) - \mathbb {E}  \hat\sigma_{n}^{\zeta(M)}(f) \Big) \stackrel{d}{\Rightarrow} Z,
  \]
for $f \in \mathbb{B} (W_1)$,  provided
${\rm Var} \, {\hat{\sigma}_{n}^{\zeta(M)}(f)} = \Omega(n^{\nu})$ for some $\nu > 0$.

\item  
Suppose the random field~$M$ and the point process~$\mathcal{P}$ are stationary 
(necessarily jointly so, due to their independence) with~$\mathcal{P}$ having intensity~$\rho$, 
and suppose that~$\zeta$ is translation invariant, 
i.e., $\zeta(x,\cdot) = \zeta(\cdot)$. Also assume $\zeta$ satisfies the $(1+\epsilon)$-moment condition~(equation e:M-p-moment of the paper) with respect to $M$ for some $\epsilon > 0$.
Then the mean empirical field satisfies for all $f \in \mathbb{B} (W_1)$
\begin{equation}
n^{-1} \, \mathbb{E}  \, \hat\sigma_n^{\zeta(M)}(f)
= \rho\, \mathbb {E}  \, \zeta(\0,M(\0)) \int_{W_1} f(x)\, \mathrm{d} x, \quad n\in\mathbb{N},
\end{equation}
which holds  without assuming mixing conditions on~$\mathcal{P}$ and~$M$ nor  Lipschitz conditions on $\zeta$. Moreover, under either of the mixing assumptions (a) or (b) of part~(i.CLT-infinite-zeta-field-mixing of the paper) we obtain for all $f \in \mathbb{B} (W_1)$
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty} n^{-1} {\rm Var} \, \hat\sigma_{n}^{\zeta(M)}(f)
= \sigma^2(\zeta) \int_{W_1} f(x)^2\,\mathrm{d} x,
\]
where
\begin{align}  
\sigma^2(\zeta) 
&:= \rho\, \mathbb {E}  \, \zeta^2(\0,M(\0)) \\
&\quad + \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} 
\Big( 
\mathbb {E} [\zeta(\0,M(\0))\, \zeta(x,M(x))]\, \rho^{(2)}(\0,x)
- \rho^2\, \mathbb {E} [\zeta(\0,M(\0))]\, \mathbb {E} [\zeta(x,M(x))]  
\Big)\, \mathrm{d} x \in [0, \infty) \nonumber
\end{align}
provided that~$\zeta$ satisfies the $(2+\epsilon)$-moment condition~(equation e:M-p-moment of the paper) for some $\epsilon > 0$.
\item  Let
$\boldsymbol{\zeta} := (\zeta_1, \ldots, \zeta_m)$ be a vector of translation-invariant, real-valued measurable functions 
on $\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb {M} $, with each $\zeta_i$ satisfying the $(2+\epsilon)$-moment condition~(equation e:M-p-moment of the paper) with respect to $M$ for some $\epsilon > 0$. 
Under either of the mixing assumptions (a) or (b) of part~(i.CLT-infinite-zeta-field-mixing of the paper), and under the stationarity assumption of part~(i.EVar-infinite-zeta-new of the paper)
 the multivariate central limit theorem holds as in Theorem~(t:multcltmarkedpp of the paper).
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: limit theory for the empirical distribution function of a random field

Let N be an eps-net of the unit sphere of R^n with eps in (0, 1/2), and A any m by n matrix. Then ||A|| <= (1 - eps)^{-1} sup over x in N of ||A x||; for a symmetric matrix, ||A|| <= (1 - 2 eps)^{-1} sup over x in N of |<A x, x>|. The sphere admits an eps-net of size at most (1 + 2/eps)^n, so suprema over the sphere reduce to maxima over exponentially many fixed points - the standard first step of random matrix norm bounds.

body:
[Lem 241 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\alpha,\iota > 0$ and $\fq\in [1,2)$ there exists $\epsilon = \epsilon(\alpha,\iota,\fq) > 0$ such that 
	\[
	\max\bigg\{
	\bbW_\fq(\mu,\ocM^{\Ising}(\alpha)) 
	: \mu\in \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)
	\bigg\}
	\le \iota\,.
	\]
The same statement holds with
$\ocM^{\Ising,\sym}(\alpha)$ and
$\cM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha;\epsilon)$ in place of $\ocM^{\Ising}(\alpha)$
and $\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)$. (The sets mentioned above specified by Definition~\ref{d:achievable-msrs}, \eqref{e:cM.Lip.union.L}, and \eqref{e:cM.Lip.union.L.SYM}.)

\begin{proof} Let
$\cA_N$ be an $L$-Lipschitz algorithm. 
If $\mu \in \cP_2(\R)$ satisfies $\bbW_2(\mu(\cA_N),\mu) \le \epsilon$, then Lemma~\ref{l:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound} gives, for $N$ large enough,
	\[
	\|\mu\|_{L^2} 
	\le 
	\|\mu(\cA_N)\|_{L^2} 
	+ \bbW_2(\mu(\cA_N),\mu)
	\stackrel{\eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l2}}{\le} 
	C(\alpha)^{1/2} + \epsilon
	\le (2C(\alpha))^{1/2}\,,
	\]
where the last bound holds for $\epsilon$ small enough. For such $\epsilon$, it follows by recalling \eqref{e:cM.Lip.union.L} and \eqref{e:cM.Lip} that 
	\[\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon) 
	\stackrel{\eqref{e:cM.Lip.union.L}}{=}
	\bigcup_{L>0}
		\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;L,\epsilon) \subseteq \cP_2(\R,2C(\alpha))\,.
	\]
For $\iota > 0$, define the set
	\[
		S_\iota = \Big\{\mu \in \cP_2(\R,2C(\alpha)) : \bbW_\fq(\mu,\ocM^{\Ising}(\alpha)) \ge \iota\Big\}\,.
	\]
	Now suppose for contradiction that $\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)$ intersects $S_\iota$ for all $\epsilon > 0$.
	Recall from Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.cPp.compact.Wq} that the $\cP_2(\R,2C(\alpha))$
	endowed with the $\bbW_\fq$ metric
	 is compact.
	The set $S_\iota$ is closed with respect to this metric. Thus, for any sufficiently small $\epsilon > 0$, the set
	\[
		S_\iota \cap \overline{\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)}
	\]
	(where the overline now denotes closure with respect to the $\bbW_\fq$ metric) is a nonempty closed subset of $\cP_2(\R,2C(\alpha))$ indexed by $\epsilon$, hence also compact.
	These sets form a nested family of nonempty compact sets, so their intersection is also nonempty.
	However, their intersection is
	\beq
		S_\iota \cap \bigcap_{\epsilon > 0} \overline{\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)}
		\subseteq  
		S_\iota \cap \bigcap_{\epsilon > 0} \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;2\epsilon)
		\stackrel{\eqref{e:sM.Lip}}{=} 
		S_\iota \cap \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha)
		\stackrel{\textup{Thm.~\ref{thm:control.problems.main}}}{=} S_\iota \cap \ocM^{\Ising}(\alpha)
		= \emptyset\,,
	\eeq
which yields a contradiction.
This proves that there exists $\epsilon$ such that $\bbW_\fq(\mu,\ocM^{\Ising}(\alpha)) \le \iota$ for all $\mu \in \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)$.
	The analogous claim for $\cM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha;\epsilon)$ and $\ocM^{\Ising,\sym}(\alpha)$ is proved similarly, using Theorem~\ref{thm:control.problems.sym} in place of Theorem~\ref{thm:control.problems.main} in \eqref{e:confinement.cM.lip.to.nbd.of.ideal}.
\end{proof}

[Corollary 57 (Failure of Euclidean rigidity without the
additional hypotheses) of arXiv:2609.02267, 'Locally Conformally Flat Manifolds with Positive Scalar Curvature: Kleinian Groups, Moduli'] Fix $n\geq4$, and let $K$, $M=S^n\setminus K$, and
$(g^{(t)})_{t\in(-m_0,\infty)}$ be as in Theorem~\ref{thm:counterexample-psc}.  The
manifold $M$ is connected, smooth, open, and simply connected, and
\(\widetilde H_i(M;\mathbb Z)=0\) for \(i\geq0\).
For every $t\geq0$, the metric $g^{(t)}$ is complete and locally
conformally flat, with
$\mathrm{Sc}_{g^{(t)}}\geq0$.  Moreover, the inclusion
$\iota:M\hookrightarrow S^n$ may be chosen as a developing map of
$(M,g^{(t)})$.  The omitted set, and also the topological boundary of
the developing image, is
$\Lambda:=S^n\setminus\iota(M)=\partial\iota(M)=K$,
which is a nondegenerate continuum.  Nevertheless, $M$ is not
homeomorphic to $\mathbb R^n$.

Consequently, the conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:intro-E}\textup{(ii)} can fail
when its two additional topological hypotheses are omitted
simultaneously.  The disjunction of conditions

[Lemma lem:density of arXiv:2608.12954, 'Rainbow percolation'] The events $\{O_{k,i}:k\in\mathbb{N}_0, i\in\mathbb Z\}$ are independent, and for all
$k,i$,
\[
   \mathbb P(O_{k,i})=\big(1-e^{-\beta/4}\big)^{16}
   \ \ge\ 1-16e^{-\beta/4}\ =:\ 1-\varepsilon(\beta) .
\]
For $\beta\ge31$ one has $\varepsilon(\beta)\le2^{-7}$.

[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2608.26565, 'A Horizon-Free Extrinsic Penrose Inequality'] There exist admissible minimal disks $\Gamma_0\prec\Gamma_1$, constants
	$0<t_0<t_1$, and a smooth function $v$ on the closure of the component of
	$M\setminus\Gamma_0$ containing $\mathcal E_+$. The function satisfies
	$v\to\infty$ along $\mathcal E_+$, its level sets are minimal disks, and
	\[
	 \Gamma_i=\{v=t_i\},\qquad i=0,1.
	\]
	On the component of $M\setminus\Gamma_0$ containing $\mathcal E_+$,
	\begin{equation}
	\operatorname{div}\left(
	\frac{\bar\nabla v}{|\bar\nabla v|}
	\right)=0,
	
	\end{equation}
	and on its lateral support boundary,
	\begin{equation}
	-\frac{\bar\nabla v}{|\bar\nabla v|}\cdot\nu_S>\tanh t_0.
	
	\end{equation}
	Moreover, $v$ and its minimal level-set foliation extend smoothly across $\Gamma_0$ to the side away from $\mathcal E_+$.

The G_i are independent constants, n<=F_i<=G_i<=2n, the errors are nonnegative and <=n, and F_i=G_i except on probability p_n->0. Nevertheless Var F_i=n^{2b}(1-p_n) and Var(F_1-F_2)=0. body:
[Proposition 29 of arXiv:2608.30752, '2608.30752'] Let
\(
  E(t):=\mathcal E_{u_0}(x_t).
\)
Then
\begin{equation}
  E'(0)
  =
  \frac12\int_M
  \operatorname{tr}_g\bigl(u^*k\bigr)\,d\mu_g,
  
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
  E''(0)
  =
  \frac12\int_M
  \operatorname{tr}_g\bigl(u^*l\bigr)\,d\mu_g
  -
  \mathcal I_u(W,W).
  
\end{equation}
Then \(W\) is the unique solution of
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal J_uW=S_k.
  
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
  E''(0)
  =
  \frac12\int_M
  \operatorname{tr}_g\bigl(u^*l\bigr)\,d\mu_g
  -
  \bigl\langle
    S_k,\mathcal J_u^{-1}S_k
  \bigr\rangle_{L^2}.
  
\end{equation}
Here
\(
  \langle A,B\rangle_{L^2}
  :=
  \int_M h(A,B)\,d\mu_g
\)
for sections \(A,B\in\Gamma(u^*TS)\).

[Definition of arXiv:2510.13659, 'On the energy image density conjecture of Bouleau and Hirsch'] For a $\mathbb{R}^n$-valued function $f=(f_1,\ldots,f_n) \in \mathcal{F}^n$ and $g \in \mathcal{F}$,  we define $T_{f,g}$ to be the one dimensional current on $\mathbb{R}^n$ associated with the $\mathbb{R}^n$-valued measure $(f_*(\Gamma(f_i,g)))_{1 \le i \le n}$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$; that is,
		\[
		T_{f,g} \left( \sum_{j=1}^n h_j dx_j \right):= \sum_{j=1}^n \int h_j(f(x))\,\Gamma(f_i,g)(dx)  
		\]
		for any smooth, compactly supported $1$-form  $\sum_{j=1}^n h_j dx_j$.

[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2604.21669, 'Discontinuous transition in 2D Potts:\\ II. order-order interface convergence'] Let \((\omega,U,U')\) be distributed according to \(\Psi_\mathsf{G}^{1/1}\), and let \((\sigma_\bullet,\sigma_\circ)\) with law~\(\spin_\msf{D}^{+-,+-}\) be as constructed in Lemma~\ref{lem:fk11_to_sixv}. Then~\(U'\) is independent of \((\sigma_\bullet,\sigma_\circ)\).
Consider the edge orientations corresponding to \((\sigma_\bullet,\sigma_\circ)\) (see Fig.~\ref{fig:six-vertex_arrows_spins_heights}), and construct a compatible oriented loop configuration~\(\ell_\shortrightarrow\) from them as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item each vertex in~\(\bbL_\circ\setminus(\mathsf{B}'\cup (\R\times\{-\tfrac{1}{2}\}))\) is surrounded by a clockwise oriented loop of minimal length,
\item every tile~\(t\in\bbL_\diamond\setminus\msf{A}^\rmi\) with~\(e_t^*\subset \R\times\{-\tfrac{1}{2}\}\) is of type 2 (see Figures~\ref{fig:oriented_loop_arcs} and~\ref{fig:bc_FK_loops_spins_o-o}), so that the resulting infinite paths are oriented from right to left,
\item for \(t\in\msf{A}^\rmi\) of type 1-4, there is a unique way to construct the loop arcs (see Fig.~\ref{fig:oriented_loop_arcs}); for \(t\in\msf{A}^\rmi\) of type 5-6, split the oriented edges into two right-oriented arcs (types 5B,6A) if \(U'_t<e^{\lambda/2}/\svc\) and into two left-oriented arcs (types 5A,6B) otherwise (see Fig.~\ref{fig:6V_to_oriented_loops}).
\end{itemize}
Then the law of the unique percolation configuration in~\(\{0,1\}^{\bbE^\bullet}\) associated to \(\ell_\shortrightarrow\) is given by~\(\fk_{\msf{G}}^{1/1}(\,\cdot\given\partial^+\nleftrightarrow\partial^-)\), which is the law of~\(\omega\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 6 of arXiv:2604.21669

body:
[Prop 32 of arXiv:2608.13727, 'Hitting-time mixing for the star transposition shuffle'] Let \(s\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), let \(s_n=\lfloor n\log n\rfloor\), and suppose \(s=s_n+nc_n^\star(s)\), where
    \(|c_n^\star(s)|\le \tfrac12\log\log n-4\log\log\log n\).
    Let \(T_n\subseteq[n]_\star\) satisfy \(|T_n|\le(\log n)^2\), and let \(Y_s^{\,T_n}\) denote the random variable \(Y_s\) conditioned on \(\mathcal F(T_n)\).
    Let \(\mu^{T_n}\) be the probability measure on \(\mathfrak S_n\) obtained by embedding the uniform distribution on \(\mathfrak S_{[n]\setminus T_n}\) into \(\mathfrak S_n\) via the natural inclusion.
    Then
    \[ d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(\mathcal L(Y_s^{\,T_n}),\mu^{T_n}\right) \le n^{-1/2+o(1)}, \]
    uniformly over all such \(T_n\).

[Prop 5 of arXiv:2608.30173, '2608.30173'] Let
\be
\sigma
=
r_\infty^{-\frac{n-2}{4}}
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\alpha_iPU_i.
\ee
There exist $\va_0\in(0,1)$ and $C>0$, depending only on
$\Omega$, $n$, $\ell$, and $\delta_0$, such that, if
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}|\alpha_i-1|
+
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\lambda_i^{-1}
+
\sum_{i\neq j}\Lambda_{i,j}
\leq\va_0,
\]
then
\be
\begin{aligned}
Y_\Omega(\sigma)
={}&
r_\infty
-
C_1c_0r_\infty^{-\frac{n-2}{2}}
\sum_{i\neq j}\Lambda_{i,j}\\
&+
O\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}|\alpha_i-1|^2\right)
+
o\left(\sum_{i\neq j}\Lambda_{i,j}\right)
+
O\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\lambda_i^{2-n}\right).
\end{aligned}
\ee
Here and below, the $o$-terms are uniform as
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}|\alpha_i-1|
+
\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\lambda_i^{-1}
+
\sum_{i\neq j}\Lambda_{i,j}
\longrightarrow0
\]
under the condition $d(a_i)\geq\delta_0$.

[Thm hitme of arXiv:2609.03033, 'An Overview of Einstein $4$-Manifolds'] Let $K3$ denote  the smooth oriented simply-connected  four-manifold  underlying  the  compact  complex surface 
$$\{ [t,u,v,w]\in \mathbb{CP}_3~|~ t^4 + u^4 + v^4 + w^4 =0\}.$$
Then any Einstein metric $g$ on $K3$ is Ricci-flat  and hyper-K\"ahler, in the sense that it is K\"ahler with respect to 
an $S^2$-family of orientation-compatible   integrable complex structures 
 on $K3$.  As a consequence, the moduli space $\mathscr{E} (K3)$ is therefore connected. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma lem:ub-h1-Lns of arXiv:2411.10419, 'Lower bounds on the top Lyapunov exponent for linear PDEs driven by the 2D stochastic Navi'] Let $\varrho$ be a solution to (equation e:main of the paper) with $L[u] $ satisfying
(equation e:form-PSA of the paper) or (equation e:form-LNS of the paper). Then for any $\gamma\in (2,3)$ and $0\leqslant s \leqslant t$, there exists a $C(\gamma)>1$ such that: for the projective process $\pi=\varrho/\|\varrho\|$ we have 
\[
\|\pi_{t} \|_{H^{1}}\leqslant C(\gamma) \exp\left(C(\gamma)\int_{s}^{t} \|u_{r}\|_{H^{\gamma}}\mathrm{\,d} r \right)\left(\|\pi_{s}\|_{H^{1}}+ (t-s)
\sup_{s\leqslant r \leqslant t}\|u_{r}\|_{H^{\gamma +1}}\right)\;.
\]
Therefore, for any $\mathbf{r} \geqslant 1 $ there exists a $C(\mathbf{r},t)>0$ such that 
\[
\mathbb{E} \left[ \| \pi_t\|_{H^{1}}^{\mathbf{r}} \right] \leqslant C(\mathbf{r},t) \mathbb{E} \left[\| \pi_{s}\|_{H^{1}}^{2\mathbf{r}} +1\right]^{\frac{1}{2}} V_{\mathbf{r}}^{\frac{1}{2}}(u_{0})\;,
\] 
where $V_{\mathbf{r}}$ is defined in (equation e:lyap-sns of the paper).
title: Lemma lem:ub-h1-Lns of arXiv:2411.10419

body:
[Proposition 9 of arXiv:2608.30752, '2608.30752'] Let $a$ and $b$ be the real-valued functions determined locally by
\begin{equation}
  u_t
  =
  ta+\frac{t^2}{2}b+O(t^3).
  
\end{equation}
Then, on $X_0\setminus Z(q)$,
\begin{align}
  (\Delta_0-2)a
  &=
  \mathcal D_q\log\lambda,
  
  \\
  (\Delta_0-2)b
  &=
  4\left(
    \mathcal D_q a+a^2-1
  \right).
  
\end{align}
Consequently, for every compact set
$K\Subset X_0\setminus Z(q)$ and every $k\ge 0$,
\begin{equation}
  \begin{aligned}
  \widetilde\sigma_t
  ={}&
  \sigma_0
  +
  2t\left(
    B_q+a\sigma_0
  \right)
  \\
  &+
  t^2
  \left[
    \left(
      2+b+2a^2
    \right)\sigma_0
    +
    4aB_q
  \right]
  +
  O_{C^k(K)}(t^3).
  \end{aligned}
  
\end{equation}
Equivalently,
\begin{align}
  \dot{\widetilde\sigma}_0
  &=
  2B_q+2a\sigma_0,
  
  \\
  \ddot{\widetilde\sigma}_0
  &=
  \left(
    4+2b+4a^2
  \right)\sigma_0
  +
  8aB_q.
  
\end{align}

[Corollary 8 of arXiv:2609.03881, 'Eulerian insertion operators and an Eulerian form of the Pieri rule'] For \(a,b\geq0\),
\[
 \G_a\G_b
 =\sum_{j=0}^{\min(a,b)}(-1)^j
   \frac{(a+b-j)!}{(a-j)!(b-j)!j!}\,
   (y-x)^j\G_{a+b-j},
\]
where \((y-x)^j\) acts by multiplication.

For width n>=2 and input angle theta in (0,pi), write the Gaussian preactivations as (a_i,b_i), i=1,...,n, with nonsingular covariance. Their joint density is continuous and strictly positive everywhere.

Restrict to the event that a_1,a_2,b_1,b_2 are positive near 1, and a_i,b_i for i>2 are in (-2,-1). Both output vectors then have exactly support {1,2}. Introduce coordinates (a_1,a_2,b_1,h) with b_2=(a_2 b_1+h)/a_1. This is a smooth change of variables with Jacobian 1/a_1, bounded above and below on a small compact box with a_1,a_2,b_1 near 1 and |h|<epsilon. The transformed Gaussian density is bounded below by a positive constant.

The angle alpha of the positive two-dimensional vectors satisfies

    sin(alpha) = |a_1*b_2-a_2*b_1|/(sqrt(a_1^2+a_2^2)*sqrt(b_1^2+b_2^2)) = |h|/(||a|| ||b||).

Hence the integral of 1/alpha over this box is bounded below by c times integral_{0<|h|<epsilon} dh/|h|, which is infinite. All conditions excluding extinction and exact zero angle hold throughout this punctured box.

[Theorem thm:TW of arXiv:2512.21159, '\textsc{From multitype branching Brownian motions\\ to branching Markov additive processes'] Assume (A1 of the paper), (A2 of the paper), and $\theta\in (0,\bar{\theta})$. 
\begin{enumerate}[label = (\roman*)]
    \item (Supercritical regime) If $\theta \lambda'(\theta) <\lambda(\theta)$ and $\sum_{k\geq 1}  (k\log k)\mu_j(k)<\infty$ for all $j\in\mathcal{I}$, then the function $\Phi_{\theta}(x,i) = \mathbf{E}_{x,i} \big[e^{-W_{\theta}(\infty)}\big] = \mathbf{E}_{0,i}\left[ e^{-e^{-\theta x} W_{\theta}(\infty)} \right]$ is a travelling wave solution with speed $\rho_{\theta}= \frac{\lambda(\theta)}{\theta}>\frac{\lambda(\theta^*)}{\theta^*}$. 
    \item (Critical regime) If $\theta^* \lambda'(\theta^*) =\lambda(\theta^*)$ and $\sum_{k\geq 1}  k(\log k)^2 \mu_j(k) <\infty$ for all $j\in\mathcal{I}$, then $\Phi_{\theta^*}(x,i) = \mathbf{E}_{x,i} \big[e^{-Z_{\theta^*}(\infty)}\big] = \mathbf{E}_{0,i}\left[ e^{-e^{-\theta x} Z_{\theta^*}(\infty)} \right]$ is a travelling wave solution with speed $\rho_{\theta^*} = \frac{\lambda(\theta^*)}{\theta^*}$. 
    \item (Subcritical regime) There are no travelling wave solutions with speed $\rho<\frac{\lambda(\theta^*)}{\theta^*}$. 
\end{enumerate} 
Suppose furthermore that the branching MAP is spectrally negative (that is the MAP $(\chi,\Theta)$ associated with $((\chi_i)_{i\in \mathcal{I}}, \Theta, (U_{ij})_{i,j\in \mathcal{I}})$  has no positive jumps), then the travelling wave solutions given in the supercritical and critical regimes are unique in $\mathcal{T}_1$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Existence and uniqueness of travelling waves

[Th th_fixed_x_solution of arXiv:2606.23648, '\textsc{Optimal Stopping for a Diffusion with Unobserved Bernoulli Drift}'] Fix \(x\ge0\). If the function \(\Phi_x\) of (equation def_phi of the paper) is non-decreasing on \((-x,\infty)\), then  immediate stopping is optimal for every \(y\in I_x\), and
    \(
        U_x(y)=k_x(y),\, y\in I_x.
    \)

    Suppose, on the other hand, that the one-interval regime (equation one_interval_phi_geometry of the paper) holds. Let \(q_x\) be the unique solution of (equation eq_main_balancing_condition of the paper), and \(a_x,b_x,R_x\) be defined by (equation def_ax_bx_fixed_x of the paper), (equation def_Rx_fixed_x of the paper). Then
    \(
        \mathcal C_x=(a_x,b_x)
    \)
    is the continuation region; the value function is given by
    \begin{equation}
        U_x(y)
        =
        \begin{cases}
            k_x(y), & -x\le y\le a_x,\\[0.3em]
            q_xG(y)+R_x-cyG(y), & a_x<y<b_x,\\[0.3em]
            k_x(y), & y\ge b_x;
        \end{cases}
    \end{equation}
    and the stopping time
    \[
        \tau_x^*
        \coloneqq
        \inf\{t\ge0:Y_y(t)\notin(a_x,b_x)\},
    \]

[Proposition 15 of arXiv:2605.25715, '2605.25715'] Let $\Phi \in H^{1,2}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}^d)\cap L^{\infty}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, $c_{ij}=-c_{ji}\in H^{1,2}_{loc}(\R^d)\cap L^{\infty}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}^d),\ 1\le i,j\le d$, and $\mu=\rho\,dx$, where $\rho=\exp(2 \Phi)$. Set 
$$
\overline{\mathbf{B}}:= C^T\nabla \Phi.
$$ 
(i) We have the following equivalences:
$$
\mathrm{div}_{\mu}(\mathrm{div}C)= 0 \ \Leftrightarrow \  \mathrm{div}_{\mu}(\overline{\mathbf{B}})= 0 \ \Leftrightarrow\ \big \langle \mathrm{div} C, \nabla \Phi\big \rangle=0\ \Leftrightarrow\ \mathrm{div}_{dx}(\overline{\mathbf{B}})= 0.
$$ 
(ii) Let $k_1, k_2 \in \mathbb{R}$ be constants. Then, we have:
\begin{enumerate}
\item [(a)] If either one of the four equivalent conditions in (i) holds, then 
\[
\mathbf{G} =  \nabla \Phi+ k_1C^T\nabla \Phi+ k_2\mathrm{div} C
\]
is an OHHD.
\item [(b)] If either $k_1\neq 0$ or $k_2 \neq 0$, and $\mathbf{G} =  \nabla \Phi+ k_1C^T\nabla \Phi+ k_2\mathrm{div} C$ is an OHHD, then one of the four equivalent conditions of (i) is satisfied.
\end{enumerate}

body:
Let T be a closed symmetric operator on a complex Hilbert space H, with deficiency subspaces K_+ = ker(T* − i), K_- = ker(T* + i) and deficiency indices n_± = dim K_±. Then: (1) D(T*) = D(T) ⊕ K_+ ⊕ K_-, a direct sum which is orthogonal for the graph inner product ⟨x, y⟩ + ⟨T*x, T*y⟩. (2) The closed symmetric extensions of T correspond bijectively to partial isometries from a closed subspace of K_+ into K_-; the self-adjoint extensions correspond bijectively to unitary operators U: K_+ → K_- (onto), via D(T_U) = {x + φ + Uφ : x ∈ D(T), φ ∈ K_+} and T_U(x + φ + Uφ) = Tx + iφ − iUφ. (3) Hence T has a self-adjoint extension iff n_+ = n_-; T is self-adjoint iff n_+ = n_- = 0; if n_+ = n_- = n with 1 ≤ n < ∞, the self-adjoint extensions form a family parametrized by the unitary group U(n); if exactly one of n_± is 0 and the other is not, T is maximal symmetric and has no self-adjoint extension. (4) If there is a conjugation C (antiunitary, C² = I) with C D(T) ⊂ D(T) and TC = CT, then n_+ = n_- (von Neumann's conjugation criterion; e.g. real differential operators with real coefficients). (5) If T is bounded below, n_+ = n_- (and a self-adjoint extension with the same lower bound exists, the Friedrichs extension).
H is a complex Hilbert space
T is closed and symmetric (densely defined)
for (4): a conjugation C commuting with T and preserving D(T)
for (5): T is bounded below

[Definition see, e.g., \cite{bozic_models_1984} of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] For an f-model $\mathfrak{M} = (W, \leq, \sqsubset, V)$, we define an \emph{extrinsic satisfaction relation} $\Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M}$ on $W \times \mathscr{L}_{\Box\Diamond}$ by:
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item $x \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \psi_1 \to \psi_2 \mathrel{\;\ratio\Longleftrightarrow\;} \forall x' \geq x\, (x' \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \psi_1 \mathrel{\Rightarrow} x' \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \psi_2)$
    \item $x \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \Box \varphi \mathrel{\;\ratio\Longleftrightarrow\;} \forall y \sqsupset x \, (y \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \varphi)$
    \item $x \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \Diamond \varphi \mathrel{\;\ratio\Longleftrightarrow\;} \exists y \sqsupset x\, (y \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \varphi)$
    \item The other cases are identical to the classical $\Vdash_\mathfrak{M}$.
  \end{enumerate}
  We write $\mathfrak{M} \vDash^e \varphi$ (``$\varphi$ is \emph{(e-)valid in} $\mathfrak{M}$'') to mean $\forall x \in W\,(x \Vdash^e_\mathfrak{M} \varphi)$,
  and $\mathfrak{F} \vDash^e \varphi$ (``$\varphi$ is \emph{(e-)valid on} $\mathfrak{F}$'') to mean that $\mathfrak{M} \vDash^e \varphi$ for every $\mathfrak{M}$ based on $\mathfrak{F}$.

[Thm 6 of arXiv:2604.11489, '2604.11489'] Let $\{X_n, n\ge 1\}$ be a sequence of independent and identically distributed random variables with common nonuniform distribution $\{p_i, i\ge 1\}$ satisfying
$\ee|\ln p(X_1)|^{2+\delta} < \infty$. Assume that there exist an integer valued function $K(n)$  and $0< \delta< \frac{1}{2}$ such that
\beq
K(n)\le n^{\frac{1}{2}-\delta},\ \ n^{\frac{1}{2}+\delta}\ln n\sum_{i=K(n)}^{\infty}p_i \leq C,
\ \ -n^{\frac{1}{2}+\delta}\sum_{i=K(n)}^{\infty}p_i\ln p_i\leq C,
\deq
then we have
\beq
\sup_x\left|\pp\left(\frac{\sqrt{n}(\hat{H}_{MM}-H)}{\sigma}<x\right)-\Phi(x)\right|
 \leq Cn^{-\frac{\delta}{2}},
\deq
where $\Phi$ denotes the standard normal distribution function and $\sigma^2=\Var(\ln p(X_1))$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:251a81781266638cf433fe2502cf13691ee3345ca3055e4a09442677a9b8c28c","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/25/251a81781266638cf433fe2502cf13691ee3345ca3055e4a09442677a9b8c28c.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:8c192f261b687d35b3c29a423144e220abb97e50e2555adbe984d3f3cd3b48fa","bundle_entry_key":"spherical-moments-bilinear-disagreement","bundle_id":"population.t407-draft-spherical-moment-gaussian-metric-proof","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability and statistical learning theory","draft":"w693/bundle_007.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:learning.sample_complexity:draft-spherical-fourth-moment-proof-gaussian-bilinear-disagreement-metric","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Direct Gaussian disagreement metric comparison

Target2 verification supplement for LOW-003 v2. Known geometric comparison, not a new frontier move. Status: proof (unaudited). This source-independent derivation removes one imported step from the existing lower audit; it does not prove the packing or the sample lower bound.

For d>=2 and U,V in O(d), let rho be the disagreement probability of sign(a^T U b) and sign(a^T V b), with independent standard Gaussian a,b. Then

    ||U-V||_F/(pi sqrt(3d)) <= rho <= ||U-V||_F/(2sqrt(d)).

The zero matrix case U=V is included. No small-angle, large-dimension or asymptotic hypothesis is needed.

## Angle and chord

For b!=0 put u=b/||b||. Conditional on b, the Gaussian a gives disagreement theta(u)/pi, where theta is the angle in [0,pi] between Uu and Vu. For linearly independent normals, this follows by the uniform angular distribution of the two-dimensional Gaussian projection; coincident and opposite normals give respectively0 and1. Thus the formula remains valid at the endpoints without dividing by an angle or by a cross product. The event b=0 is null.

Let X=||(U-V)u||. Since both vectors are unit, X=2sin(theta/2). For theta in [0,pi], sin(x)<=x and the concavity chord bound sin(x)>=2x/pi for x in [0,pi/2] give

    X <= theta <= (pi/2)X.

Consequently EX/pi <=rho<=EX/2. It remains to compare EX with the normalized Frobenius norm.

## Exact spherical moments

More generally let M be any real d-by-d matrix, S=M^T M, and X=||Mu|| for uniform u on the unit sphere. Put s1=tr(S)=||M||_F^2 and s2=tr(S^2). Rotational invariance and diagonalizing the symmetric positive-semidefinite S yield

    EX^2=s1/d,
    EX^4=(s1^2+2s2)/(d(d+2)).

Here is a direct derivation of all tensor constants. Symmetry gives E u_i^2=1/d. Let A=E u_1^4 and B=E u_1^2 u_2^2. Coordinate sign symmetry kills odd monomials. Invariance under the 45-degree rotation in the first two coordinates gives A=(2A+6B)/4, hence A=3B. Squaring sum_i u_i^2=1 gives dA+d(d-1)B=1, hence B=1/[d(d+2)] and A=3/[d(d+2)]. These denominators are positive for every d>=2. Expanding the square of sum_i lambda_i u_i^2 gives the displayed formula. Since all eigenvalues lambda_i>=0, s2<=s1^2. Therefore

    EX^4 <=3(EX^2)^2.

If s1=0 then M=0, so X=0 everywhere and the asserted comparison is immediate. Otherwise EX^2 and EX^4 are positive. All moments are finite because X<=||M||_op on the compact unit sphere.

Two Cauchy-Schwarz inequalities give

    (EX^2)^2 <= EX * EX^3,
    EX^3 <=sqrt(EX^2 * EX^4).

Combining and dividing by the positive latter square root yields

    EX >= (EX^2)^(3/2)/(EX^4)^(1/2) >=sqrt(EX^2/3).

Also EX<=sqrt(EX^2) by Cauchy-Schwarz. Thus

    ||M||_F/sqrt(3d) <= EX <=||M||_F/sqrt(d).

Apply M=U-V to finish the theorem. No integral limit or infinite-sum interchange occurs.

## Application and limits

The lower half supplies an explicit absolute Gaussian-metric constant for LOW-003 v2 section1. It makes the use of the metric comparison in Li-Zhang-Arora arXiv:2010.08515v2 LemmaD.4 independently transparent. The orthogonal packing and common-rotation entropy estimate still require independent audit. This is an elementary proof of a known comparison, with no novelty claim and no new score asserted.

Then, for every $q\in(0,1]$ with $\int_{\mathbb{R}^d\setminus B_{\bm{0}}(1)}|\bm{w}|^q\nu_{\bm{X}}^{\mathrm{d}}(\mathrm{d}\bm{w})<\infty$ 
we have $\mathds{E}\big[\sup_{s\in[0,1]} |\bm{R}^t_s|^q\big] = \mathcal{O} \big(t^{1-q/\alpha}G(t)^{-q}\big)$ as $t\downarrow 0$ and, if $p\ne\alpha-1$ and $q\in (0,\alpha)\cap(0,1]$ satisfy $q\notin\{\alpha/(p+1),\alpha/(\alpha\delta+1)\}$, we have, as $t \downarrow 0$,
\begin{align}
    \mathcal{W}_2\big(\bm{M}^{\bm{S}^t},\bm{M^Z}\big)
&=\mathcal{O}\big(G_2(t)+(1+G(t)^{p})t^{\min\{p/\alpha,\delta\}}\big),\\
\mathcal{W}_q\big(\bm{L}^{\bm{S}^t}, \bm{L}^{\bm{Z}}\big) 
&= \mathcal{O} \big( G_2(t)^q
    + (1+G(t)^{pq})(1+G_1(x))^{q(1+p)}
        t^{\min\{pq/\alpha,q\delta,1-q/\alpha\}}\big), \qquad \text{ and }\\
|\bm{\varpi}_{\bm{S}^t}-\bm{\varpi}_{\bm{Z}}|
        &=\begin{dcases}
            \mathcal{O}\big(G_2(t)+t^{1-1/\alpha}G(t)^{-1} 
    +(1+G_1(t))t^{\min\{1-1/\alpha,\delta\}}\\
    \qquad +G(t)^{p}(1+G_1(t))^{1+p}t^{\min\{1-1/\alpha,p/\alpha\}}\big), & \alpha \in (1,2),\\
    \mathcal{O}\big(G_2(t)+t^{p/\alpha}G(t)^{p} +t^{\delta}\big), & \alpha \in (0,1).
        \end{dcases}

body: [Defn of arXiv:2411.10318, 'Polynomial Mixing of the critical Glauber Dynamics for the Ising Model'] Let $G$ be a graph. On the vertices of $G$ fix an enumeration and let $v$ be one of the vertices of $G$. The tree of Self-Avoiding Walks $T_{\text{SAW}}(G,v)$ of $G$ rooted at $v$ is the tree of walks originating at $v$ that do not intersect themselves, except when the walk closes a cycle, at which point the walk ends. When that happens, the second copy of the twice-appearing vertex is fixed to be a $+$, if the edge closing the cycle is larger than the edge starting the cycle, and $-$ otherwise. In this case, comparing the edges really means comparing the respective vertices, with respect to the enumeration we initially fixed. It is easy to see that the degree of each vertex of $T_{\text{SAW}}(G,v)$ is at most $d$.

body:
[Theorem thm:multit of arXiv:2411.10829, 'Airy$_\beta$ line ensemble and its Laplace transform'] Choose $m\in \mathbb N$, $\vec \mathbf k \in \mathbb R^m_+ $, and $\vec \boldsymbol{\tau}\in \mathbb R_{\ge 0}^m$ such that $\boldsymbol{\tau}_1\le \cdots \le \boldsymbol{\tau}_m$, any real $C_1>0$, and a large enough $N\in \mathbb N$.
We take the $N$ dimensional DBM $\{Y_i(\tau)\}_{1\leq i\leq N, \tau>0}$ started from zero initial condition, and $\vec k \in \mathbb N^m$, $\tau_1\le \tau_2\le \dots \le \tau_m$ such that
\begin{equation}

|k_\ell-\mathbf k_\ell N^{2/3}|<C_1, \qquad \left|\frac{2}{\beta}N + \frac{2}{\beta}\boldsymbol{\tau}_\ell N^{2/3}-\tau_\ell\right|<C_1,\qquad  \text{for each }\ell\in\llbracket 1,m\rrbracket.
\end{equation}
Then as $N\to\infty$, uniformly over the ($N$--dependent) choices of $\vec k$ and $\vec \tau$ satisfying (equation eq_x2 of the paper):
\[
 \mathbb E \left[ \prod_{\ell=1}^m \left(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^N \left(\frac{Y_i(\tau_\ell)}{\sqrt{2\beta\tau_\ell N}}\right)^{k_\ell}+\left(\frac{Y_i(\tau_\ell)}{\sqrt{2\beta\tau_\ell N}}\right)^{k_\ell+1}\right) \right]\to \mathbf L_\beta(\vec \mathbf k, \vec\boldsymbol{\tau}).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let G be a finite connected graph with distinct edge weights, T its minimum spanning tree, and G_p its subgraph of edges of weight at most p. For each component C of G_p, the restriction T to C is a spanning tree and the T path between vertices of C stays in C. Therefore max_C diam_intrinsic(C)<=diam(T). A probabilistic lower bound on sublevel intrinsic component diameter transfers directly to the MST; this gives no MST upper bound or high-dimensional cluster estimate by itself.

title: Sublevel component intrinsic diameter is a lower bound for MST diameter

CLAIM: for every such V and every state x, 1 - V(x)_0 <= (1 - 1/q) (1 - x_0)^2. Consequently e_0 is the unique fixed point, 1 - x_0 decays quadratically and at least like (1 - 1/q)^n, and Theorem 5 of the source extends from two blocks to every partition. The cross-block coefficients are irrelevant. The constant is SHARP, attained when the block masses are equal and cross-block pairs never produce 0. Prior art: the xi^(s) and xi^(as)-QSO literature is a different notion, the literal Problem 10 was not found addressed, and novelty is small.

[Lemma 77 (Uniform resolvent seam) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] Let $1/3<\alpha<\beta<1/2$ and
$\norm{x}_{\beta\text{-H\"ol}}\le R$.  For $0\le v\le T-s$, put
\[
 \mathbb I_{s,s+v}^\eps(x)
 :=J_{s+v}^\eps(x)-J_s^\eps(x)-x_s\otimes x_{s,s+v}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb I_{s,s+v}^\eps(x)-J_v^\eps(\theta_sx)
 =-D_s^\eps(x)\otimes\mathcal A_v^\eps(\theta_sx),
\end{equation}
and the right-hand side is bounded by $CR^2\eps^{2\beta}$, uniformly in
$(s,v)$.  Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{s\in[0,T]}
 \rho_\alpha\!\left(
  S_2(Y_{s+\cdot}^\eps(x)-Y_s^\eps(x)),
  S_2(Y^\eps(\theta_sx))
 \right)
 \le CR(1+R)\eps^{\beta-\alpha},
\end{equation}

For 0<theta1<theta2,K>0 and s_t=t*omega+phi with omega/pi irrational, the quotient Q_t=[theta1*cos(s_t)^2+theta2*K*cos(3*s_t)^2]/[cos(s_t)^2+K*cos(3*s_t)^2], along its defined times,has accumulation set [theta1,(theta1+9*K*theta2)/(1+9*K)], whose upper endpoint is less than theta2. This follows by cos(3s)=cos(s)*(4*cos(s)^2-3), density of irrational rotations,and monotonicity of (theta1+K*theta2*z)/(1+K*z) on[0,9]. Therefore positive oscillation amplitudes alone cannot replace029 rational independence in the full-interval proof. This is a leading-mode route obstruction only; no standard Adam orbit realizing the locked phases is constructed, no nonlinear orbit counterexample or frontier move is claimed,and geometric remainder effects at common zeros remain unpaid.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:9e7bac292193bea84acf2b1f3f3c43275b7fb8ae6348b57318056c45e3d17784","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/9e/9e7bac292193bea84acf2b1f3f3c43275b7fb8ae6348b57318056c45e3d17784.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:3b2761a7c29a87f0ea620b851aac22586976a933ea436007cfb1e2edd8bf67b5","bundle_entry_key":"shared-zero-resonance","bundle_id":"population.resonant-shared-zero-obstruction-019","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"asymptotic recurrence methods","draft":"w706/bundle_019.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:analysis.asymptotics:resonant-shared-cosine-zeros-obstruct-full-weighted-curvature-interval","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"T421-W706-034 v1; kind route-failure; target1; proof (unaudited).

STATEMENT: A LIMITATION OF THE ASYMPTOTIC ROUTE, NOT AN ADAM ORBIT
Let 0<theta1<theta2, K>0, and s_t=t*omega+phi, with omega/pi irrational.
Define the exact leading modes h1(t)=cos(s_t), h2(t)=sqrt(K)*cos(3*s_t).
The weighted curvature
 Q_t=(theta1*h1(t)^2+theta2*h2(t)^2)/(h1(t)^2+h2(t)^2)
has accumulation set
 [theta1,(theta1+9*K*theta2)/(1+9*K)],
along defined times. Its upper endpoint is strictly less than theta2.
Thus positive nonzero oscillation amplitudes and a common decay rate
alone do not imply the whole interval between the two caps. One cannot
delete029's rational-independence assumption from its torus-density
step without additional frequency/phase analysis.

This is an exact fact about leading modes. No standard-initialization
Adam trajectory realizing these locked phases is constructed or claimed.
It does not refute the corresponding assertion about actual Adam orbits.
It is an auxiliary route obstruction and scores no frontier move.

PROOF
The identity cos(3s)=cos(s)*(4*cos(s)^2-3) gives, whenever cos(s)!=0,
 Q_t=F(z_t), z_t=(4*cos(s_t)^2-3)^2,
 F(z)=(theta1+K*theta2*z)/(1+K*z).
The range closure of z on the circle is [0,9]. Irrational rotation
has arbitrarily late visits to every open arc (the one-dimensional
Kronecker theorem), so its accumulation set is the entire interval.
Deleting times cos(s_t)=0 has no effect: there is at most one such
time, since two would make omega/pi rational. The expression F(z_t)
extends continuously through the deleted zeros. F'(z)=
K*(theta2-theta1)/(1+K*z)^2>0. Therefore its image interval has the
stated endpoints. The gap to theta2 is
 (theta2-theta1)/(1+9*K)>0.

COMPATIBILITY OF FREQUENCIES WITH THE SUBCRITICAL CAPS
For b=9/10, r=sqrt(b), choose any irrational omega/pi in (0,1/3),
and put theta_j=[1+b-2*r*cos(j*omega)]/(1-b), j=1,3.
Both lie in the strict complex-root cap interval of029 and theta3>theta1.
Hence the resonance is not ruled out by the possible linearized
frequencies. This frequency observation still says nothing about whether
the nonlinear standard-initialization curve produces the locked phase
relation phi3=3*phi1 modulo pi.

REMAINDERS AND THE UNPAID EXTENSION
For an actual Adam asymptotic expansion the remainders are geometric.
Away from shared leading zeros the quotient limit is legitimate. Near
shared zeros, dividing remainders by the leading amplitude requires a
quantitative lower bound or a higher-order recurrence argument. No such
bound is proved here. In particular, irrationality by itself supplies
no quantitative inhomogeneous approximation rate. Rationally independent
frequencies in029 avoid this issue by choosing subsequences with a
strictly positive limiting squared-weight sum and trapping all other
subsequences by the two caps.

SOURCE AND VERIFICATION
The trigonometric identity, monotonicity and weighted-quotient algebra
are proved above; scripts/check_resonant_extension.py checks five exact
polynomial/rational identities. Classical rotation density is the
one-dimensional Kronecker theorem (2404.00077v1 Section1, printedp1,
states the classical discrete version). This is not an independently
audited claim, a literature-newness claim, or a computer-assisted Adam
trajectory counterexample.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:77c3bddc7e6f19c3539229b7439cf6b082e473b9b6e07a0a036f16925e6589f0","revision_digest":"sha256:ff322d3a13f45255ff658c756386a79cf44de89e216a46086a1eca3e5b1652ed","source_id":"own-work:T421-W706-034","source_revision":"version 1; proof (unaudited); auxiliary route only","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Theorem 14 of arXiv:2606.06859, 'The rectangular finite free heat flow'] Let $(p_d)_{d \geq 1}$ be a sequence of monic polynomials with nonnegative real roots, where each $p_d$ has degree $d$, and suppose that the scaled empirical root distributions $\mu_{p_d}$ converge weakly to a compactly supported probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ as $d\to\infty$.
Let $n = n(d)$ be a sequence of positive integers with $d/n \to\lambda\in (0,1]$. Then for each $t \geq 0$,
\[
    \mu_{p_d \,\boxplus^n_d\, G_{n,d}^{[t]}}
    \xrightarrow{\, \ \, } \mu \boxplus_\lambda^+ \mathrm{MP}_{1/\lambda,\, 2t}
\]
weakly as $d\to\infty$.

[Definition 7 (Ewens fragmentation process $\Pp^{(n,\theta)}$) of arXiv:2604.25877, 'Asymptotic height of Plancherel random trees'] Fix $\theta>0$ and an integer $n\ge 1$.
We construct a random finite rooted tree $(\mathcal T_n , K)\in \Omega$ as follows.
Each vertex $u$ carries an integer mass $K(u)\in\{1,2,\dots\}$.
The root is denoted by $\varnothing$ and has mass
\[
K(\varnothing)=n.
\]

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Splitting rule.}
Let $u$ be a vertex.
\begin{itemize}
\item If $K(u)=1$, then $u$ is declared a leaf and produces no children.
\item If $K(u)=k\ge 2$, set $m:=k-1$ and sample an $\mathrm{Ewens}(m,\theta)$ partition with count vector
$(C^{(u)}_1,\dots,C^{(u)}_m)$ as in Definition~\ref{def:ewens}.
Let $(A^{(u)}_1 \ge A^{(u)}_2 \ge \cdots \ge A^{(u)}_{\delta(u)})$ be the corresponding partition of block sizes, i.e.
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{\delta(u)} A^{(u)}_i = m,\qquad
\#\{i: A^{(u)}_i=j\}=C^{(u)}_j.
\]
Then $u$ produces $\delta(u)$ children, denoted $(ui)_{1\le i\le \delta(u)}$, with masses
\[
K(ui):=A^{(u)}_i,\qquad i=1,\dots,\delta(u).
\]
\end{itemize}
All splitting variables at different vertices are sampled independently. We
denote $\Pp^{(n,\theta)}$ the probability measure on $(\Omega,\mathcal{F})$
corresponding to this procedure.

body:
[Theorem thm:dgt4-many-limits of arXiv:2609.02829, 'Quantitative explosion and percolation of the divisible sandpile'] Let $d\geq5$. There exists an i.i.d.\ scenery
	$(\zeta(x))_{x\in\mathbb{Z}^d}$ whose one-site law has mean zero, variance one,
	a strictly positive
	$C^\infty$ density, and
	\[
		\mathbb{E} e^{\theta|\zeta(0)|}<\infty,
		\qquad
		cr\leq-\log\mathbb{P}(\zeta(0)\leq-r)\leq Cr
	\]
	for some $c,C,\theta>0$ and every sufficiently large $r$.
	There is a sequence $R_k\uparrow\infty$ such that, for every
	$\kappa\in[3/2,2]$, there are indices
	$k_\ell\uparrow\infty$ such that, for all $T>0$ and
	$s>(d-4)/2$,
	\[
		R_{k_\ell}^{(d-4)/2}
		\left(
		u_{\lfloor TR_{k_\ell}^2\rfloor}
		-\mathbb{E} u_{\lfloor TR_{k_\ell}^2\rfloor}(0)
		\right)^{(R_{k_\ell})}
		\Longrightarrow
		\mathcal H_{\kappa,T}
		\qquad\text{in }H^{-s}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^d)\, .
	\]
	For $T>0$, the fields $\mathcal H_{\kappa,T}$ with
	$\kappa\in[3/2,2]$ have pairwise distinct laws.

[Prop approximating_G_with_G of arXiv:2506.10623, 'Polynomial slowdown in an angle-dependent 2d branching Brownian motion'] Let $\alpha \in (0,2)$ and $\beta > 0$.
	Let $L>0$, $a> (1-\kappa)/(1-\frac{\kappa}{2}) = 1-\alpha/2$ and $b>1-\kappa$.
	Then, there exists $\varepsilon_0 = \varepsilon_0(\alpha,a,b) > 0$ such that for all $\varepsilon \in (0,\varepsilon_0)$, there are $C,c>0$ such that for $s$ large enough, for any $t\geq s + s^\kappa$, any $x,y\in \mathbb{R}$ with $\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\lvertx\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\rvert \leq s^{(\kappa + \varepsilon)/2}$ and $\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft\lverty\aftergroup\egroup\originalright\rvert \leq t^{(\kappa + \varepsilon)/2}$ and any function $f$ satisfying $f^-_{L,a,b} \leq f \leq f^+_{L,a,b}$, we have
	\begin{equation*}
	\widetilde{G}(s,x;t,y) = (1+o(1)) G(s,x;t,y),
	\end{equation*}
	where the $o(1)$ holds as $s\to\infty$, uniformly in $t,x,y,f$ (but depending on $\alpha,\beta,L,a,b,\varepsilon$). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\frac12(e^{-2\beta}+M_H^\infty) \leq D_{H}^\infty \leq C(e^{-2\beta}+M_H^\infty).
\]
The same bound holds for $D_{H}$ and $\frac1{N}D_{N,H}$ up to changing $\frac{1}{2}$ and $C$ to $\frac{1}{4}$ and $2C$.

[Corollary 8 of arXiv:2511.06414, 'Non-uniform Edgeworth expansions for weakly dependent random variables and their applicati'] Let  Assumption \ref{GrowAssum} hold with some $m$ and
suppose that $B_n$ is monotone increasing. Let $(Z_j)$ be a sequence of 
 centered normal random variables 
so that $\text{Var}(Z_j)=B_{j}^2-B_{j-1}^2$, where $B_0=0$.

Set $X_i=S_i-S_{i-1}, S_0=0$. Then for every $n$ there  is a coupling of $(X_1,...,X_n)$ with $(Z_1,...,Z_n)$ so that 
$$
\left\|S_n-\sum_{j=1}^{n}Z_j\right\|_{m-1}\leq C
$$
where $C$ is a constant which does not depend on $n$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lem tree-two-edge-residual of arXiv:2609.03856, 'Consensus time for asynchronous $\ell^p$ relaxation: graph dependence'] Let $1<p<2$, let $x_0,x_1\ge0$, let
$\sigma_0,\sigma_1\in\{-1,1\}$, and let
$\rho=|\sigma_0x_0^{p-1}+\sigma_1x_1^{p-1}|$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 x_0^p\le(1+\varepsilon)x_1^p+C_p\varepsilon^{-1}
 \max\left\{\rho^q,
 \frac{\rho^2}{x_0^{p-2}+x_1^{p-2}}\right\},
 \qquad0<\varepsilon\le1,
\end{equation}
where, if $x_i=0$, we set $x_i^{p-2}=+\infty$ and interpret a finite
nonnegative number divided by $+\infty$ as zero.

[Lemma permutations of arXiv:2411.07878, 'Bernstein-type and Bennett-type inequalities for unbounded matrix martingales'] Let $Y = (Y_1, \dots, Y_n)$ be a set of i.i.d.\ random variables on a measurable space $\mathcal{Y}$.
    Let $g_i \colon \mathcal{Y}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{+}$, $i \in [n]$, be measurable and integrable functions, such that each $g_i(y_1, \dots, y_n)$ does not depend on $y_i$ and
    \[
    \sum_{i \in [n]} g_i(Y) \le M~~\text{a.s.}
    \]
    Let $I \subset [n]$ and define
    \[
    \mathscr{F}_{I} \coloneqq \sigma\lr{\left\{Y_i: i \in I  \right\} }.
    \]
    Let $\varPi_n$ be the set of permutations of $[n]$. 
    Then it holds that
    \[
    \frac{1}{n!} \sum_{\pi \in \varPi_n} \sum^n_{i=1} \E [g_{\pi(i)}(Y) | \mathscr{F}_{\pi([1, i-1])}] 
    \le \frac{n+1}{n} M~~\text{a.s.}
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma permutations of arXiv:2411.07878

[Proposition Prop:CAT(0):cD of arXiv:2512.13200, 'Martingales on a Euclidean manifold with a boundary and reflected BSDEs in non-convex doma'] {Let Assumption (ass:3 of the paper) hold.} Then, we have:
    \begin{enumerate}[i)]
        \item Minimizing geodesics are unique, and $\gamma^{x,y}$ depends continuously on $(x,y)$ in the sense of the uniform topology, i.e., with respect to
        $$d(\gamma^{x,y},\gamma^{x',y'}) := \sup_{t \in [0,1]} |\gamma^{x,y}_t - \gamma^{x',y'}_t|.$$
        \item The geodesic distance is a $\Gamma$-convex function on $\bar{\mathcal{D}} \times \bar{\mathcal{D}}$, i.e., for all minimizing geodesics $\gamma^1$ and $\gamma^2$,
        $t \mapsto d_{\bar{\mathcal{D}}}(\gamma^1_t,\gamma^2_t)$ is a (real) convex function.
        \item Any geodesic is a minimizing geodesic. 
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition prop:campanato of arXiv:2608.16915, 'Exact mean--covariance dynamics of the Weber field in the stochastic Lagrangian representa'] If $\sup_{t}\left\lVert M(t)\right\rVert_{C^\alpha_x}\le K$ then
$\mathcal X_M(z_0,r)\le C_\alpha Kr^\alpha$ for all $z_0,r$. The temporal part is not
controlled by this hypothesis: for a constant matrix $B\ne0$ and
\[
  M(t,x)=\sin\Bigl(\frac1{T-t}\Bigr)B\qquad(t<T),
\]
one has $\sup_{t<T}\left\lVert M(t)\right\rVert_{C^\alpha_x}=\left\lvert B\right\rvert$ and
$\mathcal X_M((x_0,T),r)=0$ for every $r$, yet
\[
  \lim_{r\downarrow0}\mathcal Y_M((x_0,T),r)^2
  =\lim_{r\downarrow0}\mathcal T_M((x_0,T),r)^2=\frac{\left\lvert B\right\rvert^2}{2} .
\]

body:
[Cor Q<=>V of arXiv:2411.00663, 'Ergodicity and Mixing of invariant capacities and applications'] If $V$ is an ergodic upper probability on a measurable space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F})$ with respect to a measurable transformation $T:\Omega\to \Omega$, then 
	$\operatorname{core}(V)\cap \mathcal{ M}(T)=\operatorname{core}(V)\cap \mathcal{ M}^e(T)$
	has only one element, denoted by $Q$. Moreover, for any $A\in\mathcal{F}$, 
	\[Q(A)=0\text{ if and only if }V(A)=0.\]
	In particular, $V(A)=Q(A)$ for any $A\in\mathcal{I}$.

[Definition 9 of arXiv:2512.07202, 'Hitting Probabilities for Hypoelliptic Differential Equations Driven by Fractional Brownia'] Let $\theta\in(0,1)$. A path $X:[0,T]\to \mathbb{R}^d$ is called \textit{$\theta$-H\"older rough} if there exists a constant $c>0$ such that for every $s\in[0,T]$, every $\varepsilon$ in $(0,T/2]$, and every unit vector $\zeta$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, there exists $t$ in $[0,T]$ such that $\varepsilon/2<|t-s|<\varepsilon$ and 
    $$
    |\langle\zeta,X_{s,t}\rangle|>c\varepsilon^\theta.
    $$
    The largest such constant is called the \textit{modulus of $\theta$-H\"older roughness} and is denoted as $L_\theta(X)$.
title: Definition 9 of arXiv:2512.07202

body:
[Lemma lem:charts of arXiv:2608.05123, 'A central limit theorem for the random assignment problem'] Fix \(d\in[0,1]^n\), let \(\mathcal C(d)\subset[0,1]^E\) be the
section on which the diagonal is optimal, and fix a root \(o\).  For
\(T\in\mathfrak T_o\), define
\[
 \Omega_{o,T}(d)=\left\{(q,y):q_o=0,\ 
 \begin{array}{ll}
 0<\theta_e(q)<1,&e\in T,\\
 \max\{0,\theta_e(q)\}<y_e<1,&e\notin T
 \end{array}\right\}
\]
and set
\[
 \Psi_{o,T,d}(q,y)_e=
 \begin{cases}
  \theta_e(q),&e\in T,\\
  y_e,&e\notin T.
 \end{cases}
\]
There is a null set \(\mathcal N_{d,o}\) such that the maps
\(\Psi_{o,T,d}\), as \(T\) varies, are bijections onto pairwise
disjoint subsets whose union is
\(\mathcal C(d)\setminus\mathcal N_{d,o}\).  Each chart has absolute
Jacobian one.  The set
\(\{(d,c):c\in\mathcal N_{d,o}\}\) is jointly null.  Consequently the
volume of the section at \(d\) is
\begin{equation}
 \int_{\mathbb R^{n-1}}\sum_{T\in\mathfrak T_o}
 \prod_{e\in T}I_e(q)\prod_{e\notin T}\lambda_e(q)\,\,\mathrm d q,
\end{equation}
where the dependence on $d$ has been suppressed at most places.

[Theorem 8 of arXiv:2512.00570, 'Makeenko--Migdal equations for lattice Yang--Mills--Higgs'] Let $s$ be a collection of strings.

Fix an edge $e$.

One has
\begin{equs}
C_{G,s,e}\,\phi(s) =\sum_{\mO}  \mp q(\mO) \sum_{s' \in \mO^\pm_{e}(s)}\phi(s'),
\end{equs}
where the sum is over all operations in the first table,
and $C_{G,s,e}$ is a constant depending on $G,s,e$.

Fix  $x\in \Lambda$.

One has
\begin{equs}
C_{M,s,x}\,\phi(s) =\sum_{\mO}   q(\mO) \sum_{s' \in \mO_{x}(s)}\phi(s'),
\end{equs}
where the sum is over all operations in the second table,
and $C_{M,s,x}$ is a constant depending on $M,s,x$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem 43 (Identification of the Fréchet Derivative and $\mathcal{C}^{1,\beta}_{loc}$ Regularity) of arXiv:2607.03318, 'Continuous Differentiability of the Value Function for Infinite-Dimensional Finite-Horizon'] Let Assumptions \ref{ass:smoothing}, \ref{ass:coefficients} and \ref{ass:problem_data} hold. Let the dynamic obstacle $\Phi$ be admissible in the sense of Definition \ref{def:admissible_obstacle}. Let $u_\varepsilon$ be the unique mild solution of equation \eqref{eq:hjb_penalized} and $V$ be the pointwise limit of $u_\varepsilon$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. For any fixed $t \in [0, T)$ and $x\in H$, the following properties hold:
\begin{enumerate}[label={(\textit{\roman*})}, leftmargin=*]
    \item The family of penalized Fréchet gradients $\{\nabla u_{\varepsilon}(t, x)\}_{\varepsilon > 0}$ admits a subsequence weakly convergent to a limit $g(t, x) \in H$ as $\varepsilon\to0$.
    \item For any Hölder exponent $\beta \in (0, 1)$ satisfying $\gamma(1+\beta) < 1$, the weak limit $g(t, \cdot)$ is locally $\beta$-Hölder continuous on $H$.
    \item The mapping $V(t, \cdot)$ is Fréchet differentiable on $H$. Its spatial gradient coincides with the weak limit, yielding $\mathcal{C}^{1,\beta}_{loc}(H)$ spatial regularity.
\end{enumerate}
title: Identification of the Fréchet Derivative and $\mathcal{C}^{1,\beta}_{loc}$ Regularity

For finite simple graphs G (n vertices, Laplacian L_G, eigenvalues 0 = lambda_1 <= ... <= lambda_n) and H (m vertices, L_H, 0 = mu_1 <= ... <= mu_m), the Cartesian product G box H has vertex set V(G) x V(H), with (g, h) adjacent to (g', h) when g ~ g' in G and to (g, h') when h ~ h' in H. If L_G u_i = lambda_i u_i and L_H v_j = mu_j v_j for orthonormal eigenbases, then u_i kron v_j is an eigenvector of L_{G box H} with eigenvalue lambda_i + mu_j, and these nm vectors form an orthonormal eigenbasis.

body: Let X be a topological space. The Borel sigma-algebra B(X) is the smallest sigma-algebra of subsets of X containing every open set (equivalently, every closed set); its members are the Borel sets. It is the intersection of all sigma-algebras containing the topology, so it exists and is unique. On the real line, B(R) is generated equally by the open intervals, by the closed intervals, by the half-lines (-infinity, a] with a rational, or by any base of the topology; every open, closed, F_sigma (countable union of closed sets) and G_delta (countable intersection of open sets) set is Borel, and the Borel sets are stratified by the Borel hierarchy of countable length omega_1. B(R^n) equals the product sigma-algebra of n copies of B(R). Every continuous map between topological spaces is Borel measurable (preimages of Borel sets are Borel), as is every pointwise limit of a sequence of Borel measurable real functions; but the image of a Borel set under a continuous map need not be Borel - such images are the analytic sets (Suslin, 1917). B(R) has the cardinality of the continuum, 2^{aleph_0}, while the Lebesgue measurable sets number 2^{2^{aleph_0}} (every subset of the null Cantor set is measurable), so there exist Lebesgue measurable sets that are not Borel: Lebesgue measure on B(R) is completed by adjoining all subsets of Borel null sets. Every finite Borel measure on a Polish space is regular (inner regular by compact sets: a Radon measure), which is why Borel sets are the natural domain of measures on metric spaces.

[Lem 6 of arXiv:2609.02398, '\textbf{Convex Order Comparisons for Sub-Gamma Random Variables}'] For any $b > 0$ and $t \ge 0$,
\begin{align}
&&
    S_{b\Lap}(t) &= \frac{b}{2}\,e^{-t/b}, &
    S_{b\Lap}'(t) &= -\frac{1}{2}\,e^{-t/b} = -\Prob(b\Lap > t). &
& 
\end{align}
Moreover $S_{b\Lap}$ is convex on $\R$, and $S_{b\Lap}(t) \ge 0 \vee (-t)$ for all $t \in \R$.
title: Lem 6 of arXiv:2609.02398

[Lemma lem_smooth_f of arXiv:2608.09105, 'Longest convex chains with i.i.d.\ points'] Assume (equation p_cont of the paper).
Then for every $f\in\mathcal{F}$, there exists a sequence $(f_n)_{n\geqslant1}$ in $\mathcal{F}$ with the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]

$d(f_n,f)\to0$ as $n\to\infty$.

\item 
$J(f_n) \to J(f)$ as $n\to\infty$.

\end{enumerate}

[Theorem thm:variational of arXiv:2607.24705, 'Derangetropy Operators'] Among all kernels with $\sqrt{w} \in H^{1}_{0}(0,1)$, the Fisher
		information attains its minimum uniquely at the canonical kernel:
		\begin{equation}
			w(z) = 2\sin^{2}(\pi z), \qquad \mathcal{I}(w) = 4\pi^{2}.
			
		\end{equation}
		The critical points of $\mathcal{I}$ under the same constraints,
		understood in the amplitude parametrization $w = \phi^{2}$ with
		$\phi \in H^{1}_{0}(0,1)$, are exactly the harmonic kernels, with
		critical values $\mathcal{I}(w_{k}) = 4k^{2}\pi^{2}$, and the
		Lagrange multiplier of the normalization constraint $\int w = 1$ at

body: For A a subset of a topological space (X, tau), the subspace (relative) topology on A is tau_A = { A intersect U : U in tau }: its open sets are the intersections with A of open sets of X, and likewise its closed sets are the intersections with A of closed sets of X. This is a topology - it contains A and empty, and the identities (A intersect U1) intersect (A intersect U2) = A intersect (U1 intersect U2) and union of (A intersect U_i) = A intersect (union U_i) give closure under finite intersections and arbitrary unions. It is the coarsest topology making the inclusion i: A -> X continuous, since i is continuous for a topology sigma on A iff A intersect U is sigma-open for every U in tau, i.e. iff tau_A is contained in sigma. Universal property: for any space Z, a map f: Z -> A is continuous iff the composite Z -> A -> X is continuous - the property that characterizes the subspace topology.
title: Subspace Topology

body:
[Proposition prop:sec5-boundary-fan of arXiv:2607.18070, 'The Brownian loop-catcher'] Fix $0\leq\lambda\leq1$.

\smallskip
\noindent\textup{(i) One-sided boundary probe.}
Fix $\xi\in\partial\mathbb{D}$ and $z_1,\ldots,z_r\in\mathbb{D}$, where $r\geq1$.
There is a random connected compact set
$C=C^\lambda_{\xi;z_1,\ldots,z_r}\subset\overline\mathbb{D}$ such that
$C\cap\partial\mathbb{D}=\{\xi\}$ and $z_1,\ldots,z_r\in C$, and, for every
compact $E\subset\overline\mathbb{D}$ with $\xi\notin E$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb E_C\!\left[
 \mathbf 1_{\{C\cap E=\varnothing\}}e^{-\lambda m_\mathbb{D}(C,E)}
 \right]
 =\prod_{j=1}^r
 \frac{P_{\mathbb{D}\setminus E}(\xi,z_j)}{P_\mathbb{D}(\xi,z_j)}.
 \end{equation}

\smallskip
\noindent\textup{(ii) Two-sided boundary probe.}
Fix distinct $\xi_+,\xi_-\in\partial\mathbb{D}$ and
$z_1,\ldots,z_r,w_1,\ldots,w_s\in\mathbb{D}$, where $r,s\geq1$.
There is a random compact set $C\subset\overline\mathbb{D}$ with at most two
connected components such that $C\cap\partial\mathbb{D}=\{\xi_+,\xi_-\}$, one
component contains $\xi_+,z_1,\ldots,z_r$, and one, possibly the same,
contains $\xi_-,w_1,\ldots,w_s$. Moreover, for every compact
$E\subset\overline\mathbb{D}$ with $E\cap\{\xi_+,\xi_-\}=\varnothing$,
\[
 \mathbb E_C\!\left[
 \mathbf 1_{\{C\cap E=\varnothing\}}e^{-\lambda m_\mathbb{D}(C,E)}
 \right]
 =\prod_{j=1}^r
 \frac{P_{\mathbb{D}\setminus E}(\xi_+,z_j)}{P_\mathbb{D}(\xi_+,z_j)}
 \prod_{k=1}^s
 \frac{P_{\mathbb{D}\setminus E}(\xi_-,w_k)}{P_\mathbb{D}(\xi_-,w_k)}.
\]

body: In measure theory, Lebesgue's dominated convergence theorem gives a mild sufficient condition under which limits and integrals of a sequence of functions can be interchanged. More technically it says that if a sequence of functions is bounded in absolute value by an integrable function and is almost everywhere pointwise convergent to a function then the sequence converges in to its pointwise limit, and in particular the integral of the limit is the limit of the integrals. Its power and utility are two of the primary theoretical advantages of Lebesgue integration over Riemann integration.
title: Dominated convergence theorem

[Thmx leA of arXiv:2505.13382, 'The localization transition for the directed polymer in a random environment is smooth'] The following limits are  well defined and coincide almost-surely
\begin{equation}
\mathfrak{f}(\beta):=\lim_{n\to \infty}  \frac{1}{n} {\ensuremath{\mathbb E}} \left[ \log W^{\beta}_n\right]= \lim_{n\to \infty}  \frac{1}{n} \log W^{\beta}_n.
 \end{equation}
The function $\mathfrak{f}(\beta)$ is referred to as the free energy of the directed polymer, it is continous and nonincreasing in $\beta$. Thus
there exists $\beta_c\in [0,\infty]$ such that
$$ \beta>\beta_c \quad \Leftrightarrow  \quad \mathfrak{f}(\beta)<0.$$
Furthermore the following holds:
\begin{itemize}
 \item [(i)] The function $\mathfrak{f}(\beta)+\lambda(\beta)=\lim_{n\to \infty} (1 /n)\log Z^{\beta,\omega}_n$ is convex in $\beta$.
 \item [(ii)] If $d=1,2$ we have $\beta_c=0$, while if $d\ge 3$ we have $\beta_c>0$.
\item [(iii)] When $d\ge 3$ we have $\beta_c\in (0,\infty)$  if ${\ensuremath{\mathbb P}} \left( \omega_{1,0}=\mathrm{ess\, sup}  \ \omega_{1,0}\right)<\frac{1}{2d}$.
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 3 (Cellular chain map of a parabolic projection) of arXiv:2609.01882, '\textbf{Coxeter Descents and Parabolic Homotopy Colimits}\\[2mm] \large A Hochster-type de'] Let $I\subset J\subseteq S$. For $w\in W^I$, write the parabolic factorization
\[
  w=uv,
  \qquad u\in W^J,
  \quad v\in W_J^I,
  \quad \ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(v).
\]
The projection $\pi_{I,J}:G/G_I\to G/G_J$ maps $C_w^I$ onto $C_u^J$. On cellular chains,
\[
  (\pi_{I,J})_\#(e_w^I)=
  \begin{cases}
    e_w^J,&v=e\ \text{(equivalently }w\in W^J\text{)},\\
    0,&v\ne e.
  \end{cases}
\]
Thus the cellular Schubert diagram is strictly isomorphic to the abstract diagram $\cW$ of \eqref{eq:parabolicmap}.

body:
[Lemma 26 (Fixed spectrum and fixed diagonal version) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] \lab{lem:fixed-spectrum-fixed-diagonal}
Let \(w>0\) and \(u\geq 0\), and let
\[
        X=wG+uD,
\]
where \(G\) is a GUE matrix and \(D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_n)\) is
fixed.  Let
\[
        \lambda=\spec(X),
        \qquad
        a=\diag(X).
\]
For \(1\leq k\leq n\), let \(\lambda^{(k)}\) be the ordered eigenvalue vector
of the \(k\times k\) northwest principal minor of \(X\), and write
\[
        \Gamma=(\lambda^{(1)},\ldots,\lambda^{(n)}).
\]
Then, conditional on both
\[
        \spec(X)=\lambda
        \qquad\text{and}\qquad
        \diag(X)=a,
\]
the minor process \(\Gamma\) is uniformly distributed, with respect to
Lebesgue measure, on the Gelfand-Tsetlin fiber
\[
        \GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel a}.
\]
Equivalently, its conditional density is
\[
        \frac{1}{|\GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel a}|}
        \mathbf 1_{\{\Gamma\in \GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel a}\}} .
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2606.14443, 'SEMICLASSICAL LIMIT OF POLYAKOV-LIOUVILLE MEASURE and Q-Curvature Uniformization ON EVEN-D'] Let $(M,g)$ be an admissible manifold with $Q(M)\le0$. For $\kappa\in\R$, let $u_\kappa$ be the unique smooth solution to \eqref{const-Q}. 
	\begin{enumerate}[$(i)$]
		\item Under $\Q_{\kappa,\gamma}$, the rescaled augmented fields $\frac\gamma n h$ converge in law as $\gamma\to0$ 
		
		towards $u_\kappa$. 
		\item Under $\Q_{\kappa,\gamma}$, the fields $h-\frac n\gamma u_\kappa$ converge in law towards an augmented massive field $\tilde h$ on $(M,\hat g)$, where $\hat g=e^{2u_\kappa}g$, with mass $na_n\Lambda_\kappa$. 
		
			
			
	\end{enumerate}
	In both cases, the respective fields are regarded as random variables with values in $H^{-1}(M)$. In the borderline case $Q(M)=0$, the ``massive’’ field $\tilde h$ in $(ii)$ actually is mass-less. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Prop 2 (Stretching covariance of the burglars) of arXiv:2609.03968, 'A one-parameter family of local-time conditioned processes : the generalized Brownian burg'] Let $\Lambda$ be an admissible capacity on an interval $I$, and let $x,x_0 \in \overline{I}$. Let $X$ be a Brownian burglar of intensity $\nu \in\R$ and initial capacity $\Lambda$, starting from $x$ and targeting $x_0$. Let $g$ be a stretching morphism mapping $\Lambda$ to an other admissible capacity $\rho$ on some interval $J$.
Then, the process $g(X)$ has (up to time-reparametrization) the law of a Brownian burglar of intensity $\nu$ and initial capacity $\rho$, starting from $g(x)$ and targeting $g(x_0)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

For each $x\in\mathbb{T}_N$, let $\varphi_{x}:[0,T]\times \mathcal{D}_{\Omega_N}[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}$ be independent of the occupation-values in $\{x+w+r,x+y\}_{r\in B_{L}}$, and such that $\text{c}_{t,\varphi}:=\int_0^t\sup_{x\in\mathbb{T}_N,\eta\in\Omega_N}|\varphi_x(\cdot,s)|\mathrm{d} s<\infty $.

        \eta_{N^2s}(x+w)

        4\sqrt{2\text{c}_\alpha}c_{T,\varphi}\frac{\mathrm{d}(w,z)}{\sqrt{\min\{\mathbf{r}_{\beta,\ell_N}\}TN^2}}

    \end{align}

body: [Lemma 15 of arXiv:2608.23450, 'The Oldest Allele in a Moran Model'] For $\delta>0$, define the $\delta$-hitting time mapping $\tau^{\delta}: D_{[0,1]}[0,\infty) \to [0,\infty]$ by $\tau^{\delta}(x) = \inf\{t \ge 0 : x(t) \le \delta\}$. The mapping $x \mapsto \tau^{\delta}(x)$ is continuous at any path $x \in D_{[0,1]}[0,\infty)$ as long as $x$ is continuous at $\tau^{\delta}(x)$ and $\tau^{\delta}(x) = \tilde{\tau}^{\delta}(x)$, where $\tilde{\tau}^{\delta}(x) = \inf\{t \ge 0 : x(t) < \delta\}$. If $Z$ is the continuous diffusion process governed by $G$ on $[0,1]$, then the mapping $\tau^{\delta}$ is continuous almost surely with respect to the distribution of $Z$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 15 of arXiv:2608.23450

[Cor eq:CR_variance of arXiv:2608.10215, 'The variance of the Pitman--Yor process: a Cifarelli--Regazzini identity and inversion for'] Let $\theta > 1/2$, and let $\mathsf{G}$ be a probability measure on $[0, +\infty)$ satisfying $\int_0^{+\infty} \log(1 + x^2) \mathsf{G}(\mathrm{d} x) < +\infty$. 
Then, for any $t \ge 0$, there holds
\begin{align}
\mathbb{E}_{\theta}\left[ \left(\frac{1}{1 + t\mathfrak{V}}\right)^{\theta - 1/2} \right] &= \int_0^1 {\mathcal B eta}(\mathrm{d}\rho; 1/2, \theta - 1/2) \times \nonumber \\
& \times \frac 12 \left\{ \Psi_{+,0}(\sqrt{t \rho (1 - \rho)}, t(1 - \rho)) + \Psi_{-,0}(\sqrt{t \rho (1 -\rho)}, t(1 - \rho)) \right\} \mathrm{d} \rho 
\end{align}
with
\[
\Psi_{\pm, 0}(u, v) := \exp\left\{ -\theta\int_0^{+\infty}  \log(1 \pm 2ux + vx^2) \mathsf{G}(\mathrm{d} x) \right\} \ .
\]
Moreover, if $\theta > 3/2$, one has
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}_{\theta}\left[\frac{1}{z + \mathfrak{V}}\right] &= \int_0^{+\infty} \frac{f_{\mathfrak{V}}(x)}{z + x} \mathrm{d} x \nonumber \\
&= z^{\theta - 1} \int_{\Delta_2} {\mathcal D ir}(\mathrm{d}\xi \mathrm{d}\eta; 1/2, 1, \theta - 3/2) 
\left[\frac{\Phi_{+,0}(z; \xi, \eta) + \Phi_{-,0}(z; \xi, \eta) }{2} \right]
\end{align*}
with
\begin{displaymath}
\Phi_{\pm, 0}(z; \xi, \eta) := \exp\left\{ -\theta\int_0^{+\infty}  \log(z \pm 2\sqrt{z \xi\eta} x + \eta x^2) \mathsf{G}(\mathrm{d} x) \right\}\ . 
\end{displaymath} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Cor eq:CR_variance of arXiv:2608.10215

body: In mathematics, Minkowski's theorem is the statement that every convex set in which is symmetric with respect to the origin and which has volume greater than contains a non-zero integer point. The theorem was proved by Hermann Minkowski in 1889 and became the foundation of the branch of number theory called the geometry of numbers. It can be extended from the integers to any lattice and to any symmetric convex set with volume greater than , where denotes the covolume of the lattice.

body:
[Proposition 97 (Typed Hoffman interface and collision kernel) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] Let $E$ be finite dimensional and fix a stochastic weight $N\ge2$.  Enlarge
the weight-one alphabet $\mathscr V_E=E$ by the collision letters
\[
 \mathscr C_{E,N}=\bigoplus_{k=2}^N E^{\odot k}.
\]
The finite-weight It\^o iterated integrals of an $E$-valued semimartingale
form a quasi-shuffle character on this typed alphabet.  Hoffman's exponential
and logarithm give inverse coalgebra maps and turn it into a shuffle
character without deleting collision letters.  The subsequent projection
$p:\mathscr V_E\oplus\mathscr C_{E,N}\to\mathscr V_E$ induces the exact
primitive sequence
\begin{equation}
 0\longrightarrow\mathfrak I_{E,N}
 \longrightarrow\mathfrak L(\mathscr V_E\oplus\mathscr C_{E,N})
 \longrightarrow\mathfrak L(\mathscr V_E)\longrightarrow0,
 
\end{equation}
where $\mathfrak I_{E,N}$ is the Lie ideal generated by the collision
letters.  Geometricization and the quotient commute with convolution,
bounded spatial maps, deterministic evolution transport, truncation, and
fixed-terminal stopping.  At degree two the weight-one geometric tensor is
\[
 \mathbb Y^H_{s,t}=\mathbb Y^I_{s,t}+\frac12[Y]_{s,t}
 =\frac12Y_{s,t}^{\otimes2}+\operatorname{Alt}_2\mathbb Y^I_{s,t}.
\]
Thus the quotient retains the geometric ancestry while the typed parent
retains optional collision information.

[Lemma 17 of arXiv:2608.17509, '2608.17509'] Let \(\Lambda:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be finite, \(C^1\), and strictly convex,
and define
\[
        J(x):=\sup_{\theta\in\mathbb R}\{\theta x-\Lambda(\theta)\},
        \qquad x\in\mathbb R.
\]
Set \(m_-:=\lim_{\theta\to-\infty}\Lambda'(\theta)\) and
\(m_+:=\lim_{\theta\to+\infty}\Lambda'(\theta)\), allowing infinite limits.
Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item For every \(x\in(m_-,m_+)\), the supremum defining \(J(x)\) is attained
at the unique \(\theta(x)\in\mathbb R\) satisfying
\(\Lambda'(\theta(x))=x\), and
\[
J(x)=\theta(x)x-\Lambda(\theta(x)).
\]

\item The function \(J\) is differentiable on \((m_-,m_+)\), with
\(J'(x)=\theta(x)\). In particular, \(J\) is strictly convex on
\((m_-,m_+)\).

\item For every \(\theta\in\mathbb R\),
\(J(\Lambda'(\theta))=\theta\Lambda'(\theta)-\Lambda(\theta)\).

\item If \(\Lambda(0)=0\) and \(\Lambda'(0)\in(m_-,m_+)\), then
\(J(x)\ge0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R\), and \(J\) vanishes uniquely at
\(x=\Lambda'(0)\).
\end{enumerate}

body: In mathematics, the free group over a given set consists of all words that can be built from members of , considering two words to be different unless their equality follows from the group axioms. The members of are called generators of , and the number of generators is the rank of the free group. An arbitrary group is called free if it is isomorphic to for some subset of , that is, if there is a subset of such that every element of can be written in exactly one way as a product of finitely many elements of and their inverses.

[Lemm 9 of arXiv:2605.23292, 'Second-order Poincaré inequalities and localization on the Poisson space'] (closeness in $d_{BL}$ implies closeness of mixed moments, unbounded case)
Let $X_1,...X_4,X_1',...,X_4'$ be random variables such that
\[
d_{BL}\big( (X_1,...,X_4),\ (X_1',...,X_4') \big) \leq \alpha,
\]
with $0\leq\alpha \leq 2$. Assume that there exists $M>0$ and $q \in \N$ such that $\E|X_i|^{q+1},\E|X_i'|^{q+1}\leq M$ for all $i=1,...,4$. Then for all non-negative integers $p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4$ with $p_1+p_2+p_3+p_4=q$, it is the case that
\[
| \E \Pi_{i=1}^4 X_i^{p_i} - \E \Pi_{i=1}^4 X_i'^{p_i}| \leq (36q+16) \max(1,M^{q/(q+1)}) \alpha^{1/(q+1)}.
\]

body:
[Proposition prop:rectangular-laguerre-recurrence of arXiv:2608.12147, 'The Average Singular Value of a Complex Gaussian Random Matrix Strictly Decreases with Dim'] Let $\lambda\in\mathbb N_0$ and $N\geqslant 1$. 

Then 
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \Delta_{N+1}^{(\lambda)}(x)-\Delta_N^{(\lambda)}(x)
 ={}&
 \frac{\Gamma(N+1)}{\Gamma(N+\lambda+1)}
 \Bigl[
 \delta_N \left(L_N^{(\lambda)}(x)\right)^2 \\
 &\quad
 +\widetilde\delta_N xL_N^{(\lambda+1)}(x)L_{N-1}^{(\lambda+1)}(x)\\
 &\quad
 -\lambda\widetilde\delta_N L_{N-1}^{(\lambda+1)}(x)L_N^{(\lambda)}(x)
 \Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]
title: Laguerre recurrence with fixed rectangularity

body:
The Hardy-Littlewood maximal inequality is WEAK type (1,1), never strong type (1,1), and Marcinkiewicz interpolation gives nothing at p = 1 (its constant contains p/(p - p_0) and blows up as p -> 1+). Precisely: if f is in L^1(R^n) and f is not a.e. 0, then Mf is NOT in L^1(R^n). Global counterexample: pick R with c = int_{B(0,R)} |f| > 0; for |x| >= R the ball B(x, 2|x|) contains B(0,R), so Mf(x) >= c / (v_n (2|x|)^n), which is not integrable at infinity. Local counterexample showing the failure is not only at infinity: f(x) = |x|^{-n} (log(1/|x|))^{-2} 1_{{|x| < 1/2}} is in L^1, but averaging over B(x, 2|x|) gives Mf(x) >= c' |x|^{-n} (log(1/|x|))^{-1} near 0, which is not locally integrable. The correct endpoint substitutes are: (i) the weak (1,1) bound |{Mf > t}| <= 3^n ||f||_1 / t; (ii) Stein's L log L theorem: for f supported in a ball B, Mf is integrable over B if and only if int_B |f| log^+ |f| < infinity. So a proof that applies 'M is bounded on L^p' at p = 1, or that interpolates strong (1,1) with strong (infinity, infinity), is wrong; the same warning applies to any operator known only to be weak (1,1), such as the Calderon-Zygmund singular integrals and the Hilbert transform.
Lebesgue measure on R^n
M is the centered or uncentered Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator
title: Pitfall: the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator is not bounded on L^1 (the endpoint is only weak type)

body:
For f in L^1_loc(R^n) (Lebesgue measure |.|), the centered Hardy-Littlewood maximal function is Mf(x) = sup_{r>0} (1/|B(x,r)|) int_{B(x,r)} |f(y)| dy, with values in [0, infinity]. The uncentered version is M'f(x) = sup over all open balls B containing x of (1/|B|) int_B |f|; one has Mf <= M'f <= 2^n Mf. The set {Mf > t} is open for every t (so Mf is lower semicontinuous, hence Borel measurable), M is sublinear, M(f) = M(|f|), and ||Mf||_infinity <= ||f||_infinity. Cubes in place of balls give a pointwise comparable operator (constants depending only on n).
f is locally integrable on R^n
balls are Euclidean and |.| is Lebesgue measure
title: Hardy-Littlewood maximal function

[Proposition prop-intensity measure of point process of arXiv:2505.24043, 'Weak solutions of Navier-Stokes Equation with purely discontinuous L\'evy Noise'] Suppose that $(X, \mathscr{B}_X) $ is a non-empty measure space  and
$\bigl( {\Omega}, {\mathscr{F}}, {\mathbb{P}}  \bigr)$ is a probability space.
If a map $p: \Omega \to \Pi_X$ is a point process, we put
\[
  n_p((0,t]\timesU)= \mathbb{E} \bigl[  \eta_p((0,t]\timesU) \bigr],  \;\; t>0,\;\;U \in \mathscr{B}_X.
\]
Then the function $n_p$ has a unique extension to a $\sigma$-additive $\bar{\mathbb{N}}:=\mathbb{N}\cup \{\infty\}$-valued function on the set $\mathscr{B}(0,\infty)\otimes \mathscr{B}_X$. \\
It is called the intensity measure of the point process $p$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Prop prop_ge_general of arXiv:2608.29914, 'Fixed points in abstract provability structures'] Let $S$ be a consistent APS and let $\triangle v$ be a one-variable APS term of the form
\[
    \triangle v = \Box^{k_0}\boxtimes\Box^{k_1}\boxtimes\cdots \boxtimes\Box^{k_n}v,
\]
where $n\geq 1$.
Let $k=\min\{k_0,k_1,\ldots,k_{n-1}\}$.
Suppose that $\mathsf{E}_S(\boxtimes\Box^k)$ holds.
Then $\triangle\top$ is not refutable in $S$.

[Thm 12 of arXiv:2609.03819, 'Stochastic damped wave and Euler-Bernoulli equations with singular locally H\"older contin'] Assume that hypotheses \ref{H0}, \ref{H1}, \ref{H2b}, \ref{H3} hold and 
\begin{equation}
\beta+\delta<\frac12\min\{\alpha,1-\alpha\}.
\end{equation}
Then, there exists ${\mathfrak{c}}_0\geq 1$ such that for every $\mathfrak{c}>{\mathfrak{c}}_0$, $n\in\N$, $k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, $i\in\{-,+\}$ and continuous function $g:[0,T]\times H_n\rightarrow \R$ verifying 
\[
\sup_{t\in [0,T]}\norm{g(t,\cdot)}_{C^\theta_b(H_n)}<\infty,
\]
there exists a unique solution $u_{n,k}^{(i)}\in C^{0,1+\theta}_{b,\mathcal{V}_n}([0,T]\times H_n)$ to \eqref{Def:Unki} and
\begin{align}
&\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\norm{u_{n,k}^{(i)}(t,\cdot)}_{C^{1+\theta}_{b,\mathcal{V}_n}(H_n)}\leq  \mathfrak{C}_0\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\norm{g(t,\cdot)}_{C^{\theta}_b(H_n)},\\
&\mathfrak{C}_0=\frac{4(2+\varepsilon^{-\gamma_2})M_0}{(\varepsilon\mathfrak c)^{1-\gamma_2}(1-\gamma_2)}\left(1+\sup_{t\geq 0}\|C(t,\cdot)\|_{C^\theta_b(H;U)}\right),
\end{align}
where $M_0\geq 1$ and $0<\gamma_2<1$ are the constants given by Lemma \ref{lemma:stima_ind_n} and $\varepsilon\in (0,1]$ is given by \eqref{r-eps}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2608.31164, 'The anisotropic Michael-Simon inequality'] For $A \in \textup{End}(P)$, we will consider the smallest eigenvalue function
\[
    \lambda_m(A) := \lambda_{\min} ( \textup{sym} \, A), \qquad \text{where } \; \textup{sym} \, A := \tfrac{1}{2} (A + A^t).
\]
Equivalently, $\lambda_m(A) = \min_{ |v| = 1 } \la A v , v \rg$.
The function $\lambda_m$ is superadditive on matrices and defines a concave barrier with $|\lambda_m(A) - \lambda_m(B)| \leq \|A - B\|_{\textup{op}}$ and $\lambda_m (R^t AR) = \lambda_m(A)$ for every $R \in O(P)$.

Then, the $A$-localized state $\mu_A$ for this model, see Proposition (prop: Bounds A-loc. states of the paper), fulfills the following properties:
     \begin{enumerate}[label=\roman*)]
         \item $\mu_A$ is not extremal in $\mathscr{G}(\gamma)$ and moreover,
         \item the corresponding extremal decomposition measure $\alpha_{\mu_A}$, see (equation eq: extremal decomposition measure of the paper), appearing in the extremal decomposition 
                    \begin{equation}
        \mu_A=\int_{\text{ex }\mathscr{G}(\gamma)} \nu \cdot \alpha_{\mu_A}(d\nu)
    \end{equation}

     \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Satz thm:HigherOrderPI of arXiv:2507.08692, 'Some notes on higher order concentration of measure'] Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on ${\mathbb R}^n$ which satisfies a Poincar\'{e}-type inequality with constant $\sigma^2 > 0$, and let $f\colon {\mathbb R}^n \to {\mathbb R}$ be a $\mathcal{C}^d$-smooth function with ${\mathbb E} f = 0$.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item Assuming that $\lVert f^{(j)} \rVert_{\mathrm{op},1} \le \sigma^{d-j}$ for all $j=1,\ldots,d-1$ and $\lVert f^{(d)} \rVert_{\mathrm{op},\infty} \le 1$, it holds that
		\[
		\int \exp\Big\{\frac{c}{\sigma} |f|^{1/d} \Big\} d\mu \le 2,
		\]
		where we may choose $c=2^{1/(2d)}/(4e)$.
		\item For any $t\ge 0$, it holds that
		\[
		\mu(|f| \ge t)\le
		2 \exp\Big\{- \frac{C_d}{d\sigma} \min\Big(\min_{j=1, \ldots,d-1} \Big(\frac{t}{\lVert f^{(j)} \rVert_{\mathrm{op},1}}\Big)^{1/j}, \Big(\frac{t}{\lVert f^{(d)} \rVert_{\mathrm{op},\infty}}\Big)^{1/d}\Big)\Big\},
		\]
		where we may choose $C = \log(2)/(\sqrt{2}e)$.
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 6 of arXiv:2506.18558, '2506.18558'] Suppose that  Assumption {\rm\ref{A2}} holds. Then the class of measures $\{\mu^x_{t}\}_{t\in\RR}$ given in Lemma $\ref{Le3.3}$ is an evolution system of measures for $\{P^x_{s,t}\}_{t\ge s}$. Moreover, for any Lipschitz continuous function $\phi$ on $\RR^m$, $t\ge s$ and $x\in \RR^m$,
\begin{align}
\left|P^x_{s,t} \phi(y)-\int_{\RR^m}\phi(z)\,\mu^x_t(dz)\right|\le  C {\rm Lip(\phi)} (1+|x|+|y|)e^{-\beta(t-s)}.
\end{align}
Furthermore, if $\{\nu^x_{t}\}_{t\in\RR}$ is another evolution system of measures for $\{P^x_{s,t}\}_{t\ge s}$ that satisfies
$$
\sup_{t\in\RR}\int_{\RR^m}|y|\nu^x_t(dy)<\infty,\quad   x\in\RR^n,
$$
then $\nu^x_t=\mu^x_t$ for all $t\in\RR$ and $x\in\RR^n$.
